meta.title: Korean Language Mastery Roadmap
meta.subtitle: 16 levels across 6 phases — from Hangeul & phonetics to professional fluency & native mastery

phases.name: Foundations
phases.themeLabel: Hangeul, sound system, survival Korean, grammar engines I & II
phases.goal: Build the substrate everything else sits on: a sound system you can actually produce, a reading system that works on words you have never seen, and the grammar engine that generates sentences instead of storing them. By the end of this phase you read anything aloud correctly, survive a week in Korea without English, conjugate any verb in any tense, and talk about your past for three minutes.
phases.rule: **The rule of this phase:** you do not "know" a pattern until you have produced it out loud, unprompted, in a sentence about your own life. Reading an explanation is preparation for learning, not learning.

dashboard.study commitment: 2–3 hours per day, 6 days per week; the 7th day is a checkpoint
dashboard.core tools: Anki, a recorder, Naver Dictionary, *Korean Grammar in Use – Beginning*, a tutor from L2
dashboard.final outcome: Read at 60+ syllables/min with all sound rules; hold a 3-minute unprepared conversation on your own life; produce 55 grammar patterns; command 700 active words.

levels.title: HANGEUL AND THE SOUND SYSTEM
levels.goal: Read any Korean text aloud correctly — including words you have never seen — with all seven sound-change rules applied without conscious thought. Then produce the sounds well enough that a native speaker does not have to work to understand you.
levels.mainProject: **`sound-lab`** — a recorded corpus proving you can read and pronounce

levels.title: BEGINNER KOREAN (ABSOLUTE BEGINNER → BASIC COMMUNICATION)
levels.goal: Master Level 1 completely following the university standard (SNU Korean+ inspired 5-step pedagogy: 대화 → 어휘 → 문법 → 말하기·듣기 → 읽기·쓰기). By the end, communicate smoothly across all 16 units: read/write Hangul, introduce yourself, order food/drinks, buy items with counters and Won, describe daily routines, make appointments, talk about past experiences, navigate public transit, and deliver connected life narratives.
levels.mainProject: **`korean-level1-mastery`** — Complete spoken simulation + written essay across all 4 Checkpoints (A, B, C, D)

levels.title: THE GRAMMAR ENGINE I
levels.goal: Stop memorising sentences and start generating them. By the end you can conjugate any regular verb into any of three tenses, negate four ways, and place every core particle correctly.

levels.title: THE GRAMMAR ENGINE II
levels.goal: Connect clauses into discourse, handle all the irregulars fluently, use honorifics in the full system, and tell a three-minute story about your own life that a native speaker would call fluent.

elements.text: **The brief.** Spend sixty minutes entirely in Korean. No English, no dictionary app, no switching. One conversation, one topic, one hour.

items.text: **Duration.** 55–65 minutes, continuous, with a tutor, an exchange partner, or a native speaker.
**No English.** Zero English words, zero code-switching. If you cannot say something, you must circumlocute — describe it another way.
**Topic coverage.** At least four of: your work or study, your family, your city, a trip you took, a film or book you liked, a plan for next year.
**Grammar coverage.** At least one instance each of: past, present, future, negation (both 안 and 못), a connector, a noun modifier, an honorific sentence.
**Repair.** At least three instances of asking for clarification *in Korean*, and at least one of correcting yourself mid-sentence.
**The recording and the transcript.** Full audio, plus a 15-line transcript of the most and least successful exchanges.
**The retrospective.** Written, in Korean if possible, answering: what did I avoid saying, and what structure would have let me say it?

elements.code:
first-hour/
├── recording.mp3
├── topic_map.md            ← the four topics, in order, with what you wanted to say vs said
├── grammar_checklist.md    ← each required pattern, with the timestamp where you used it
├── repair_log.md           ← three clarifications + one self-correction
├── transcript.md           ← 15 lines: best and worst exchanges
└── retrospective.md        ← what I avoided, and the structure I needed

rows: you understood ≥ 85% of what the partner said
≤ 3 topics abandoned for lack of vocabulary

items.text: Do it on the phone, with no visual cues.
Do it with two people at once.
Do it on a topic you have never discussed in any language.

elements.text: Rather than a list to read, the core is a **deck specification**. Build it yourself, because building it is half the learning.

elements.label: The rule for card design
elements.value: every card has a **sentence**, not a word. Front: the English situation. Back: the Korean sentence, read aloud by you. A word in isolation is not learned; a sentence is.

elements.text: **Phase 2 — Everyday Fluency · Levels 4–6**

rows: Housing, banking, healthcare, bureaucracy, phone calls — the vocabulary of existing in Korea
Natural-speed comprehension, contraction rules, native rhythm
News, short fiction, diary, formal messages, spacing rules

elements.text: Phase 2 assumes Phase 1 completely: you will listen to natives who speak at a speed your grammar cannot yet predict, and you will read texts whose vocabulary you do not have. The foundation is what lets you survive that.
*Phase 1 of 7 · Levels 0–3 of 18 · Foundations*

phases.name: Everyday Fluency
phases.themeLabel: daily life domains, listening & pronunciation mastery, reading & writing
phases.goal: Move from *can form sentences* to *can live in the language*. By the end of this phase you handle housing, banking, hospitals, bureaucracy, phone calls and workplace Korean without preparation; you understand natural-speed everyday speech at 90%; and you read a news brief and write a 300-word diary with correct spacing and register.  **The shift.** Phase 1 taught you to construct. Phase 2 teaches you to *operate*. The grammar stops being new and starts being recombined at speed, in domains where a wrong word has a real consequence — a deposit, a prescription, a deadline.
phases.rule: **The rule of this phase:** every domain must be *performed*, not *studied*. Reading a list of hospital vocabulary is not healthcare Korean. Standing in a room, saying "열이 나고 기침이 나요" to a partner who then asks a follow-up question, is.

dashboard.study commitment: 2–3 hours per day, 6 days per week
dashboard.core tools: Anki, recorder, tutor (weekly, now essential), Naver Dictionary, *Korean Grammar in Use – Intermediate*, graded readers, a news app
dashboard.final outcome: Twelve life domains handled in Korean; native-speed listening at 90%; newspaper headlines read; a 300-word diary and a formal email written correctly.

levels.title: DAILY LIFE DOMAINS
levels.goal: Handle the twelve situations that make up an actual life in Korea. Not tourist Korean — the Korean of a lease, a prescription, a bank transfer, and a phone call from someone who expects an answer.
levels.mainProject: **`life-kit`** — twelve domains, each with vocabulary, dialogues, and a recorded performance

levels.title: LISTENING AND PRONUNCIATION MASTERY
levels.goal: Close the gap between the Korean you can read and the Korean you can hear. By the end of this level you understand natural-speed everyday speech at 90%, catch the contractions that are never written, recognise the major dialects by ear, and produce rhythm and intonation that no longer sounds translated.

levels.title: READING AND WRITING FOUNDATIONS
levels.goal: Read a news brief and a short story with 90% comprehension; write a 300-word diary, a formal email, and a message thread — each in the correct register, with correct spacing.
levels.mainProject: **`text-lab`** — a reading log, a diary, an email, and an error taxonomy

elements.text: **The brief.** Live one full day in Korean, and document it. Not a day of study — a day of use. From waking to sleeping, every Korean interaction is either real or simulated, and every one is logged.

items.text: **Morning (07:00–09:00).** A two-minute voice note in Korean describing your plan for the day, in future tense.
**A news brief (09:00).** Read one article, skim then close-read, and write a 100-word summary in -다 style.
**A phone call (11:00).** A real or simulated call of 3+ minutes — booking, enquiring, or rescheduling.
**A listening block (14:00).** A 10-minute audio clip, transcribed with an error map and a genre label.
**A conversation (17:00).** Fifteen minutes with a tutor or partner, on a topic neither of you prepared.
**A diary entry (21:00).** 150 words, -다 style, covering the day.
**An evening reflection (22:00).** A five-minute voice note in Korean: what was hard, what you avoided, and what you will practise tomorrow.

elements.text: **Phase 3 — Intermediate Range · Levels 7–9**

rows: quoting others, being acted upon, causing events
해요체 / 합니다체 / 해체 / 반말 without slipping; reading tone

elements.text: Phase 3 is where the language stops being a set of situations and becomes a way of thinking. You will argue, report, hedge, and joke — and the grammar for those is a different order of difficulty from ordering a coffee.
*Phase 2 of 7 · Levels 4–6 of 18 · Everyday fluency*

phases.name: Intermediate Range
phases.themeLabel: discourse & connectors, reported speech & passive/causative, register & nuance
phases.goal: Move from *can handle situations* to *can think in the language*. By the end of this phase you argue a position for five minutes with structure and concession, quote other people accurately with the right hearsay marker, describe events in the passive and the causative, and move between four registers without slipping.  **The shift.** Phases 1 and 2 taught you to survive situations. Phase 3 teaches you to hold a *position* — and the grammar for that is a different order of difficulty. A request is one clause. An argument is a structure: claim, reason, example, concession, conclusion — each with its own ending, and each with a politeness level that has to stay consistent across all five.
phases.rule: **The rule of this phase:** every new form is produced in *three registers* before the block is closed — 해요체, 합니다체, and -다. A pattern you can only use politely is a pattern you cannot use in writing, and vice versa.

dashboard.study commitment: 2–3 hours per day, 6 days per week
dashboard.core tools: Anki, recorder, tutor twice weekly, *Korean Grammar in Use – Intermediate/Advanced*, a debate podcast, a drama with subtitles off
dashboard.final outcome: A five-minute structured argument; accurate reported speech; passive and causative; four registers used without a slip; nuance endings read correctly.

levels.title: DISCOURSE AND CONNECTORS
levels.goal: Hold the floor. Say something for five minutes that has a beginning, three reasons, a concession, and an end — in the right register, without the listener having to work to follow you.
levels.mainProject: **`argument-lab`** — a five-minute argument with a Q&A

levels.title: REPORTED SPEECH, PASSIVE, AND CAUSATIVE
levels.goal: Move other people's words, and change the direction of a verb. By the end you report what someone said with the correct hearsay marker, describe being acted upon without sounding like a translated English sentence, and distinguish the passive from the causative where Korean uses the same suffix for both.
levels.mainProject: **`voice-lab`** — a retelling, a news summary, and a voice audit

levels.title: REGISTER AND NUANCE
levels.goal: Say the same thing four different ways, and know which one a situation demands. By the end of this level you move between 해요체, 합니다체, 해체, and 반말 without a slip, and you can hear the difference between a neutral statement, a reproach, a discovery, and a joke — which in Korean is carried almost entirely by the final ending.
levels.mainProject: **`register-lab`** — one piece of content, four registers

elements.text: **The brief.** Sit on a three-person panel, in Korean, for thirty minutes. Deliver a five-minute opening statement on an assigned topic, take questions, disagree with someone politely, and summarise the discussion at the end — all in the correct register for a semi-formal setting.

items.text: **The opening statement.** Five minutes, structured with the five-part skeleton from 7.6, in 합니다체.
**The Q&A.** Ten minutes, including one hostile question and one you cannot answer.
**The disagreement.** Disagree with another panellist twice, using two different concession patterns, without dropping the register.
**The summary.** Three minutes at the end, summarising the panel's positions — including one you disagree with, reported fairly using quoted speech.
**The register log.** Every register switch, with the trigger.
**The recording and transcript.** Full thirty minutes, with the transcript annotated for structure.
**The reflection.** Written in Korean, 200 words, on what you avoided saying.

elements.text: **Phase 4 — Advanced Grammar and Vocabulary · Levels 10–12**

rows: the TOPIK 4–5 set: supposition, regret, inevitability, hearsay, and forty more
1,800 Hanja roots; decoding unfamiliar words on sight

elements.text: Phase 4 is where vocabulary stops being a list and becomes a system. The grammar at L10 is mostly combination — patterns built from patterns you already have — and L11 is the single largest return on time in the entire roadmap, because it triples your vocabulary without adding cards.
*Phase 3 of 7 · Levels 7–9 of 18 · Intermediate range*

phases.name: Advanced Grammar & Vocabulary
phases.themeLabel: TOPIK 4-5 patterns, 1,800 Hanja roots, idioms, proverbs & plain form
phases.goal: Bridge the gap between upper-intermediate communication and advanced stylistic fluency. In this phase, Korean vocabulary stops being a random memorisation list and transforms into a generative root system via 1,800 Sino-Korean Hanja morphemes; advanced grammar patterns (supposition, regret, inevitability, and hearsay) become subconscious speech habits; and culturally dense idioms (사자성어), proverbs (속담), and mimetic words (의성어·의태어) grant your Korean texture, humour, and expressive authority.
phases.rule: **The rule of this phase:** You do not study vocabulary by memorising isolated headwords. You study the morphemes (roots) that generate them. A learner who knows 300 Hanja roots commands 6,000 words on sight.

dashboard.study commitment: 2–3 hours per day, 6 days per week
dashboard.core tools: Naver Hanja Dictionary, Anki (Sino-Korean root decks), *Korean Grammar in Use – Advanced*, Korean editorial podcasts, language partner
dashboard.final outcome: Sight-decode unfamiliar 3- and 4-syllable Sino-Korean words instantly; produce 80+ advanced grammar patterns without pauses; deploy 50 사자성어 and 30 proverbs in natural argument; write a 1,200-word essay in 해라체 (plain form).

levels.title: ADVANCED GRAMMAR PATTERNS
levels.goal: Master the TOPIK Level 4–5 grammar architecture: multi-clause hypothetical conditions, nuanced supposition, regret, inevitability, and concessive constructions. Transition from "correct sentences" to expressing exact degrees of probability, intention, and emotional stance.
levels.mainProject: `grammar-engine-ii` — live oral drill matrix of 80 advanced grammar patterns

levels.title: THE SINO-KOREAN VOCABULARY ENGINE
levels.goal: Decode 1,800 Hanja roots to unlock exponential vocabulary growth. In this level, polysyllabic Sino-Korean words (which comprise over 60% of modern Korean vocabulary) stop being isolated strings of sound and become transparent morphological compounds.
levels.mainProject: `hanja-lexicon` — personal 300-root cross-reference network decoding 1,500 advanced words

levels.title: IDIOMS, PROVERBS, AND EXPRESSIVE LANGUAGE
levels.goal: Acquire the cultural and rhetorical layer that separates mechanical fluency from native-adjacent expressive mastery: four-character idioms (사자성어), living proverbs (속담), evocative sound-symbolic words (의성어·의태어), and writing in plain form (해라체).
levels.mainProject: `expressive-voice` — a 1,200-word published-grade opinion column in 해라체

elements.text: **The Discourse Dossier**

**Goal.** Prove that your Korean has moved past transactional utility into stylistic authority. The phase capstone combines all three levels into an integrated deliverable: an advanced analytical essay and an unprepared 10-minute speech.

items.text: Written entirely in 해라체.
Must demonstrate Level 10 grammar synthesis (at least 15 distinct advanced patterns).
Must utilize Level 11 Sino-Korean vocabulary compounds deconstructed accurately.
Must include at least 6 사자성어 and 3 속담 seamlessly integrated.
Delivered in formal 하십시오체 with spontaneous connectors.
Defend a controversial thesis without reading from a script.
Address 3 hypothetical counterarguments using concessive and hypothetical structures (`-더라도`, `-을망정`, `-느니 차라리`).
Spontaneously produce hypothetical clauses with `-(으)ㄹ 텐데`.
Accurately distinguish `-은 모양이다` from `-나 보다`.
Conjugate without hesitation using `-을 뻔했다` and `-을 걸 그랬다`.
Recognize 300 productive Hanja roots on hearing.
Decode unknown 3-syllable compounds in newspaper headlines on sight.
Explain homophonic distinctions in common pairs (e.g. `전기`, `수도`, `사고`).
Active recall of 40 사자성어 in conversational debates.
Flawless 해라체 plain form consistency in long-form writing.
Mastery of sound symbolism in 의성어/의태어.

phases.name: Specialization
phases.themeLabel: professional Korean, business meetings & negotiations, literature & media
phases.goal: Up to now, every level has been about the language itself. This phase splits it by *purpose*. By the end you can run a meeting, present to a client, negotiate, write a business proposal, and interview in Korean — and you can also read a novel chapter, a journal abstract, and a political editorial with full comprehension.  **The shift.** You are no longer learning Korean. You are learning *two Koreans*: the institutional one and the literary one. They share grammar and diverge almost completely in vocabulary, rhythm, and what counts as a good sentence. A manager's Korean and a novelist's Korean are not the same language spoken at different speeds.  **Why both, even if you only need one.** The professional register is what you use to earn. The literary register is what makes the professional one legible — because newspapers, editorials, and any marketing copy that is any good are written in the literary voice.
phases.rule: **The rule of this phase:** every section produces an artefact that a professional or a reader would recognise as belonging to the genre. A "business email" that reads like a textbook exercise fails, even if every particle is correct.

dashboard.study commitment: 2–3 hours per day, 6 days per week
dashboard.core tools: A real workplace or simulated one, business-writing corpora, a novel, a journal database, two tutors (one professional, one literary)
dashboard.final outcome: A 20-minute presentation, a 3,000-word report, a negotiation, a mock interview, a literary analysis, and an academic abstract written in Korean.

levels.title: PROFESSIONAL KOREAN
levels.goal: Operate inside a Korean organisation. Not "survive a business trip" — function as a colleague: attend and run meetings, present to a room that outranks you, write documents that get approved, negotiate without rupturing the relationship, and interview for a job.
levels.mainProject: **`professional-kit`** — a meeting, a presentation, a proposal, and an interview

levels.title: MEDIA, LITERATURE, AND ACADEMIC KOREAN
levels.goal: Read the Korean that is written to be *read*, not spoken. By the end of this level you read a newspaper editorial and identify its argument, a short story and identify its narrative technique, a journal abstract and extract the method, and a poem and hear what it does with sound — and you can write an abstract and a literary analysis of your own.
levels.mainProject: **`canon-lab`** — an analysis, a translation, and an abstract

elements.text: **The brief.** Produce one professional deliverable and one literary deliverable, both in Korean, both at a standard a Korean professional or an editor would accept — then defend them in conversation.

items.text: **The professional deliverable.** A 2,000-word report or proposal on a real problem, nine-section structure, plus a 10-minute presentation of it.
**The literary deliverable.** A 1,200-word critical essay on a Korean short story, with quoted evidence.
**The translation.** 800 words of the story translated into English, with a translator's note.
**The defence.** A 30-minute recorded interview where a native questions both deliverables: the report's method, the essay's reading.
**The register comparison.** One page contrasting the professional and literary registers, with a quoted sentence from each and an analysis of the difference.
**The reading record.** The full L13–L14 log, with comprehension estimates.
**The error ledger.** 200 entries from this phase, classified by category.

elements.text: **Phase 6 — Precision and Certification · Levels 15–16**

rows: the exam as a skill: format, timing, and the 230/300 score

elements.text: Phase 6 is the first phase with an *external* marker. Everything so far has been judged by a tutor or by you; L15 is judged by a national exam, and L16 by whether a professional would publish your translation. That external standard is why the phase exists.
*Phase 5 of 7 · Levels 13–14 of 18 · Specialization*

phases.name: Precision & Certification
phases.themeLabel: TOPIK II mastery (Levels 5–6), professional translation & interpretation
phases.goal: Two things happen here at once. First, you take the language you already have and make it *measurable* — an externally judged score you can put on a document. Second, you learn a craft that forces you to understand Korean more deeply than fluency ever does: translation.  **The shift.** Everything before this was about *using* Korean. This phase is about *accountability*. A tutor can be generous. An examiner is not. A client is not.  **Why these two belong together.** TOPIK 6 is roughly the level at which professional translation into Korean becomes possible. And translation is the single fastest way to find the exact holes in your grammar that a score of 230 will expose but never explain. The exam tells you that you have a gap. Translation tells you where it is.
phases.rule: **The rule of this phase:** nothing counts until it is scored by someone who has no reason to be kind to you. Self-assessment is allowed everywhere else in this roadmap. Here it is not.

dashboard.study commitment: 2–3 hours per day, 6 days per week
dashboard.core tools: Official TOPIK past papers, a timer, a writing tutor who has marked TOPIK scripts, parallel corpora, a recorder, an interpreting tutor
dashboard.final outcome: A timed mock score ≥ 230/300, and a translation portfolio with a consecutive interpretation that a professional would sign their name to.

levels.title: TOPIK II MASTERY
levels.goal: Score 230 or above on a full, timed, cold TOPIK II paper. Not 230 on a practice set you have seen before, and not 230 assembled from your best section scores on different days — 230 in one sitting, under exam conditions, with the clock running.
levels.mainProject: **`topik-kit`** — three full timed mocks, a writing portfolio, and an error ledger

levels.title: TRANSLATION AND INTERPRETATION
levels.goal: Move meaning between Korean and one other language without losing the things that make it mean. By the end you can translate a 3,000-word document with a translator's note explaining every hard choice, and perform fifteen minutes of consecutive interpreting from audio you have never heard.
levels.mainProject: **`bridge-kit`** — a translation portfolio, a 300-term glossary, and a recorded consecutive performance

elements.text: Take one short text — a paragraph of a corporate apology — and translate it three ways: into formal English, into neutral English, and into a deliberately over-formal English that a Korean reader might produce.

elements.text: **Phase 7 — Mastery · Levels 17–18**

rows: the things no exam measures: humour, subtext, silence, rapid register switching, cultural fluency
the ability to explain the language, and the maintenance regime that keeps it alive for decades

elements.text: Phase 7 has no external examiner, because there is no exam above TOPIK 6. The judge becomes a native speaker who forgets you are foreign, and then the only remaining judge is you.
*Phase 6 of 7 · Levels 15–16 of 18 · Precision and Certification*

phases.name: Mastery
phases.themeLabel: native-adjacent fluency, cultural depth, teaching & lifelong maintenance
phases.goal: Close the distance that no exam can measure, and then build the machinery that keeps the language alive for the rest of your life.  **The shift.** Every previous phase added capability. This one removes the last visible seams. There is no new grammar in L17 and almost no new vocabulary. What is left is timing, subtext, humour, cultural reference, and the hundred small choices that make a sentence sound like it came from a person rather than a learner.  **The honest framing.** This is the phase that never ends, and it is the only one that cannot be completed by finishing a file. L17 has a finish line — a native speaker has to forget, for a measurable stretch of time, that you are foreign. L18 has none, because teaching and maintenance are practices, not milestones.
phases.rule: **The rule of this phase:** nothing here can be done alone for long. Every gate in L17 requires a native speaker, and every gate in L18 requires a learner. That is not an accident — it is the design. The last 5% of a language exists only between people.

dashboard.suggested duration: 6–12 months to the L17 pass; then indefinite
dashboard.study commitment: 2 hours per day, but the *shape* changes: less study, more living
dashboard.core tools: Native friends who will not flatter you, a recorder, a class you teach, Korean-language media as a default rather than a study object
dashboard.final outcome: Sixty minutes of unprepared speech, a short story in Korean, a lesson you taught, and a written plan for the next twenty years.

levels.title: NATIVE-ADJACENT FLUENCY
levels.goal: Be mistaken for a native for a sustained stretch — not on the phone for thirty seconds, and not because you said one idiom correctly, but for twenty minutes in a conversation you did not prepare.  **What this level is not.** It is not accent elimination. Some learners reach near-native prosody and some never do, and the difference is mostly age of onset and ear. Accent is the least important thing in this level and the thing learners obsess over most. **Being mistaken for native and being native-adjacent are different targets, and only the second one is required here.**
levels.mainProject: **`fluency-proof`** — a 60-minute unprepared talk, a 3,000-word short story, and a native-blind test

levels.title: TEACHING AND LIFELONG MASTERY
levels.goal: Two things. First, be able to *explain* Korean — which is the deepest test of understanding there is, and the only one that exposes the gaps that fluency hides. Second, build the regime that keeps the language alive for decades, because the single most common outcome of reaching an advanced level is losing it by neglect.  **Why teaching is the final level.** A user of a language can be excellent and still not know why anything works. A teacher must be able to say what the rule is, when it bends, which exceptions matter, and why the learner's version was wrong rather than merely different. That knowledge cannot be faked, and building it fixes things fluency never touched.
levels.duration: 3–6 months to the teaching certification; the maintenance regime is permanent
levels.mainProject: **`the-teacher`** — a taught unit, a diagnosis, a curriculum, and a rubric

elements.text: **The brief.** There is no exam above TOPIK 6, so the capstone is the invention of one: a panel of three native speakers who do not know you well, a day of performance, and a verdict you cannot appeal.  **Why it is called the Passing.** Because the thing being tested is not knowledge. It is whether you can pass — as a colleague, as a conversation partner, as a writer, as a teacher — in front of people with no reason to be generous.
Speak for **60 minutes**, unprepared, on a topic drawn at random from a set you submitted a week in advance (twenty topics, so you cannot prepare them all).

*End of the roadmap. Everything from here is maintenance, and maintenance is the whole point.*

levels.title: HANGEUL AND THE SOUND SYSTEM
levels.goal: Read any Korean text aloud correctly — including words you have never seen — with all seven sound-change rules applied without conscious thought. Then produce the sounds well enough that a native speaker does not have to work to understand you.

dashboard.core tools: Anki, a recorder, a native-speaker audio source, a syllable chart
dashboard.main project: **`sound-lab`** — a recorded corpus proving you can read and pronounce
dashboard.final outcome: 60+ syllables/min on unseen text, correct sound rules, and a phoneme inventory you can produce on demand.

sections.title: Why Hangeul is a design problem, not a memorisation problem

items.text: Every consonant shape encodes where the sound is made: `ㄱ` the tongue rising at the back; `ㄴ` the tongue at the ridge; `ㅁ` the shape of a mouth; `ㅅ` the shape of teeth; `ㅇ` the throat, empty.
Consonants come in families — plain, aspirated, tensed — and the aspiration is drawn *as an extra stroke*: `ㄱ` → `ㅋ`, `ㄷ` → `ㅌ`, `ㅂ` → `ㅍ`, `ㅈ` → `ㅊ`.
Vowels are built from three elements: a dot (sky, ㅗ/ㅏ), a horizontal line (earth, ㅡ), a vertical line (human, ㅣ). Every compound vowel is a combination.
There are no capitals, no cursive, and no positional letter variants.

elements.text: This is why the script is learnable in days. It is one of the few writing systems in the world that a literate adult can acquire analytically rather than by rote.

items.text: It is phonemic, not phonetic: it spells the *morpheme*, not the sound. `꽃이` is written with ㅊ and pronounced [꼬치].
Sound changes are unwritten. The gap between spelling and speech is the whole difficulty of Korean listening.
Spacing (띄어쓰기) carries grammatical information and is a separate skill (L6).

elements.text: **Module completion gate (0.1).** You can explain, in two sentences, why Hangeul is fast to learn and why that does not make Korean fast to learn.

rows: between English *g* and *k*; no puff of air
Spanish *pero* between vowels; *l* as a final
a placeholder at the start of a syllable

items.text: English has a two-way distinction (voiced/voiceless). Korean has three: **plain** (ㄱ), **aspirated** (ㅋ), **tensed** (ㄲ).
Say the triplet `가 / 카 / 까` until a native speaker or a recording confirms all three are distinct.
Do not rely on voicing ([g] vs [k]) — Korean's plain series is voiced between vowels and voiceless elsewhere, which is not a distinction English ears track.
Hold a sheet of paper in front of your mouth: ㅋ and ㅌ should move it, ㄱ and ㄲ should not, and ㄲ should feel tighter in the throat than ㄱ.

elements.text: **Why this matters now.** If you cannot distinguish these three at the start, you cannot hear them later — and Korean is full of minimal pairs that depend on them: `불` fire / `풀` grass / `뿔` horn.
**Module completion gate (0.2).** You produce all nineteen consonants on demand from a random order, and a recording of yourself saying 가/카/까, 다/타/따, 바/파/빠 is audibly three-way different.

rows: teeth together, lips flat, a grunt — **not** *oo*
*bed*, shorter; merged with ㅐ for most speakers under 50
glide; as the possessive particle it is pronounced 에

modules.title: The two collapses to fix now

items.text: **ㅓ vs ㅗ.** English speakers round ㅓ into ㅗ. Say pairs: 어-오, 어-오. Then `언어` (language) — it must not become 오노.
**ㅡ vs ㅜ.** ㅡ is unrounded; ㅜ is rounded. Say pairs: 크-쿠, 크-쿠. Then `그` (that) versus `구` (nine).
Record both pairs and listen back with headphones. This self-check catches what your ear will not.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (0.3).** You read the full vowel chart from memory, and your recording of 어/오 and 크/쿠 is distinguishable by a native speaker or by a language-exchange partner.

items.text: Every syllable is `(initial consonant) + vowel + (final consonant)`.
Six shapes: `가` (C+V), `강` (C+V+C), `과` (C+V+V), `아` (ㅇ+V), `안` (ㅇ+V+C), `완` (C+V+V+C).
ㅇ is silent in the initial position and *ng* in the final position.
Stroke order: top-left first, then right, then bottom. Learn it once, correctly.
Write each of the 40 letters ten times, saying the sound aloud.
Write your own name in Hangeul, then a Koreanised version of three friends' names.
Write ten words from dictation given by a text-to-speech voice.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (0.4).** You handwrite 20 random syllables from dictation with correct block construction and legible stroke order.

headers: Written letters that collapse into it
rows: ㄷ ㅅ ㅆ ㅈ ㅊ ㅌ ㅎ

items.text: ㄺ → ㄱ before a consonant: 읽다 [익따], 맑다 [막따], 닭 [닥]
ㄻ → ㅁ: 삶 [삼]
ㄼ → ㄹ: 여덟 [여덜], 넓다 [널따]
ㅄ → ㅂ: 값 [갑], 없어요 [업써요]
ㄵ → ㄴ: 앉아요 [안자요]
ㄶ → ㄴ, with the ㅎ dropped: 많아요 [마나요]
A final stop (ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ) is never released in Korean — no puff of air at the end. `밥` ends with the lips closed, not with a *p*.
This is the single most audible marker of a foreign accent. Practise stopping the sound in your mouth.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (0.5).** Given any batchim word, you state its seven-sound collapse without a reference, and your recording of 밥/밤/밥 does not release the final.

items.text: This is the most frequent rule in the language. At normal speed, words bleed into each other constantly.
Drill: read 30 two-syllable words where the second begins with ㅇ, applying liaison every time.

modules.title: Aspiration (격음화): ㅎ fuses with a stop

elements.text: ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ + ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ/ㅅ/ㅈ → tensed.
ㄱ/ㄷ/ㅂ + ㄴ/ㅁ → ㅇ/ㄴ/ㅁ.
ㄴ + ㄹ or ㄹ + ㄴ → [ㄹㄹ].

**The sentence that identifies a beginner.** `괜찮아요` said as *gwaen-chan-a-yo*, with a full ㅎ, is understood — and immediately placed. Say [괜차나요]. Record yourself until it sounds like one word, not four syllables.

**Module completion gate (0.6).** You read 20 unseen words containing sound changes, state which rule applies to each, and your spoken version matches the rule. You can list all seven rules from memory.

items.text: Korean is syllable-timed, not stress-timed. Every syllable gets roughly equal duration; do not crush unstressed syllables the way English does.
Consequence: Korean speech sounds *flatter and faster* than English to a learner, and your English rhythm sounds *lumpy* to a Korean.
Korean uses pitch at the phrase level, not the word level: a rise at the end of a question, a fall at the end of a statement.
Long vowels carry emotional weight: `네~` (yes, drawn out) signals hesitation or disbelief.
There is no lexical tone — pitch does not change word meaning, but it changes *attitude*, which is where misunderstanding lives.

rows: slight rise on each, fall on last

elements.text: **Module completion gate (0.7).** You shadow a 60-second native clip and your recording has the same contour shape — checked visually on a pitch track or by comparing lengths of matched phrases.

items.text: Take a 100-syllable passage, read aloud, time it, divide.
Count errors separately. A fast read with wrong sound rules is not progress.
Start with syllable charts, then word lists, then short sentences, then a paragraph of a children's book.
Read *novel* text every session — re-reading the same passage inflates speed without building decoding.
Read aloud, always. Silent reading at this stage trains nothing.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (0.8).** 60 syllables per minute on unseen text at 98% rule accuracy, measured three days in a row.

modules.title: Dictation as a test of perception

items.text: Dictate 20 words per session from an audio source, in Hangeul.
Mark every miss. Group the misses: was it a consonant, a vowel, a batchim, or a sound rule?
The group with the most misses is your training target for the next session.
Pass 1 blind; pass 2 sentence-by-sentence dictation; pass 3 compare and mark.
Re-listen to the missed spots immediately, three times, before moving on.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (0.9).** 20-word dictation at 95% accuracy, with misses classified by cause rather than simply corrected.

sections.title: Level 0 assessment
sections.objective: **Level 0 completion rule.** If you can read quickly but a native speaker cannot transcribe your speech, you have completed a decoding course, not this level. Repeat 0.6–0.9 until the corpus passes.

elements.text: **Objective.** Produce a recorded, reviewable corpus that proves the level's outcome — not a claim that you "know the alphabet".

items.text: **The alphabet corpus.** You record all 40 letters, isolated, in a single take, with no reading from a list you can see mid-recording.
**The minimal-pair corpus.** Ten triplets (가/카/까 and nine others) recorded twice, with a 2-second gap.
**The sound-rule corpus.** Twenty sentences, each containing at least one sound-change rule, recorded at natural speed.
**The reading corpus.** Three unseen passages of 100+ syllables, read aloud, timed, with the time and syllable count written down.
**The dictation log.** Ten sessions of 20 words, with accuracy per session and a running list of your recurring phoneme errors.
**The self-assessment.** One paragraph, written, naming your three weakest sounds and the drill you used for each.

sections.title: Unit 0 — Hangul: The Alphabet & Sound System (한글과 발음 기초)

modules.title: 0.1 — Meeting Korean Letters: Vowels, Consonants & Syllable Blocks (기본 모음과 기본 자음)

elements.text: **Situation & Objective.** Understanding the featural design of King Sejong's alphabet and forming two-letter syllable blocks.

items.text: **Dialogue Practice:** Listen to and practice the dialogue between 선생님 and 학생 and 선생님.
`한글 모음 "ㅏ, ㅓ, ㅗ, ㅜ"를 소리 내어 읽어 보세요.` (Try reading the Hangul vowels "a, eo, o, u" aloud.) — *Note: Bright vowels (ㅏ, ㅗ) vs Dark vowels (ㅓ, ㅜ).*
`ㅏ, ㅓ, ㅗ, ㅜ. 자음 "ㄱ, ㄴ, ㄷ"도 같이 읽어요?` (a, eo, o, u. Shall we also read consonants "g, n, d" together?)
`네, "가, 나, 다"처럼 모음과 합쳐서 소리를 만듭니다.` (Yes, just like "ga, na, da", combine consonants with vowels to create sounds.)
**Cultural Etiquette & Pragmatics:** Hangul letters are never written in a linear row like English (n-a-m-u); they are stacked into syllable blocks representing CV or CVC sounds (나무).
**Core Target Words:** Memorise and pronounce all target words for this lesson:
`한글` (han-geul) [Noun]: Hangeul (Korean alphabet) — e.g., "한글은 읽기 쉬운 글자입니다." (*Hangeul is an easy-to-read script.*)
`모음` (mo-eum, Hanja: 母音) [Noun]: Vowel (literally "mother sound") — e.g., "기본 모음은 열 자입니다." (*There are ten basic vowels.*)
`자음` (ja-eum, Hanja: 子音) [Noun]: Consonant (literally "child sound") — e.g., "기본 자음은 14자입니다." (*There are 14 basic consonants.*)
`나무` (na-mu) [Noun]: Tree / wood — e.g., "공원에 큰 나무가 있어요." (*There is a big tree in the park.*)
`아이` (a-i) [Noun]: Child / baby — e.g., "아이가 활짝 웃어요." (*The child smiles brightly.*)
**Grammar Pattern: `Syllable Block Formation (음절 블록 구조)`** (Combining Initial Consonant (초성) + Medial Vowel (중성))
Formula: `Initial Consonant (C) + Medial Vowel (V)`

Explanation: Every Korean syllable block MUST begin with a consonant letter. When a syllable begins with a vowel sound, the silent placeholder consonant "ㅇ" must be placed in the initial position (e.g., 아, 오, 우).
Rule: Vertical vowels (ㅏ, ㅑ, ㅓ, ㅕ, ㅣ) place the consonant on the left: ㄱ + ㅏ = 가.
Rule: Horizontal vowels (ㅗ, ㅛ, ㅜ, ㅠ, ㅡ) place the consonant on top: ㄱ + ㅗ = 고.
Rule: Silent "ㅇ" has no sound value at the start of a syllable: ㅇ + ㅣ = 이 (pronounced "ee").
Example: `가, 나, 다, 라, 마, 바, 사` — *ga, na, da, ra, ma, ba, sa*
Example: `고, 노, 도, 로, 모, 보, 소` — *go, no, do, ro, mo, bo, so*
Example: `우유, 오이, 모자, 바지` — *milk, cucumber, hat, pants*
**Shadowing & Repetition Drill:** Listen carefully to the contrast between bright and dark vowels, then repeat aloud.
Prompt: "Read vowel pair: a vs eo" → Speak aloud: `아이 / 어디` (*child / where*)
Prompt: "Read vowel pair: o vs u" → Speak aloud: `오이 / 우유` (*cucumber / milk*)
Prompt: "Read consonant contrast: g vs n" → Speak aloud: `가구 / 나라` (*furniture / country*)
**Reading Passage:** "First Korean Syllables"
Text: `아이. 오이. 나무. 모자. 다리. 비누. 고기.`
Translation: *Child. Cucumber. Tree. Hat. Bridge/leg. Soap. Meat.*
Check: Which word means "tree"? → Answer: `나무 (na-mu)` (*ㄴ + ㅏ = 나, ㅁ + ㅜ = 무.*)
Check: Which word means "cucumber"? → Answer: `오이 (o-i)` (*ㅇ + ㅗ = 오, ㅇ + ㅣ = 이.*)
**Guided Writing Task:** Write the 4 syllable blocks for "cow" (소), "tree" (나무), "water" (물), and "shoes" (구두).
Sample Model Answer: `소, 나무, 물, 구두`

modules.title: 0.2 — Aspirated & Tense Consonants & Compound Vowels (거센소리와 된소리, 이중 모음)

elements.text: **Situation & Objective.** Distinguishing plain, aspirated, and tense sounds that change word meanings in Korean.

items.text: **Dialogue Practice:** Listen to and practice the dialogue between 선생님 and 학생 and 선생님.
`"달", "탈", "딸"의 소리 차이를 들어 보세요.` (Listen to the sound differences between "dal" (moon), "tal" (mask), and "ttal" (daughter).)
`"탈"은 공기가 많이 나오고, "딸"은 목에 힘이 들어가네요.` ("Tal" has a lot of air coming out, and "ttal" has tension in the throat.)
`정확해요! 한국어에서는 이 세 소리가 완전히 다른 단어입니다.` (Exactly! In Korean, these three sounds create completely different words.)

**Cultural Etiquette & Pragmatics:** Korean does not distinguish voiced/voiceless sounds (B vs P) as phonemes; it distinguishes three-way phonation: Plain (ㄱ), Aspirated (ㅋ - puff of air), and Tense (ㄲ - tight vocal cords).
**Core Target Words:** Memorise and pronounce all target words for this lesson:
`달` (dal) [Noun]: Moon / month — e.g., "밤하늘에 밝은 달이 떴어요." (*A bright moon rose in the night sky.*)
`탈` (tal) [Noun]: Mask (traditional) — e.g., "전통 하회탈을 썼습니다." (*I put on a traditional Hahoe mask.*)
`딸` (ttal) [Noun]: Daughter — e.g., "우리 딸은 일곱 살입니다." (*Our daughter is seven years old.*)
`사과` (sa-gwa) [Noun]: Apple / apology — e.g., "달콤한 사과를 씻었어요." (*I washed a sweet apple.*)
`회사` (hoe-sa, Hanja: 會社) [Noun]: Company / office — e.g., "내일 아침에 회사에 갑니다." (*I am going to the company tomorrow morning.*)
**Grammar Pattern: `The 3-Way Consonant Phonation Matrix (평음 · 격음 · 된소리)`** (Plain vs Aspirated vs Tense Consonants)
Formula: `Plain (ㄱ, ㄷ, ㅂ, ㅅ, ㅈ) ↔ Aspirated (ㅋ, ㅌ, ㅍ, —, ㅊ) ↔ Tense (ㄲ, ㄸ, ㅃ, ㅆ, ㅉ)`

Explanation: Placing a hand or sheet of paper in front of your mouth reveals the difference: Plain causes slight air, Aspirated blows the paper vigorously, and Tense emits almost zero air while tensing the glottis.
Rule: 불 (fire - plain) vs 풀 (grass - aspirated) vs 뿔 (horn - tense).
Rule: 방 (room - plain) vs 빵 (bread - tense).
Rule: 자다 (to sleep - plain) vs 차다 (to kick - aspirated) vs 짜다 (to be salty - tense).
Example: `방 / 빵` — *room / bread*
Example: `자다 / 차다 / 짜다` — *to sleep / to kick / to be salty*
Example: `가다 / 카드 / 까다` — *to go / card / to peel*
**Shadowing & Repetition Drill:** Listen and distinguish plain vs aspirated vs tense consonants.
Prompt: "Distinguish: bang vs ppang" → Speak aloud: `방 / 빵` (*room / bread*)
Prompt: "Distinguish: dal vs tal vs ttal" → Speak aloud: `달 / 탈 / 딸` (*moon / mask / daughter*)
Prompt: "Distinguish: jada vs chada vs jjada" → Speak aloud: `자다 / 차다 / 짜다` (*sleep / kick / salty*)
**Reading Passage:** "Consonant Distinctions Passage"
Text: `아침에 빵을 먹어요. 시원한 차를 마셔요. 날씨가 조금 추워요. 회사에 가요.`
Translation: *I eat bread in the morning. I drink cool tea. The weather is a bit cold. I go to the office.*
Check: What does the speaker eat? → Answer: `빵 (bread)` (*Tense consonant ㅃ in 빵.*)
Check: Where is the speaker going? → Answer: `회사 (company/office)` (*Compound vowel ㅚ in 회.*)
**Guided Writing Task:** Write down the contrasting pairs: "room" (방) and "bread" (빵); "foot" (발) and "arm" (팔).
Sample Model Answer: `방 - 빵 / 발 - 팔`

modules.title: 0.3 — Final Consonants (받침) & The 7 Sound-Change Rules (받침과 7개 대표음, 연음 규칙)

elements.text: **Situation & Objective.** Mastering syllable codas and smooth liaison when reading words in sequence.

items.text: **Dialogue Practice:** Listen to and practice the dialogue between 안내원 and 승객.
`출구 쪽에 "꽃집 [꼳찝]" 간판이 보이세요?` (Do you see the "flower shop [kkot-jjip]" sign by the exit?) — *Note: 꽃 [꼳] neutralizes to [ㄷ], causing tensification on 집 [찝].*
`네, 보여요! "한국어 [한구거]" 책도 거기서 파나요?` (Yes, I see it! Do they also sell "Korean [han-gu-geo]" books there?) — *Note: 한국어 undergoes liaison: ㄱ moves to empty ㅇ space -> [한구거].*

**Cultural Etiquette & Pragmatics:** Although 27 different consonants and double-consonant clusters can be written as 받침, they can only make 7 phonetic sounds at the end of a syllable: [ㄱ, ㄴ, ㄷ, ㄹ, ㅁ, ㅂ, ㅇ].
**Core Target Words:** Memorise and pronounce all target words for this lesson:
`꽃` (kkot) [Noun]: Flower (pronounced [꼳]) — e.g., "장미꽃 [장미꼳] 이 참 예뻐요." (*The rose flower is very pretty.*)
`한국어` (han-gu-geo, Hanja: 韓國語) [Noun]: Korean language (pronounced [한구거]) — e.g., "한국어를 열심히 공부해요." (*I study Korean diligently.*)
`감사합니다` (gam-sa-ham-ni-da, Hanja: 感謝합니다) [Expression]: Thank you (pronounced [감사함니다]) — e.g., "도와주셔서 감사합니다." (*Thank you for helping me.*)
`책` (chaek, Hanja: 冊) [Noun]: Book — e.g., "책을 매일 읽어요." (*I read books every day.*)
`지하철` (ji-ha-cheol, Hanja: 地下鐵) [Noun]: Subway (pronounced [지하철]) — e.g., "지하철을 타고 학교에 가요." (*I take the subway to school.*)
**Grammar Pattern: `Liaison Rule (연음 법칙)`** (Carrying Syllable-Final Consonants into Vowel Placeholders)
Formula: `Syllable with 받침 + Syllable starting with ㅇ → 받침 sound moves to ㅇ`

Explanation: When a syllable with a final consonant is immediately followed by a syllable starting with the silent placeholder consonant "ㅇ", the final consonant naturally leaps over to become the initial sound of the next syllable.
Rule: 한국어 [한구거]: ㄱ carries over into 어.
Rule: 음악 [으막]: ㅁ carries over into 악.
Rule: 집에 [지베]: ㅂ carries over into 에.
Example: `한국어 → [한구거]` — *Korean language*
Example: `음악 → [으막]` — *music*
Example: `밥을 먹어요 → [바블 머거요]` — *eat rice*
**Grammar Pattern: `Syllable-Final Neutralization (음절의 끝소리 규칙)`** (7 Representative Coda Sounds)
Formula: `All codas reduce to: [ㄱ, ㄴ, ㄷ, ㄹ, ㅁ, ㅂ, ㅇ]`
Explanation: In isolation or before a consonant, no matter how complex the written coda is, it collapses into one of the 7 sounds. In particular: ㅅ, ㅆ, ㅈ, ㅊ, ㅌ, ㅎ all neutralize to phonetic [ㄷ].
Rule: 옷 [옫] (clothes), 꽃 [꼳] (flower), 낮 [낟] (daytime), 빛 [빋] (light) all end in phonetic [ㄷ].
Rule: 앞 [압] (front), 잎 [입] (leaf) neutralize to phonetic [ㅂ].
Rule: 부엌 [부억] (kitchen) neutralizes to phonetic [ㄱ].
Example: `옷 [옫], 꽃 [꼳], 빛 [빋]` — *clothes, flower, light -> all [ㄷ]*
Example: `앞 [압], 숲 [숩]` — *front, forest -> all [ㅂ]*
**Shadowing & Repetition Drill:** Practice moving final consonants into the following vowel smoothly.
Prompt: "Liaison: ba-beul meo-geo-yo" → Speak aloud: `밥을 먹어요 [바블 머거요]` (*eat a meal*)
Prompt: "Liaison: ha-neul-e" → Speak aloud: `하늘에 [하느레]` (*in the sky*)
Prompt: "Neutralization: kkot-jip" → Speak aloud: `꽃집 [꼳찝]` (*flower shop*)
**Reading Passage:** "Reading Seoul Subway Signs"
Text: `서울역 1번 출구입니다. 오른쪽으로 가면 꽃집과 약국이 있습니다. 환승역은 시청역입니다.`
Translation: *It is Exit 1 of Seoul Station. If you go right, there is a flower shop and a pharmacy. The transfer station is City Hall Station.*
Check: How is "꽃집" pronounced? → Answer: `[꼳찝]` (*꽃 neutralizes to [ㄷ], triggering tensification [찝].*)
Check: Which exit is mentioned? → Answer: `1번 출구 (Exit 1)` (*일 번 출구.*)
**Guided Writing Task:** Transcribe the spoken sounds of: 1) 한국어, 2) 음악, 3) 밥을.
Sample Model Answer: `1) [한구거], 2) [으막], 3) [바블]`

sections.title: Unit 1 — Unit 1: Greetings & Self-Introductions (제1과: 인사와 자기소개)

modules.title: 1.1 — Meeting Someone for the First Time: Greetings & Farewells (처음 만났을 때의 인사)

elements.text: **Situation & Objective.** Meeting a new language exchange partner or acquaintance in Seoul.

items.text: **Dialogue Practice:** Listen to and practice the dialogue between 민수 and 사라 and 민수 and 사라.
`안녕하세요! 처음 뵙겠습니다.` (Hello! Pleased to meet you for the first time.) — *Note: 처음 뵙겠습니다 is the formal introductory greeting to someone new.*
`안녕하세요! 만나서 반갑습니다.` (Hello! Nice to meet you.) — *Note: 만나서 반갑습니다 is used by both parties after first greetings.*
`오늘 시간 내 주셔서 감사합니다. 안녕히 가세요!` (Thank you for making time today. Goodbye (to the person leaving)!) — *Note: 안녕히 가세요 (Go in peace) is said to the person who is departing.*
`네, 민수 씨도 안녕히 계세요!` (Yes, goodbye (stay in peace), Min-su!) — *Note: 안녕히 계세요 (Stay in peace) is said to the person remaining.*

**Cultural Etiquette & Pragmatics:** In Korean, bowing at approximately 15 to 30 degrees while saying "안녕하세요" conveys genuine respect. Never shake hands with just one hand to an elder or superior; support your right forearm with your left hand.
**Core Target Words:** Memorise and pronounce all target words for this lesson:
`안녕하세요` (an-nyeong-ha-se-yo) [Expression]: Hello / Good morning / How are you? — e.g., "선생님, 안녕하세요!" (*Teacher, hello!*)
`만나서 반갑습니다` (man-na-seo ban-gap-seum-ni-da) [Expression]: Nice to meet you — e.g., "처음 뵙겠습니다. 만나서 반갑습니다." (*Pleased to make your acquaintance. Nice to meet you.*)
`안녕히 가세요` (an-nyeong-hi ga-se-yo) [Expression]: Goodbye (said to someone who is leaving) — e.g., "손님, 안녕히 가세요!" (*Customer, goodbye!*)
`안녕히 계세요` (an-nyeong-hi gye-se-yo) [Expression]: Goodbye (said to someone who is staying) — e.g., "저는 먼저 갈게요. 안녕히 계세요!" (*I will head out first. Goodbye (stay well)!*)
`죄송합니다` (joe-song-ham-ni-da, Hanja: 罪悚합니다) [Expression]: I am sorry (polite/formal) — e.g., "늦어서 정말 죄송합니다." (*I am truly sorry for being late.*)
`감사합니다` (gam-sa-ham-ni-da, Hanja: 感謝합니다) [Expression]: Thank you (polite/formal) — e.g., "도와주셔서 감사합니다." (*Thank you for helping me.*)
**Grammar Pattern: `안녕히 가세요 vs 안녕히 계세요`** ("Go peacefully" vs "Stay peacefully")
Formula: `가다 (to go) + -세요 → 가세요 // 계시다 (honorific of to stay) + -세요 → 계세요`
Explanation: Korean distinguishes whether the person you are parting with is leaving or staying. If both people are leaving the place, both say "안녕히 가세요!"
Rule: The speaker leaves, the other person stays: say 안녕히 계세요.
Rule: The speaker stays, the other person leaves: say 안녕히 가세요.
Rule: Both people leave: both say 안녕히 가세요.
Example: `카페를 나갈 때: "안녕히 계세요!"` — *When leaving a cafe: "Stay in peace!"*
Example: `집을 나서는 손님에게: "안녕히 가세요!"` — *To a guest leaving your house: "Go in peace!"*
**Shadowing & Repetition Drill:** Shadow each native speaker line with authentic bowing intonation.
Prompt: "Say hello respectfully" → Speak aloud: `안녕하세요! 처음 뵙겠습니다.` (*Hello! Pleased to meet you.*)
Prompt: "Say nice to meet you" → Speak aloud: `만나서 반갑습니다.` (*Nice to meet you.*)
Prompt: "Farewell to person staying" → Speak aloud: `안녕히 계세요!` (*Goodbye (stay in peace)!*)
Prompt: "Farewell to person leaving" → Speak aloud: `안녕히 가세요!` (*Goodbye (go in peace)!*)
**Reading Passage:** "First Day Greetings at the Institute"
Text: `안녕하세요. 처음 뵙겠습니다. 저는 민수입니다. 만나서 반갑습니다. 안녕히 계세요.`
Translation: *Hello. Pleased to meet you for the first time. I am Min-su. Nice to meet you. Goodbye.*
Check: What is the speaker's name? → Answer: `민수 (Min-su)` (*저는 민수입니다.*)
Check: Is the speaker staying or leaving at the end? → Answer: `Leaving` (*He says "안녕히 계세요" to the people staying.*)
**Guided Writing Task:** Write a short 3-sentence greeting introducing yourself to a new acquaintance.
Sample Model Answer: `안녕하세요! 저는 마이클입니다. 만나서 반갑습니다.`

modules.title: 1.2 — Introducing Yourself: Names, Nationalities & Occupations (자기소개: 국적과 직업 말하기)

elements.text: **Situation & Objective.** First day of Korean language class at Seoul National University.

items.text: **Dialogue Practice:** Listen to and practice the dialogue between 사라 and 민수 and 사라 and 민수 and 사라.
`안녕하세요? 저는 사라예요. 미국 사람이에요.` (Hello? I am Sarah. I am American.) — *Note: 사라 ends in a vowel, so it takes 예요. 사람 ends in a consonant, so it takes 이에요.*
`반가워요, 사라 씨! 저는 김민수예요. 한국 사람이에요.` (Nice to meet you, Sarah! I am Kim Min-su. I am Korean.)
`민수 씨는 학생이에요?` (Are you a student, Min-su?)
`네, 저는 대학생이에요. 사라 씨는 회사원이에요?` (Yes, I am a university student. Are you an office worker, Sarah?)
`아니요, 저도 학생이에요.` (No, I am also a student.) — *Note: 도 means "also/too", replacing the topic particle 은/는.*

**Cultural Etiquette & Pragmatics:** The title "씨" (e.g. 민수 씨, 사라 씨) is polite and respectful between peers and adult classmates. Never attach "씨" to your own name (e.g., saying "저는 사라 씨예요" is incorrect; say "저는 사라예요").
**Core Target Words:** Memorise and pronounce all target words for this lesson:
`사람` (sa-ram) [Noun]: Person / people — e.g., "저는 미국 사람이에요." (*I am an American person.*)
`한국` (han-guk, Hanja: 韓國) [Noun]: Korea — e.g., "한국에 여행을 왔어요." (*I came on a trip to Korea.*)
`미국` (mi-guk, Hanja: 美國) [Noun]: United States of America — e.g., "미국 뉴욕에서 살았어요." (*I lived in New York, USA.*)
`학생` (hak-saeng, Hanja: 學生) [Noun]: Student — e.g., "저는 한국어 학생이에요." (*I am a Korean language student.*)
`선생님` (seon-saeng-nim, Hanja: 先生님) [Noun]: Teacher (honorific) — e.g., "선생님, 질문이 있습니다." (*Teacher, I have a question.*)
`회사원` (hoe-sa-won, Hanja: 會社員) [Noun]: Office worker / company employee — e.g., "제 친구는 회사원이에요." (*My friend is an office worker.*)
`의사` (ui-sa, Hanja: 醫師) [Noun]: Doctor / physician — e.g., "병원에 의사 선생님이 계세요." (*The doctor is at the clinic.*)
**Grammar Pattern: `Noun + 이에요 / 예요`** (Am / Is / Are (Polite Identification Copula))
Formula: `Noun ending in Consonant + 이에요 // Noun ending in Vowel + 예요`
Explanation: The identification copula equates the subject to a noun ("A is B"). In spoken Korean (해요체), the form depends entirely on whether the preceding noun ends with a consonant (받침) or a vowel.
Rule: Ends in Consonant (받침 O): 학생 + 이에요 → 학생이에요.
Rule: Ends in Vowel (받침 X): 의사 + 예요 → 의사예요.
Rule: Question form has the exact same spelling with rising intonation: 학생이에요? (Are you a student?)
Example: `저는 학생이에요.` — *I am a student.*
Example: `저는 의사예요.` — *I am a doctor.*
Example: `한국 사람이에요?` — *Are you Korean?*
**Grammar Pattern: `Topic Particle: Noun + 은 / 는`** ("As for N..." / Topic Marker)
Formula: `Noun ending in Consonant + 은 // Noun ending in Vowel + 는`
Explanation: Marks the topic of the sentence ("As for me...", "Speaking of Min-su..."). It sets the stage or creates a contrast with other topics.
Rule: Ends in Consonant: 사람 + 은 → 사람은.
Rule: Ends in Vowel: 저 + 는 → 저는.
Example: `저는 사라예요.` — *As for me, I am Sarah.*
Example: `민수 씨는 학생이에요.` — *As for Min-su, he is a student.*
**Shadowing & Repetition Drill:** Substitute nationalities and professions into the pattern "저는 [Country] 사람이에요".
Prompt: "Say: I am American" → Speak aloud: `저는 미국 사람이에요.` (*I am American.*)
Prompt: "Say: I am Japanese" → Speak aloud: `저는 일본 사람이에요.` (*I am Japanese.*)
Prompt: "Say: I am an office worker" → Speak aloud: `저는 회사원이에요.` (*I am an office worker.*)
Prompt: "Ask: Are you a teacher?" → Speak aloud: `선생님이에요?` (*Are you a teacher?*)
**Reading Passage:** "Classmate Self-Introduction Card"
Text: `안녕하세요? 제 이름은 타쿠야예요. 저는 일본 사람이에요. 저는 서울대학교 학생이에요. 반갑습니다.`
Translation: *Hello? My name is Takuya. I am Japanese. I am a Seoul National University student. Nice to meet you.*
Check: Where is Takuya from? → Answer: `일본 (Japan)` (*저는 일본 사람이에요.*)
Check: What is his occupation? → Answer: `대학생 (University student)` (*서울대학교 학생이에요.*)
**Guided Writing Task:** Write your own 4-sentence Korean self-introduction using: greeting, name, nationality, and occupation.
Sample Model Answer: `안녕하세요? 저는 안나예요. 저는 독일 사람이에요. 저는 회사원이에요. 반갑습니다!`

sections.title: Unit 2 — Unit 2: Classroom Korean & Everyday Objects (제2과: 교실 한국어와 사물)

modules.title: 2.1 — Classroom Survival: Asking the Teacher for Help (선생님, 질문 있어요!)

elements.text: **Situation & Objective.** Asking for clarification and instructions during Korean language class.

items.text: **Dialogue Practice:** Listen to and practice the dialogue between 선생님 and 학생 and 선생님 and 학생.
`책 15쪽을 펴세요. 다 읽으셨어요?` (Please open your books to page 15. Have you all read it?)
`선생님, 질문 있어요! 잘 모르겠어요.` (Teacher, I have a question! I don't understand well.) — *Note: 질문 있어요 (I have a question) + 잘 모르겠어요 (I don't know/understand well).*
`네, 어떤 단어를 모르겠어요?` (Yes, which word do you not understand?)
`천천히 다시 말씀해 주세요.` (Please say it again slowly.) — *Note: 천천히 (slowly) + 다시 (again) + 말씀해 주세요 (please speak honorifically).*

**Cultural Etiquette & Pragmatics:** When you do not understand something in class, saying "다시 말씀해 주세요" (Please say it again) is polite and expected. Saying just "뭐요?" is considered blunt and rude to an instructor.
**Core Target Words:** Memorise and pronounce all target words for this lesson:
`질문` (jil-mun, Hanja: 質問) [Noun]: Question — e.g., "질문이 있으면 손을 드세요." (*If you have a question, please raise your hand.*)
`책` (chaek, Hanja: 冊) [Noun]: Book — e.g., "책을 펴세요." (*Please open your book.*)
`천천히` (cheon-cheon-hi) [Adverb]: Slowly — e.g., "천천히 읽어 주세요." (*Please read slowly.*)
`다시` (da-si) [Adverb]: Again / once more — e.g., "다시 한번 들어 보세요." (*Please listen once more.*)
`공책` (gong-chaek, Hanja: 空冊) [Noun]: Notebook — e.g., "공책에 필기하세요." (*Please take notes in your notebook.*)
**Grammar Pattern: `Verb Stem + -(으)세요 (Polite Request)`** (Please do [Action] / Imperative Request)
Formula: `Consonant stem + 으세요 // Vowel stem + 세요`
Explanation: Used by teachers and elders to give polite directions or instructions. Common classroom verbs: 읽다 → 읽으세요 (please read), 보다 → 보세요 (please look).
Rule: 닫다 (to close) → 닫으세요.
Rule: 쓰다 (to write) → 쓰세요.
Rule: 듣다 (to listen - ㄷ irregular) → 들으세요.
Example: `책을 보세요.` — *Please look at the book.*
Example: `따라 읽으세요.` — *Please read along.*
**Shadowing & Repetition Drill:** Practice requesting help from the teacher clearly.
Prompt: "Request: Please speak slowly" → Speak aloud: `천천히 말씀해 주세요.` (*Please speak slowly.*)
Prompt: "Request: Please say it once more" → Speak aloud: `다시 한번 말씀해 주세요.` (*Please say it once again.*)
Prompt: "Statement: I have a question" → Speak aloud: `선생님, 질문 있어요!` (*Teacher, I have a question!*)
**Reading Passage:** "Classroom Instruction Board"
Text: `여러분, 교재를 펴세요. 오디오를 들으세요. 그리고 공책에 정답을 쓰세요. 질문이 있으면 손을 드세요.`
Translation: *Everyone, please open your textbooks. Listen to the audio. And write the correct answers in your notebook. If you have questions, please raise your hand.*
Check: Where should students write answers? → Answer: `공책에 (in notebook)` (*공책에 정답을 쓰세요.*)
Check: What should you do if you have a question? → Answer: `손을 들다 (raise hand)` (*손을 드세요.*)
**Guided Writing Task:** Write 3 polite requests you would say to your Korean teacher in class.
Sample Model Answer: `선생님, 질문 있어요. 천천히 말씀해 주세요. 감사합니다.`

modules.title: 2.2 — Asking What an Object Is: Demonstratives & Negation (이거, 그거, 저거와 사물 이름)

elements.text: **Situation & Objective.** Asking about unfamiliar items in a stationery shop or on a desk.

items.text: **Dialogue Practice:** Listen to and practice the dialogue between 지우 and 민호 and 지우 and 민호.
`민호 씨, 저게 뭐예요?` (Min-ho, what is that over there?) — *Note: 저것이 contracted to 저게 in natural speech.*
`저거요? 저거는 전자사전이에요.` (That over there? That is an electronic dictionary.)
`아, 스마트폰이 아니에요?` (Ah, is it not a smartphone?) — *Note: 아니에요 is the negative copula ("is not").*
`네, 스마트폰이 아니에요. 사전이에요.` (Yes, it is not a smartphone. It is a dictionary.)
**Cultural Etiquette & Pragmatics:** 이거 (this near speaker), 그거 (that near listener), 저거 (that over there far from both). When spoken casually, 이것/그것/저것 contracted to 이거/그거/저거.
**Core Target Words:** Memorise and pronounce all target words for this lesson:
`이거` (i-geo) [Noun]: This item (near speaker) — e.g., "이거 얼마예요?" (*How much is this?*)
`그거` (geu-geo) [Noun]: That item (near listener) — e.g., "그거 보여 주세요." (*Please show me that.*)
`저거` (jeo-geo) [Noun]: That item over there (far from both) — e.g., "저거 참 예쁘네요." (*That over there is really pretty.*)
`시계` (si-gye, Hanja: 時計) [Noun]: Clock / watch — e.g., "벽에 시계가 있어요." (*There is a clock on the wall.*)
`가방` (ga-bang) [Noun]: Bag / backpack — e.g., "가방이 아주 무거워요." (*The bag is very heavy.*)
`지갑` (ji-gap, Hanja: 紙匣) [Noun]: Wallet / purse — e.g., "지갑에 현금이 없어요." (*There is no cash in my wallet.*)
**Grammar Pattern: `Demonstratives: 이거 / 그거 / 저거`** (This / That (near you) / That (over there))
Formula: `이거 (near speaker) // 그거 (near listener) // 저거 (distant from both)`
Explanation: Refers to physical objects based on proximity to the speaker and listener. When attached to nouns as modifiers, use 이 [Noun], 그 [Noun], 저 [Noun] (e.g., 이 책, 그 가방, 저 건물).
Rule: 이것이 → 이게 (Subject).
Rule: 이것은 → 이건 (Topic).
Rule: 이것을 → 이걸 (Object).
Example: `이게 뭐예요? — 시계예요.` — *What is this? — It is a watch.*
Example: `그건 제 가방이에요.` — *That is my bag.*
Example: `저 시계가 비싸요.` — *That watch over there is expensive.*
**Grammar Pattern: `Noun Negation: Noun + 이/가 아니에요`** (Am not / Is not / Are not Noun)
Formula: `Consonant noun + 이 아니에요 // Vowel noun + 가 아니에요`
Explanation: The negative counterpart of 이에요/예요. Always requires the subject particle 이 or 가 attached to the preceding noun.
Rule: 학생 (consonant) + 이 아니에요 → 학생이 아니에요 (I am not a student).
Rule: 의사 (vowel) + 가 아니에요 → 의사가 아니에요 (I am not a doctor).
Example: `저는 일본 사람이 아니에요.` — *I am not Japanese.*
Example: `이건 제 지갑이 아니에요.` — *This is not my wallet.*
**Shadowing & Repetition Drill:** Ask what an object is and deny incorrect guesses.
Prompt: "Ask: What is this?" → Speak aloud: `이게 뭐예요?` (*What is this?*)
Prompt: "Answer: It is a wallet" → Speak aloud: `지갑이에요.` (*It is a wallet.*)
Prompt: "Deny: It is not a smartphone" → Speak aloud: `스마트폰이 아니에요.` (*It is not a smartphone.*)
**Reading Passage:** "Desk Inspection Note"
Text: `책상 위에 물건이 많아요. 이건 한국어 책이에요. 공책이 아니에요. 저건 제 스마트폰이에요. 지갑은 가방 안에 있어요.`
Translation: *There are many items on the desk. This is a Korean book. It is not a notebook. That over there is my smartphone. The wallet is inside the bag.*
Check: Is the item on the desk a notebook? → Answer: `No` (*공책이 아니에요 (It is not a notebook).*)
Check: Where is the wallet? → Answer: `가방 안에 (inside the bag)` (*가방 안에 있어요.*)
**Guided Writing Task:** Write 3 sentences identifying 3 objects on your desk and negating what they are not.
Sample Model Answer: `이건 제 노트북이에요. 태블릿이 아니에요. 저건 제 텀블러예요.`

sections.title: Unit 3 — Unit 3: People & Belongings (제3과: 사람과 물건 (소유))

modules.title: 3.1 — Asking About a Friend's Bag: Possession (의) (이 가방 누구 거예요?)

elements.text: **Situation & Objective.** Finding a lost bag in a study lounge and locating the owner.

items.text: **Dialogue Practice:** Listen to and practice the dialogue between 유진 and 민수 and 유진 and 민수.
`민수 씨, 이 검은색 가방 민수 씨 거예요?` (Min-su, is this black bag yours?) — *Note: 민수 씨 거예요? = Is it Min-su's?*
`아니요, 제 가방이 아니에요. 제 가방은 파란색이에요.` (No, it is not my bag. My bag is blue.) — *Note: 저의 (my) contracts to 제. 나 + 의 contracts to 내.*
`그럼 이 가방은 누구 거예요?` (Then whose bag is this?)
`마이클 씨의 가방이에요. 아까 찾고 있었어요.` (It is Michael's bag. He was looking for it earlier.)

**Cultural Etiquette & Pragmatics:** The possessive particle "의" is pronounced [에] in spoken conversational Korean (e.g. 민수의 is pronounced [민수에]). In everyday speech, "의 것" (thing of...) contracts to "거" (누구 거예요? = Whose is it?).
**Core Target Words:** Memorise and pronounce all target words for this lesson:
`누구` (nu-gu) [Noun]: Who / whose — e.g., "저 사람은 누구예요?" (*Who is that person over there?*)
`제` (je) [Noun]: My (polite, contracted from 저의) — e.g., "이건 제 책이에요." (*This is my book.*)
`내` (nae) [Noun]: My (casual, contracted from 나의) — e.g., "내 우산 어디 있어?" (*Where is my umbrella?*)
`우산` (u-san, Hanja: 雨傘) [Noun]: Umbrella — e.g., "비가 오니까 우산을 챙기세요." (*Since it is raining, take an umbrella.*)
`모자` (mo-ja, Hanja: 帽子) [Noun]: Hat / cap — e.g., "이 모자 정말 멋져요." (*This hat is really cool.*)
**Grammar Pattern: `Possessive Particle: Noun + 의`** ("Of" / Possessive 's)
Formula: `Noun + 의 (pronounced [에] in speech)`
Explanation: Attaches to a noun to show ownership. Common contractions: 저의 → 제 (my, polite), 나의 → 내 (my, casual), 너의 → 네 / 네 [pronounced 니] (your).
Rule: 선생님의 책 [선생니메 책] = Teacher's book.
Rule: 누구의 것 → 누구 거 = Whose item.
Rule: 제 우산 = My umbrella.
Example: `이건 제 친구의 가방이에요.` — *This is my friend's bag.*
Example: `누구 거역시요? — 제 거예요.` — *Whose is it? — It is mine.*
**Shadowing & Repetition Drill:** Practice claiming and identifying who items belong to.
Prompt: "Ask: Whose watch is this?" → Speak aloud: `이 시계 누구 거예요?` (*Whose watch is this?*)
Prompt: "Answer: It is my watch" → Speak aloud: `제 시계예요.` (*It is my watch.*)
Prompt: "State: It is Min-su's umbrella" → Speak aloud: `민수 씨 우산이에요.` (*It is Min-su's umbrella.*)
**Reading Passage:** "Lost & Found Notice"
Text: `휴게실에 검은색 가방이 있습니다. 이 가방은 선생님의 가방이 아닙니다. 마이클 씨의 가방입니다. 3층 교무실로 오세요.`
Translation: *There is a black bag in the lounge. This bag is not the teacher's bag. It is Michael's bag. Please come to the 3rd floor teachers' office.*
Check: Whose bag is it? → Answer: `마이클 씨 (Michael)` (*마이클 씨의 가방입니다.*)
Check: Where should he pick it up? → Answer: `3층 교무실 (3rd floor teachers' office)` (*3층 교무실로 오세요.*)
**Guided Writing Task:** Write 3 sentences describing 3 items you have and who they belong to.
Sample Model Answer: `이건 제 스마트폰이에요. 저건 제 룸메이트의 우산이에요. 이 열쇠는 누구 거예요?`

modules.title: 3.2 — Asking What Someone Has: 있어요 and 없어요 (펜 있어요? — 있어요와 없어요)

elements.text: **Situation & Objective.** Borrowing stationery and asking if a classmate has something.

items.text: **Dialogue Practice:** Listen to and practice the dialogue between 지민 and 유진 and 지민 and 유진.
`유진 씨, 혹시 파란색 펜 있어요?` (Yu-jin, by any chance do you have a blue pen?) — *Note: 혹시 (by any chance) + 펜 있어요? (Do you have a pen?)*
`네, 필통에 펜 있어요. 여기 있어요.` (Yes, I have a pen in my pencil case. Here it is.)
`지우개도 있어요?` (Do you have an eraser too?)
`아니요, 지우개는 없어요. 연필만 있어요.` (No, I don't have an eraser. I only have a pencil.) — *Note: 만 means "only", attached directly to the noun.*

**Cultural Etiquette & Pragmatics:** 있어요 means both "to exist / be located" AND "to possess / have".없어요 is its single negative counterpart ("does not exist" or "do not have"). Korean does not use "안 있어요".
**Core Target Words:** Memorise and pronounce all target words for this lesson:
`있다` (it-da) [Verb]: To have / to exist (polite: 있어요) — e.g., "저는 지금 시간이 있어요." (*I have time right now.*)
`없다` (eop-da) [Verb]: To not have / to not exist (polite: 없어요) — e.g., "지갑에 돈이 없어요." (*I have no money in my wallet.*)
`펜` (pen) [Noun]: Pen — e.g., "펜으로 이름을 쓰세요." (*Please write your name with a pen.*)
`지우개` (ji-u-gae) [Noun]: Eraser — e.g., "지우개로 글씨를 지웠어요." (*I erased the writing with an eraser.*)
`돈` (don) [Noun]: Money — e.g., "교통카드를 살 돈이 있어요." (*I have money to buy a transit card.*)
**Grammar Pattern: `Noun + 이/가 있어요 / 없어요 (Possession)`** (To have / To not have Noun)
Formula: `Consonant noun + 이 있어요 // Vowel noun + 가 있어요`
Explanation: Expresses possession. Notice that Korean puts the subject particle 이/가 on the item you have, unlike English where the item is a direct object.
Rule: 시간이 있어요 = I have time.
Rule: 친구가 없어요 = I don't have friends.
Rule: Never say "안 있어요" — the opposite of 있어요 is always 없어요.
Example: `우산이 있어요?` — *Do you have an umbrella?*
Example: `네, 있어요. / 아니요, 없어요.` — *Yes, I have it. / No, I don't.*
**Shadowing & Repetition Drill:** Ask and answer about items in your bag using 있어요 / 없어요.
Prompt: "Ask: Do you have money?" → Speak aloud: `돈이 있어요?` (*Do you have money?*)
Prompt: "Answer: No, I don't have money" → Speak aloud: `아니요, 돈이 없어요.` (*No, I don't have money.*)
Prompt: "Ask: Do you have time today?" → Speak aloud: `오늘 시간 있어요?` (*Do you have time today?*)
**Reading Passage:** "What is Inside Sarah's Backpack?"
Text: `제 가방 안에 책과 공책이 있어요. 필통도 있어요. 필통 안에 볼펜이 있어요. 하지만 지우개는 없어요. 스마트폰도 가방에 있어요.`

Translation: *Inside my bag there are books and notebooks. There is also a pencil case. Inside the pencil case there is a ballpoint pen. However, there is no eraser. My smartphone is also in the bag.*
Check: What is inside the pencil case? → Answer: `볼펜 (ballpoint pen)` (*필통 안에 볼펜이 있어요.*)
Check: Does Sarah have an eraser? → Answer: `No` (*지우개는 없어요.*)
**Guided Writing Task:** Write 4 sentences describing what you have and do not have in your bag right now.
Sample Model Answer: `제 가방에 지갑이 있어요. 이어폰도 있어요. 하지만 우산은 없어요. 현금도 없어요.`

modules.title: 4.1 — Finding an Object in a Room (방에서 물건 찾기)

elements.text: **Situation & Objective.** Describe the location of household and classroom objects using location marker 에 and 있어요/없어요.

items.text: **Dialogue Practice:** Listen to and practice the dialogue between Sarah (사라) and Minsu (민수) and Sarah (사라) and Minsu (민수) and Sarah (사라).
`민수 씨, 제 한국어 책이 어디에 있어요?` (Min-su, where is my Korean book?) — *Note: 어디에 = "at where" (어디 + 에 location marker).*
`책상 위에 있어요. 안경도 책상 위에 있어요.` (It is on the desk. The glasses are also on the desk.) — *Note: 책상 위 = desk top; 위 = above/on.*
`아, 찾았어요! 그러면 제 가방은 어디에 있어요?` (Ah, I found it! Then where is my bag?) — *Note: 그러면 = "then / in that case".*
`가방은 의자 밑에 있어요. 침대 옆이 아니에요.` (The bag is under the chair. It is not next to the bed.) — *Note: 밑 = under/below; 침대 옆 = next to the bed.*
`정말 고마워요, 민수 씨!` (Thank you so much, Min-su!) — *Note: Friendly polite expression of thanks.*

**Cultural Etiquette & Pragmatics:** In Korean homes and student dormitories (기숙사), asking where shared or personal study materials are located is everyday conversation. When indicating positions, Korean places the reference noun before the position noun: [Noun] + [위/밑/앞/뒤/옆] + 에 있어요 (e.g. 책상 위에 있어요, literally "desk top-at is").
**Core Target Words:** Memorise and pronounce all target words for this lesson:
`방` (bang, Hanja: 房) [Noun]: room — e.g., "제 방이 아주 따뜻해요." (*My room is very warm.*)
`책상` (chaeksang, Hanja: 冊床) [Noun]: desk — e.g., "책상 위에 컴퓨터가 있어요." (*There is a computer on the desk.*)
`의자` (uija, Hanja: 椅子) [Noun]: chair — e.g., "의자에 앉으세요." (*Please sit on the chair.*)
`침대` (chimdae, Hanja: 寢臺) [Noun]: bed — e.g., "침대 밑에 슬리퍼가 있어요." (*There are slippers under the bed.*)
`위` (wi) [Noun]: top / above / on — e.g., "탁자 위에 커피가 있어요." (*There is coffee on the table.*)
`밑 / 아래` (mit / arae) [Noun]: bottom / below / underneath — e.g., "의자 밑에 고양이가 있어요." (*There is a cat under the chair.*)
`어디` (eodi) [Noun]: where (interrogative pronoun) — e.g., "화장실이 어디예요?" (*Where is the restroom?*)
**Grammar Pattern: `Noun + 에 있어요/없어요`** (to exist / not exist in/at a place (Location marker 에))
Formula: `[Noun (Location)] + 에 + [Subject]이/가 + 있어요/없어요`
Explanation: The particle -에 marks static location where someone or something exists, sits, or remains. Contrast this with action location marker -에서 which marks where an action takes place.
Rule: Attach -에 directly to the place noun, regardless of whether it ends in a vowel or consonant: 방 + 에 -> 방에, 학교 + 에 -> 학교에.
Rule: Use 있어요 to state that the subject is present at that location.
Rule: Use 없어요 to state that the subject is absent from that location.
Contrast Note: Do not confuse location "에" (static existence with 있어요/없어요, 살아요, 있어요) with destination "에" (direction with 가요/와요).
Example: `선생님이 교실에 있어요.` — *The teacher is in the classroom.* [선생님 (teacher) + 이 (subject) + 교실 (classroom) + 에 (at) + 있어요 (is)]
Example: `민수 씨는 지금 집에 없어요.` — *Minsu is not at home right now.* [민수 씨는 (As for Minsu) + 지금 (now) + 집 (home) + 에 (at) + 없어요 (is not)]
**Grammar Pattern: `Noun + [위/밑/앞/뒤/옆/안/밖] + 에`** (on / under / in front of / behind / beside / inside / outside)
Formula: `[Reference Noun] + [Position Word] + 에`

Explanation: In Korean, positional words like 위 (top), 밑 (under), 앞 (front), 뒤 (back), 옆 (side), 안 (inside), and 밖 (outside) act as spatial nouns. You place the reference object first, followed by the spatial noun, followed by the location particle 에.
Rule: 책상 위 (desk top) + 에 = 책상 위에 (on the desk)
Rule: 의자 밑 (chair bottom) + 에 = 의자 밑에 (under the chair)
Rule: 가방 안 (bag inside) + 에 = 가방 안에 (inside the bag)
Example: `스마트폰이 가방 안에 있어요.` — *The smartphone is inside the bag.* [스마트폰 + 이 (subject) + 가방 (bag) + 안 (inside) + 에 (at) + 있어요]
Example: `고양이가 침대 밑에 있어요.` — *The cat is underneath the bed.* [고양이 (cat) + 가 (subject) + 침대 (bed) + 밑 (under) + 에 (at) + 있어요]
**Shadowing & Repetition Drill:** Listen carefully, repeat aloud, and substitute the nouns to describe where things are located.
Prompt: "Where is the book? (On the desk)" → Speak aloud: `책이 책상 위에 있어요.` (*The book is on the desk.*)
Prompt: "Where is the wallet? (Under the chair)" → Speak aloud: `지갑이 의자 밑에 있어요.` (*The wallet is under the chair.*)
Prompt: "Where is the pencil? (Inside the pencil case)" → Speak aloud: `연필이 필통 안에 있어요.` (*The pencil is inside the pencil case.*)
Prompt: "Is Min-su at home right now?" → Speak aloud: `아니요, 지금 집에 없어요.` (*No, he is not at home right now.*)
**Reading Passage:** "사라의 방 (Sarah's Room)"
Text: `여기는 제 방이에요. 제 방에 큰 책상이 있어요. 책상 위에 노트북과 한국어 사전이 있어요. 책상 옆에 편안한 의자가 있어요. 침대 위에는 베개와 이불이 있어요. 하지만 방에 텔레비전은 없어요.`

Translation: *This is my room. In my room, there is a big desk. On the desk, there is a laptop and a Korean dictionary. Beside the desk, there is a comfortable chair. On the bed, there are pillows and a blanket. However, there is no television in the room.*
Check: What is on Sarah's desk? → Answer: `노트북과 한국어 사전 (Laptop and Korean dictionary)` (*책상 위에 노트북과 한국어 사전이 있어요.*)
Check: Is there a television in Sarah's room? → Answer: `No` (*하지만 방에 텔레비전은 없어요.*)
**Guided Writing Task:** Describe your study room or bedroom in 5 Korean sentences using location words (위, 밑, 옆, 안) and 있어요/없어요.
Sample Model Answer: `여기는 제 방이에요. 방에 책상이 있어요. 책상 위에 컴퓨터가 있어요. 책상 옆에 침대가 있어요. 하지만 방에 텔레비전은 없어요.`

modules.title: 4.2 — Asking Where a Place or Building Is (카페가 어디예요?)

elements.text: **Situation & Objective.** Inquire about and give directions to facilities, stores, and buildings using 앞, 뒤, 옆, and 건너편.

items.text: **Dialogue Practice:** Listen to and practice the dialogue between David (데이비드) and Passerby (행인) and David (데이비드) and Passerby (행인) and David (데이비드).
`실례합니다, 여기 스타벅스 카페가 어디예요?` (Excuse me, where is the Starbucks cafe here?) — *Note: 실례합니다 = "Excuse me" (standard polite opener when asking a stranger).*
`저기 지하철역 출구 앞을 보세요. 은행이 있어요.` (Look in front of the subway station exit over there. There is a bank.) — *Note: 출구 = exit; 은행 = bank.*
`네, 국민은행이 보여요.` (Yes, I see the KB Kookmin Bank.) — *Note: 보여요 = "is visible / I see it".*
`카페는 은행 바로 옆에 있어요. 약국 뒤예요.` (The cafe is right next to the bank. It is behind the pharmacy.) — *Note: 바로 = "right / immediately"; 약국 = pharmacy.*
`아, 찾았습니다. 정말 감사합니다!` (Ah, I found it. Thank you very much!) — *Note: Formal polite acknowledgment and gratitude.*

**Cultural Etiquette & Pragmatics:** When asking strangers on the street for directions in Seoul, start with "실례합니다" (Excuse me). Koreans frequently use visible landmarks such as subway station exits (지하철역 출구), convenience stores (편의점), and banks (은행) as navigational anchors.
**Core Target Words:** Memorise and pronounce all target words for this lesson:
`카페` (kape) [Noun]: cafe / coffee shop — e.g., "카페에서 친구를 만나요." (*I meet a friend at the cafe.*)
`지하철역` (jihacheol-yeok, Hanja: 地下鐵驛) [Noun]: subway station — e.g., "강남역 2번 출구로 오세요." (*Please come to Gangnam Station Exit 2.*)
`은행` (eunhaeng, Hanja: 銀行) [Noun]: bank — e.g., "은행이 우체국 옆에 있어요." (*The bank is next to the post office.*)
`약국` (yakguk, Hanja: 藥局) [Noun]: pharmacy — e.g., "약국에서 감기약을 사요." (*I buy cold medicine at the pharmacy.*)
`앞` (ap) [Noun]: front — e.g., "학교 앞에서 만나요." (*Let us meet in front of the school.*)
`뒤` (dwi) [Noun]: back / behind — e.g., "건물 뒤에 주차장이 있어요." (*There is a parking lot behind the building.*)
`옆` (yeop) [Noun]: side / next to — e.g., "제 옆에 앉으세요." (*Please sit next to me.*)
`건너편 / 맞은편` (geonneopyeon / majeunpyeon) [Noun]: across the street / opposite side — e.g., "서점이 길 건너편에 있어요." (*The bookstore is across the street.*)
**Grammar Pattern: `Noun + 이/가 어디예요? / 어디에 있어요?`** (Where is [Noun]?)
Formula: `[Noun] + 이/가 어디예요? OR [Noun] + 은/는 어디에 있어요?`
Explanation: Both forms ask for location. "어디예요?" asks what/where the location identity is, while "어디에 있어요?" asks at what physical point the subject is located. Both are completely natural.
Rule: Noun ends in consonant: 화장실이 어디예요? / 화장실은 어디에 있어요?
Rule: Noun ends in vowel: 카페가 어디예요? / 카페는 어디에 있어요?
Example: `편의점이 어디예요?` — *Where is the convenience store?* [편의점 (convenience store) + 이 (subject) + 어디예요? (where is it?)]
Example: `지하철역은 어디에 있어요?` — *As for the subway station, where is it located?* [지하철역 (subway station) + 은 (topic) + 어디 (where) + 에 (at) + 있어요? (is it?)]
**Grammar Pattern: `Noun 1 + [앞/뒤/옆/사이/건너편] + 에 있어요`** (It is in front of / behind / next to / between / across from Noun 1)
Formula: `[Reference Building] + [Spatial Relation] + 에 있어요`
Explanation: Provides exact spatial orientation relative to a well-known building or landmark.
Rule: 건물 앞 = in front of the building -> 건물 앞에 있어요
Rule: 식당 뒤 = behind the restaurant -> 식당 뒤에 있어요
Rule: 은행과 우체국 사이 = between the bank and post office -> 은행과 우체국 사이에 있어요
Example: `약국이 병원 바로 옆에 있어요.` — *The pharmacy is right next to the hospital.* [약국 (pharmacy) + 이 (subject) + 병원 (hospital) + 바로 (right) + 옆 (side) + 에 있어요]
Example: `버스 정류장은 백화점 맞은편에 있어요.` — *The bus stop is across from the department store.* [버스 정류장 (bus stop) + 은 (topic) + 백화점 (dept store) + 맞은편 (opposite side) + 에 있어요]
**Shadowing & Repetition Drill:** Practice asking for everyday city landmarks and answering using spatial prepositions.
Prompt: "Ask where the subway station is." → Speak aloud: `실례합니다, 지하철역이 어디예요?` (*Excuse me, where is the subway station?*)
Prompt: "Answer: It is behind the school." → Speak aloud: `학교 뒤에 있어요.` (*It is behind the school.*)
Prompt: "Ask where the convenience store is." → Speak aloud: `편의점이 어디에 있어요?` (*Where is the convenience store?*)
Prompt: "Answer: It is right next to the bank." → Speak aloud: `은행 바로 옆에 있어요.` (*It is right next to the bank.*)
**Reading Passage:** "우리 동네 지도 (Our Neighborhood Map)"
Text: `우리 동네는 아주 살기 좋아요. 지하철역 1번 출구 앞에 편의점이 있어요. 편의점 건너편에 맛있는 빵집이 있어요. 빵집 옆에는 큰 병원이 있어요. 그리고 병원 뒤에 조용한 도서관이 있어요.`

Translation: *Our neighborhood is very pleasant to live in. There is a convenience store in front of subway station Exit 1. Across from the convenience store, there is a delicious bakery. Next to the bakery, there is a large hospital. And behind the hospital, there is a quiet library.*
Check: What is located across from the convenience store? → Answer: `빵집 (bakery)` (*편의점 건너편에 맛있는 빵집이 있어요.*)
Check: Where is the library located? → Answer: `병원 뒤 (behind the hospital)` (*병원 뒤에 조용한 도서관이 있어요.*)
**Guided Writing Task:** Write 5-6 sentences describing the buildings and landmarks around your home or school campus.
Sample Model Answer: `제 학교 근처에 많은 건물이 있어요. 정문 앞에 지하철역이 있어요. 지하철역 옆에 편의점이 있어요. 편의점 건너편에는 서점이 있어요. 학교 뒤에 아름다운 공원도 있어요.`

modules.title: 5.1 — Ordering a Drink at a Café (카페에서 음료 주문하기)

elements.text: **Situation & Objective.** Order drinks, request quantities with native numbers (하나, 둘, 셋) and counter 잔, and use 주세요 politely.

items.text: **Dialogue Practice:** Listen to and practice the dialogue between Barista (바리스타) and Sarah (사라) and Barista (바리스타) and Sarah (사라) and Barista (바리스타).
`어서 오세요! 주문하시겠어요?` (Welcome! Would you like to order?) — *Note: 주문하시겠어요? = Standard honorific polite greeting at food establishments.*
`네, 따뜻한 아메리카노 한 잔 주세요.` (Yes, please give me one warm Americano.) — *Note: 따뜻한 = warm/hot; 한 잔 = one cup.*
`더 필요하신 것은 없으세요?` (Is there anything else you need?) — *Note: Standard polite question checking for additional items.*
`그리고 치즈 케이크 하나 주세요. 포장해 주세요.` (And please give me one cheese cake. Please wrap it to go.) — *Note: 포장해 주세요 = "Please package it / to go".*
`네, 알겠습니다. 진동벨을 받으세요.` (Yes, understood. Please take the buzzer pager.) — *Note: 진동벨 = vibrating buzzer pager ubiquitous in Korean cafes.*

**Cultural Etiquette & Pragmatics:** In Korean cafes, the default iced drink is often abbreviated: "아아" (아이스 아메리카노).
