Translation: *Today Seoul's morning temperature is 3 degrees, which is very chilly. Therefore, people's clothing has become thicker. Today I wore a cozy ivory knit sweater. And I wore comfortable black slacks. When going outside, I put on a long beige trench coat and wore brown leather dress shoes. Around my neck, I wrapped a checkered scarf. It is a warm yet very stylish outfit.*
Check: What kind of shoes did the writer wear? → Answer: `갈색 가죽 구두 (Brown leather dress shoes)` (*갈색 가죽 구두를 신었습니다.*)
Check: What color knit sweater did the writer wear? → Answer: `아이보리색 (Ivory color)` (*포근한 아이보리색 니트를 입었습니다.*)
**Guided Writing Task:** Write 5-6 sentences describing what you are wearing today based on the weather, specifying the item, color, and corresponding wearing verb.
Sample Model Answer: `오늘 날씨는 조금 쌀쌀해요. 그래서 저는 흰색 셔츠와 파란색 스웨터를 입었어요. 그리고 편안한 검은색 바지를 입었어요. 신발은 하얀 운동화를 신었어요. 햇빛이 강해서 선글라스도 썼어요. 아주 편안한 옷차림이에요.`

sections.title: Unit 14 — Transport and Going Out (교통과 길 찾기)

modules.title: 14.1 — Asking How to Get Somewhere (어떻게 가요? 와 대중교통)

elements.text: **Situation & Objective.** Inquire about transit routes with 어떻게 and specify modes of transport (지하철, 버스, 택시) using -(으)로.

items.text: **Dialogue Practice:** Listen to and practice the dialogue between Sarah (사라) and Seoul Resident (시민) and Sarah (사라) and Seoul Resident (시민) and Sarah (사라).
`실례합니다, 서울역까지 어떻게 가요?` (Excuse me, how do I get to Seoul Station?) — *Note: 어떻게 가요? = "How do I get there?"; 까지 = "until / up to".*
`여기서 지하철 4호선으로 가세요. 가장 빨라요.` (Go by subway Line 4 from here. It is the fastest.) — *Note: 4호선으로 = by Line 4 (consonant + 으로); 가장 빨라요 = is the fastest.*
`시간이 얼마나 걸려요?` (How long does it take?) — *Note: 얼마나 걸려요? = "How long does it take?" (걸리다 = to take time).*
`이십 분 정도 걸려요. 환승 안 해도 돼요.` (It takes about twenty minutes. You don't even need to transfer.) — *Note: 정도 = "about / approximately"; 환승 = transit transfer.*
`친절하게 알려 주셔서 정말 감사합니다!` (Thank you very much for kindly letting me know!) — *Note: 알려 주셔서 감사합니다 = Polite gratitude for directions.*

**Cultural Etiquette & Pragmatics:** Seoul possesses one of the world's most punctual and comprehensive metropolitan transit systems (수도권 전철). Lines are designated by numbers and distinct colors (Line 1: Dark Blue, Line 2: Green Circle Line, Line 4: Sky Blue, etc.). Transferring (환승) between subway lines or buses within 30 minutes using a T-money card (교통카드) is free or heavily discounted.
**Core Target Words:** Memorise and pronounce all target words for this lesson:
`지하철 / 전철` (jihacheol / jeoncheol, Hanja: 地下鐵 / 電鐵) [Noun]: subway / metro train — e.g., "지하철 2호선을 타요." (*I take subway Line 2.*)
`시내버스 / 고속버스` (sinaebeoseu / gosokbeoseu) [Noun]: city bus / express highway bus — e.g., "정류장에서 시내버스를 기다려요." (*I wait for the city bus at the bus stop.*)
`택시 / 기차 (KTX)` (taeksi / gicha) [Noun]: taxi / bullet train (KTX) — e.g., "짐이 많아서 택시를 탔어요." (*I had lots of luggage, so I took a taxi.*)
`어떻게` (eotteoke) [Noun]: how (method / way) — e.g., "명동에 어떻게 가요?" (*How do I get to Myeongdong?*)
`얼마나 걸리다` (eolmana geollida) [Verb]: how long does it take (time) — e.g., "집에서 학교까지 삼십 분 걸려요." (*It takes thirty minutes from home to school.*)
`타다 / 내리다 / 갈아타다` (tada / naerida / garatada) [Verb]: to ride/take / to get off / to transfer — e.g., "시청역에서 1호선으로 갈아타세요." (*Please transfer to Line 1 at City Hall Station.*)
**Grammar Pattern: `Noun (Transport Method) + (으)로`** (by means of / by transport)
Formula: `Consonant (except ㄹ) + 으로 | Vowel or ㄹ + 로`
Explanation: Attach -(으)로 to vehicles and instruments to express the method of traveling.
Rule: Ends in consonant: 지하철 + 으로 = 지하철로 (note: ㄹ ends take 로 -> 지하철로)
Rule: Ends in vowel: 버스 + 로 = 버스로, 택시 + 로 = 택시로, 비행기 + 로 = 비행기로
Rule: By foot: 걸어서 가요 (special expression)
Example: `저는 매일 아침 버스로 통학해요.` — *I commute to school by bus every morning.* [버스 (bus) + 로 (by) + 통학해요 (commute to school)]
Example: `부산까지 KTX 기차로 두 시간 반 걸려요.` — *It takes two and a half hours to Busan by KTX train.* [KTX 기차 (train) + 로 (by) + 걸려요]
**Shadowing & Repetition Drill:** Formulate travel instructions specifying the exact transit vehicle and -(으)로.
Prompt: "Ask: How do I get to Incheon Airport?" → Speak aloud: `인천공항까지 어떻게 가요?` (*How do I get to Incheon Airport?*)
Prompt: "Answer: Go by airport railroad train." → Speak aloud: `공항철도로 가세요.` (*Go by airport railroad train.*)
Prompt: "Ask: How long does it take by taxi?" → Speak aloud: `택시로 시간이 얼마나 걸려요?` (*How long does it take by taxi?*)
Prompt: "Answer: It takes about 40 minutes." → Speak aloud: `사십 분 정도 걸려요.` (*It takes about 40 minutes.*)
**Reading Passage:** "서울 대중교통 이용 안내 (Seoul Transit Guide)"
Text: `서울에서는 지하철과 버스를 이용하면 아주 편리합니다. 교통카드를 태그하고 타면 요금이 할인되고, 다른 노선으로 갈아탈 때 무료 환승 혜택도 받을 수 있습니다. 강남역에서 명동역까지 갈 때는 지하철 2호선을 타고 사당역에서 4호선으로 갈아타면 약 35분이 걸립니다. 출퇴근 시간에는 지하철이 버스보다 훨씬 빠릅니다.`

Translation: *Using the subway and bus in Seoul is very convenient. If you tap and ride with a transit card, fares are discounted, and you can also receive free transfer benefits when changing to different lines. When traveling from Gangnam Station to Myeongdong Station, if you ride Line 2 and transfer to Line 4 at Sadang Station, it takes approximately 35 minutes. During rush hours, the subway is far faster than the bus.*
Check: At which station do you transfer when going from Gangnam to Myeongdong? → Answer: `사당역 (Sadang Station)` (*사당역에서 4호선으로 갈아타면*)
Check: Why is the subway better during rush hours? → Answer: `버스보다 훨씬 빨라요 (It is much faster than the bus)` (*출퇴근 시간에는 지하철이 버스보다 훨씬 빠릅니다.*)
**Guided Writing Task:** Write 5 sentences explaining how to get from your home to your school or workplace using transport modes, -(으)로, and duration expressions.
Sample Model Answer: `제 집에서 서울대학교까지 지하철로 가요. 먼저 합정역에서 지하철 2호선을 타요. 그리고 서울대입구역에서 내려요. 그곳에서 버스로 갈아타요. 전체 시간은 약 40분 정도 걸려요.`

modules.title: 14.2 — Finding Places in Town and Directions (길 찾기와 방향 안내)

elements.text: **Situation & Objective.** Guide pedestrians using directional particles -(으)로 and directional verbs (쭉 가세요, 오른쪽으로 도세요, 건너세요).

items.text: **Dialogue Practice:** Listen to and practice the dialogue between Tourist (관광객) and Local Guide (안내원) and Tourist (관광객) and Local Guide (안내원) and Tourist (관광객).
`실례합니다, 인사동 쌈지길이 어디예요?` (Excuse me, where is Insadong Ssamziegil?) — *Note: 쌈지길 = famous spiral handicraft mall in Insadong.*
`이 길로 똑바로 100미터쯤 쭉 가세요.` (Go straight along this street for about 100 meters.) — *Note: 이 길로 = along this road; 똑바로 / 쭉 = straight.*
`100미터 직진한 후에 어디로 가요?` (After going straight 100 meters, where do I go?) — *Note: 어디로 = toward where; 직진 = moving straight ahead.*

`사거리에서 오른쪽으로 도세요. 횡단보도를 건너면 바로 보여요.` (Turn right at the 4-way intersection. If you cross the pedestrian crosswalk, you will see it right away.) — *Note: 오른쪽으로 = to the right; 횡단보도 = crosswalk; 건너면 = if you cross.*
`자세히 설명해 주셔서 정말 감사합니다!` (Thank you so much for explaining in detail!) — *Note: 자세히 = in detail.*

**Cultural Etiquette & Pragmatics:** Giving directions in Korean uses clear spatial and directional commands ending in the polite imperative -(으)세요: "쭉 가세요" (go straight), "오른쪽으로 가세요" (go to the right), "왼쪽으로 도세요" (turn left), and "횡단보도를 건너세요" (cross the crosswalk).
**Core Target Words:** Memorise and pronounce all target words for this lesson:
`오른쪽 / 왼쪽 / 똑바로 (직진)` (oreunjjok / oenjjok / ttokbaro) [Noun]: right side / left side / straight — e.g., "사거리에서 왼쪽으로 가세요." (*Go to the left at the four-way intersection.*)
`사거리 / 삼거리` (sageori / samgeori, Hanja: 四거리 / 三거리) [Noun]: four-way intersection / three-way T-junction — e.g., "신호등 있는 사거리에서 멈추세요." (*Stop at the intersection with the traffic light.*)
`횡단보도 / 신호등` (hoengdanbodo / sinhodeung, Hanja: 橫斷步道 / 信號燈) [Noun]: pedestrian crosswalk / traffic light — e.g., "초록불에 횡단보도를 건너요." (*Cross the crosswalk on the green light.*)
`건너다 / 건너세요` (geonneoda / geonneoseyo) [Verb]: to cross -> please cross — e.g., "길을 조심히 건너세요." (*Please cross the street carefully.*)
`돌다 / 도세요` (dolda / doseyo) [Verb]: to turn -> please turn — e.g., "약국 모퉁이에서 우회전하세요 (오른쪽으로 도세요)." (*Turn right at the pharmacy corner.*)
**Grammar Pattern: `Direction Noun + (으)로 (Directional Marker: Towards)`** (towards / in the direction of)
Formula: `Consonant + 으로 | Vowel or ㄹ + 로`
Explanation: When attached to spatial words (오른쪽, 왼쪽, 위, 아래, 앞, 뒤), -(으)로 marks orientation or movement path.
Rule: 오른쪽 (consonant) + 으로 = 오른쪽으로 (to the right)
Rule: 왼쪽 (consonant) + 으로 = 왼쪽으로 (to the left)
Rule: 위 (vowel) + 로 = 위로 (upward)
Example: `다음 골목에서 왼쪽으로 도세요.` — *Please turn left at the next alley.* [다음 골목 (next alley) + 에서 + 왼쪽 (left) + 으로 (toward) + 도세요 (turn)]
**Shadowing & Repetition Drill:** Give clear walking directions using directional adverbs and -(으)로.
Prompt: "Instruct: Go straight ahead." → Speak aloud: `앞으로 똑바로 가세요.` (*Go straight ahead.*)
Prompt: "Instruct: Turn to the right at the bank." → Speak aloud: `은행에서 오른쪽으로 도세요.` (*Turn right at the bank.*)
Prompt: "Instruct: Turn to the left at the pharmacy." → Speak aloud: `약국에서 왼쪽으로 도세요.` (*Turn left at the pharmacy.*)
Prompt: "Instruct: Cross the crosswalk over there." → Speak aloud: `저기 횡단보도를 건너세요.` (*Cross the crosswalk over there.*)
**Reading Passage:** "우리 집 찾아오는 길 (Directions to My House)"
Text: `친구들을 제 생일 파티에 초대합니다. 우리 집 찾아오는 방법을 알려 드릴게요. 지하철 3호선 안국역 2번 출구로 나오세요. 나온 후에 편의점 쪽으로 50미터 직진하세요. 베이커리 빵집이 나오면 오른쪽 골목으로 도세요. 골목 안으로 30미터쯤 들어오면 1층에 꽃집이 있는 흰색 빌라 건물 302호입니다.`

Translation: *I invite my friends to my birthday party. Let me tell you how to find my house. Come out of Exit 2 of Anguk Station on Subway Line 3. After coming out, go straight for 50 meters toward the convenience store. When the bakery appears, turn into the right alley. If you walk in about 30 meters into the alley, it is Apartment 302 of the white villa building with a flower shop on the first floor.*
Check: Which subway station exit should guests use? → Answer: `안국역 2번 출구 (Anguk Station Exit 2)` (*지하철 3호선 안국역 2번 출구로 나오세요.*)
Check: What store is located on the first floor of the building? → Answer: `꽃집 (Flower shop)` (*1층에 꽃집이 있는 흰색 빌라 건물*)
**Guided Writing Task:** Write 5 sentences providing clear walking directions from a local subway station or bus stop to your home, favorite cafe, or classroom.
Sample Model Answer: `홍대입구역 9번 출구로 나오세요. 출구 앞에서 앞으로 100미터 똑바로 직진하세요. 올리브영 화장품 가게가 보이면 왼쪽으로 도세요. 횡단보도를 하나 건너세요. 건너편에 우리가 만날 카페가 바로 있어요.`

modules.title: 15.1 — Inviting a Friend and Future Plansㄹ 거예요) (친구 초대와 -(으)

elements.text: **Situation & Objective.** Formulate future commitments, intentions, and vacation plans using Verb Stem + -(으)ㄹ 거예요.

items.text: **Dialogue Practice:** Listen to and practice the dialogue between Min-su (민수) and Sarah (사라) and Min-su (민수) and Sarah (사라) and Min-su (민수).
`사라 씨, 이번 주말에 특별한 계획이 있어요?` (Sarah, do you have special plans this weekend?) — *Note: 특별한 계획 = special plans.*

`토요일에 한국인 튜터와 어학원에서 공부할 거예요. 일요일에는 계획 없어요.` (On Saturday I am going to study at the language academy with my Korean tutor. On Sunday I have no plans.) — *Note: 공부할 거예요 = 공부하다 + ㄹ 거예요 (future intention).*

`그러면 일요일에 같이 야구장에 갈래요? 재미있는 경기가 있을 거예요.` (In that case, would you like to go to the baseball stadium together on Sunday? There will be an interesting match.) — *Note: 야구장 = baseball stadium; 있을 거예요 = there will be.*
`와, 정말 신나요! 한국 야구 응원을 꼭 보고 싶었어요.` (Wow, that sounds so exciting! I really wanted to see Korean baseball cheering.) — *Note: 신나요 = exciting; 응원 = cheering/fan songs.*
`제가 티켓을 예매할게요. 잠실야구장에서 만나요!` (I will reserve the tickets. Let's meet at Jamsil Baseball Stadium!) — *Note: 예매할게요 = I will book/reserve.*

**Cultural Etiquette & Pragmatics:** Korean professional baseball (KBO) at venues like Jamsil Baseball Stadium (잠실야구장) is legendary for its participatory fan culture. Fans sing individual cheer songs for every batter, eat fried chicken and beer (치맥), and cheer rhythmically with thundersticks.
**Core Target Words:** Memorise and pronounce all target words for this lesson:
`계획` (gyehoek, Hanja: 計劃) [Noun]: plan / project — e.g., "미래 계획을 세워요." (*I make future plans.*)
`야구장 / 경기장` (yagujang / gyeonggijang, Hanja: 野球場 / 競技場) [Noun]: baseball stadium / sports stadium — e.g., "야구장에서 신나게 응원해요." (*We cheer excitedly at the baseball stadium.*)
`예매하다 / 예약하다` (yemaehada / yeyakhada, Hanja: 豫買 / 豫約) [Verb]: to purchase tickets in advance / to reserve — e.g., "영화표를 미리 예매했어요." (*I reserved the movie tickets in advance.*)
`내일 / 다음 주 / 내년` (naeil / daeumju / naenyeon, Hanja: 來日 / ── / 來年) [Noun]: tomorrow / next week / next year — e.g., "다음 주에 고향 친구가 와요." (*My hometown friend is coming next week.*)
**Grammar Pattern: `Verb Stem + -(으)ㄹ 거예요 (Future / Probable Tense)`** (will / am going to [do verb])
Formula: `Consonant ends (받침 O) + 을 거예요 | Vowel ends (받침 X) or ㄹ ends + ㄹ 거예요`
Explanation: Expresses future intention, planned action, or objective probability.
Rule: Stem ends in vowel: 가다 -> 가 + ㄹ 거예요 = 갈 거예요
Rule: Stem ends in consonant: 먹다 -> 먹 + 을 거예요 = 먹을 거예요
Rule: Stem ends in ㄹ: 살다 -> 살 거예요, 만들다 -> 만들 거예요
Rule: 하다 verbs: 하다 -> 할 거예요, 공부하다 -> 공부할 거예요
Example: `저는 주말에 친구들과 삼겹살을 먹을 거예요.` — *I am going to eat pork belly with friends on the weekend.* [먹 (eat) + 을 거예요 (will eat)]
Example: `내일은 날씨가 아주 맑을 거예요.` — *Tomorrow the weather will be very clear.* [맑 (clear) + 을 거예요 (will be)]
**Shadowing & Repetition Drill:** Conjugate each verb into the future tense -(으)ㄹ 거예요.
Prompt: "Conjugate: 만나다 (to meet) -> [I will meet Sarah tomorrow]." → Speak aloud: `내일 사라 씨를 만날 거예요.` (*I will meet Sarah tomorrow.*)
Prompt: "Conjugate: 읽다 (to read) -> [I will read a book tonight]." → Speak aloud: `오늘 밤에 책을 읽을 거예요.` (*I will read a book tonight.*)
Prompt: "Conjugate: 여행하다 (to travel) -> [I will travel to Busan next month]." → Speak aloud: `다음 달에 부산을 여행할 거예요.` (*I will travel to Busan next month.*)
Prompt: "Conjugate: 만들다 (to make) -> [I will make Korean food]." → Speak aloud: `한국 음식을 만들 거예요.` (*I will make Korean food.*)
**Reading Passage:** "사라의 여름방학 계획서 (Sarah's Summer Vacation Plan)"
Text: `이번 여름방학은 두 달 동안 아주 알차게 보낼 거예요. 첫 번째 달에는 서울대학교 어학당에서 2급 한국어 과정을 열심히 공부할 거예요. 한국어 말하기를 매일 연습할 거예요. 두 번째 달에는 친구들과 제주도와 경주로 일주일 동안 여행을 갈 거예요. 한국의 전통 유적지를 둘러보고 맛있는 지역 음식도 많이 먹을 거예요. 방학이 정말 기다려져요.`

Translation: *This summer vacation, I am going to spend two months very productively. In the first month, I will study the Level 2 Korean course diligently at the SNU Language Education Center. I will practice Korean speaking every day. In the second month, I will go on a one-week trip to Jeju Island and Gyeongju with friends. I will tour Korea's traditional historical sites and eat lots of delicious regional food. I am really looking forward to vacation.*
Check: What course will Sarah study in the first month? → Answer: `2급 한국어 과정 (Level 2 Korean course)` (*2급 한국어 과정을 열심히 공부할 거예요.*)
Check: Which cities will Sarah visit in the second month? → Answer: `제주도와 경주 (Jeju Island and Gyeongju)` (*친구들과 제주도와 경주로 일주일 동안 여행을 갈 거예요.*)
**Guided Writing Task:** Write a 6-sentence paragraph describing your goals and plans for next week or your next holiday using the future tense -(으)ㄹ 거예요.
Sample Model Answer: `저는 다음 주말에 많은 계획이 있어요. 먼저 토요일 아침에 밀린 청소와 빨래를 할 거예요. 오후에는 강남 서점에 갈 거예요. 서점에서 재미있는 한국어 소설을 살 거예요. 저녁에는 친구를 만나서 불고기를 먹을 거예요. 아주 보람찬 주말을 보낼 거예요.`

modules.title: 15.2 — Accepting and Declining Invitationsㄹ까요?) (초대 수락과 거절: -(으)

elements.text: **Situation & Objective.** Propose joint activities using -(으)ㄹ까요?, accept warmly, or politely decline with considerate excuses.

items.text: **Dialogue Practice:** Listen to and practice the dialogue between David (데이비드) and Yujin (유진) and David (데이비드) and Yujin (유진) and David (데이비드).
`유진 씨, 오늘 수업 끝나고 같이 커피 한잔할까요?` (Yu-jin, shall we have a cup of coffee together after class today?) — *Note: 커피 한잔할까요? = "Shall we have a cup of coffee together?"*
`정말 미안해요, 데이비드 씨. 오늘은 치과 예약이 있어요.` (I am really sorry, David. Today I have a dentist appointment.) — *Note: 치과 = dentist; 예약 = appointment.*
`아, 그렇군요! 그러면 내일은 어때요?` (Ah, I see! Then how about tomorrow?) — *Note: 내일은 어때요? = Polite alternative proposal.*
`내일은 좋아요! 내일 점심 같이 먹을까요?` (Tomorrow is good! Shall we eat lunch together tomorrow?) — *Note: 점심 같이 먹을까요? = "Shall we eat lunch together?"*
`네, 좋아요! 내일 열두 시에 학생회관 앞에서 봐요.` (Yes, sounds great! See you tomorrow at 12:00 in front of the Student Hall.) — *Note: 학생회관 = Student Center/Hall.*

**Cultural Etiquette & Pragmatics:** In Korean etiquette, declining an invitation directly with a flat "아니요" (No) can sound blunt or abrasive. Koreans soften refusals by opening with "미안해요" (I'm sorry) or "아쉽지만..." (It's regrettable, but...) followed by a clear reason ("선약이 있어요" - I have a prior engagement, or "시험공부를 해야 해요" - I must study for exams).
**Core Target Words:** Memorise and pronounce all target words for this lesson:
`미안해요 / 죄송해요` (mianhaeyo / joesonghaeyo, Hanja: 未安 / 罪悚) [Expression]: I am sorry (polite informal / formal polite) — e.g., "늦어서 정말 죄송합니다." (*I am truly sorry for being late.*)
`선약` (seonyak, Hanja: 先約) [Noun]: prior engagement / previous appointment — e.g., "그날은 선약이 있어서 곤란해요." (*I have a prior engagement that day, so it is difficult.*)
`좋아요 / 괜찮아요` (joayo / gwaenchanayo) [Expression]: Sounds good / That is fine — e.g., "네, 그 시간이면 괜찮아요." (*Yes, if it is that time, it is fine.*)
`다음에 / 나중에` (daeume / najung-e) [Noun]: next time / later on — e.g., "다음에 꼭 같이 가요." (*Let us definitely go together next time.*)
**Grammar Pattern: `Verb Stem + -(으)ㄹ까요? (Shall we...? / Shall I...?)`** (Shall we [do verb] together?)
Formula: `Consonant ends + 을까요? | Vowel ends + ㄹ까요?`
Explanation: Used to ask the listener's opinion or propose a shared activity.
Rule: Vowel ends: 가다 -> 갈까요? (Shall we go?), 보다 -> 볼까요? (Shall we watch?)
Rule: Consonant ends: 먹다 -> 먹을까요? (Shall we eat?), 앉다 -> 앉을까요? (Shall we sit?)
Rule: Accepting: 네, 좋아요! 같이 [아요/어요].
Rule: Declining: 미안해요, [이유]이/가 있어서 못 가요.
Example: `우리 오늘 저녁에 한식 먹을까요?` — *Shall we eat Korean food this evening?* [우리 (we) + 먹 (eat) + 을까요? (shall we eat?)]
**Shadowing & Repetition Drill:** Propose suggestions with -(으)ㄹ까요? and respond politely.
Prompt: "Suggest: Shall we drink coffee together?" → Speak aloud: `우리 같이 커피 마실까요?` (*Shall we drink coffee together?*)
Prompt: "Accept: Yes, sounds great! Let's go together." → Speak aloud: `네, 좋아요! 같이 가요.` (*Yes, sounds great! Let's go together.*)
Prompt: "Decline: I am sorry. I have an exam today." → Speak aloud: `미안해요. 오늘은 시험이 있어요.` (*I am sorry. Today I have an exam.*)
Prompt: "Suggest alternative: Then let's meet on Friday." → Speak aloud: `그러면 금요일에 만나요.` (*Then let's meet on Friday.*)
**Reading Passage:** "동아리 회식 초대장 (Club Dinner Invitation)"
Text: `한국어 회화 동아리 회원 여러분, 안녕하세요? 이번 주 금요일 저녁 6시에 신촌 고깃집에서 중간 모임을 가질 예정입니다. 맛있는 삼겹살을 먹으면서 한국어 연습도 하고 친목을 다질 예정입니다. 참석이 가능하신 분은 목요일까지 회장에게 카톡으로 알려 주세요. 혹시 선약이 있으신 분은 다음에 꼭 함께해요!`

Translation: *Hello members of the Korean Conversation Club! This Friday at 6 PM, we plan to hold a midterm gathering at a Sinchon barbecue restaurant. While eating delicious pork belly, we will practice Korean and build camaraderie. Those who can attend, please notify the president via KakaoTalk by Thursday. If anyone has prior plans, please be sure to join us next time!*
Check: When and where is the club gathering held? → Answer: `금요일 저녁 6시 신촌 고깃집 (Friday 6 PM at Sinchon BBQ)` (*이번 주 금요일 저녁 6시에 신촌 고깃집에서*)
Check: By when must members notify their attendance? → Answer: `목요일까지 (By Thursday)` (*참석이 가능하신 분은 목요일까지*)
**Guided Writing Task:** Write a realistic 5-line message declining an invitation from a classmate due to prior study commitments, and proposing an alternative time.
Sample Model Answer: `민수 씨, 저녁 식사에 초대해 줘서 고마워요. 하지만 금요일에는 한국어 말하기 시험공부가 있어서 갈 수 없어요. 정말 아쉽고 미안해요. 대신 시험이 끝나는 토요일 점심에 같이 먹을까요? 그때 제가 맛있는 커피 살게요!`

sections.title: Unit 16 — Everyday Communication and Integration (종합 의사소통과 정리)

modules.title: 16.1 — Explaining a Problem and Conversation Repair (대화 수리와 문제 설명)

elements.text: **Situation & Objective.** Keep conversations going when confused by asking native speakers to repeat, slow down, or explain words.

items.text: **Dialogue Practice:** Listen to and practice the dialogue between Sarah (사라) and Teacher (선생님) and Sarah (사라) and Teacher (선생님) and Sarah (사라).
`선생님, 죄송하지만 방금 하신 말씀을 다시 한번 말씀해 주시겠어요?` (Teacher, I am sorry, but could you please say what you just said once more?) — *Note: 다시 한번 = once more; 말씀해 주시겠어요 = respectful request.*
`네, 그럼요. 조금 더 천천히 말해 줄게요.` (Yes, of course. I will speak a little more slowly for you.) — *Note: 천천히 = slowly.*
`감사합니다. 그런데 그 단어의 뜻을 잘 모르겠어요. 설명해 주세요.` (Thank you. But I don't know the meaning of that word well. Please explain it.) — *Note: 모르겠어요 = I don't know; 뜻 = meaning; 설명해 주세요 = please explain.*
`이 단어는 쉬운 말로 "약속"이라는 뜻이에요.` (This word means "appointment / promise" in simple words.) — *Note: 쉬운 말로 = in simple words.*
`아, 이제 이해했어요! 정말 감사합니다.` (Ah, I understand now! Thank you so much.) — *Note: 이제 이해했어요 = "Now I understood".*

**Cultural Etiquette & Pragmatics:** Never remain silent when you don't understand something in Korea! Native speakers deeply appreciate proactive communication repair. Essential conversational survival phrases include: "천천히 말해 주세요" (Please speak slowly), "다시 한번 말해 주세요" (Please say it once again), and "한국어로 어떻게 말해요?" (How do you say this in Korean?).
**Core Target Words:** Memorise and pronounce all target words for this lesson:
`다시 / 또` (dasi / tto) [Adverb]: again / once more — e.g., "다시 말씀해 주세요." (*Please speak once again.*)
`천천히` (cheoncheonhi) [Adverb]: slowly — e.g., "조금만 천천히 말씀해 주시겠어요?" (*Could you please speak just a little more slowly?*)
`모르다 / 모르겠어요` (moreuda / moreugesseoyo) [Verb]: to not know -> I don't know — e.g., "이 단어 뜻을 잘 모르겠어요." (*I don't know the meaning of this word well.*)
`알다 / 알겠어요 / 이해했어요` (alda / algesseoyo / ihaehaesseoyo) [Verb]: to know -> Understood / I got it — e.g., "네, 무슨 뜻인지 잘 알겠어요." (*Yes, I understand well what it means.*)
`도와주세요` (dowajuseyo) [Expression]: please help me — e.g., "길을 잃었어요. 좀 도와주세요." (*I lost my way. Please help me a little.*)
**Grammar Pattern: `다시 말해 주세요 / 천천히 말해 주세요 / 써 주세요`** (Please repeat / Please speak slowly / Please write it down)
Formula: `[Verb Stem + 아/어] + 주세요`
Explanation: Using the polite request form -아/어 주세요 with conversational repair verbs.
Rule: 말하다 -> 말해 주세요 (Please speak)
Rule: 천천히 말해 주세요 (Please speak slowly)
Rule: 다시 한번 말해 주세요 (Please say it once again)
Rule: 종이에 써 주세요 (Please write it down on paper)
Example: `죄송하지만 한국어로 다시 말씀해 주세요.` — *I am sorry, but please say it again in Korean.* [한국어 (Korean language) + 로 (in) + 다시 (again) + 말씀해 주세요]
**Shadowing & Repetition Drill:** Practice delivering emergency comprehension phrases clearly and politely.
Prompt: "Request: Please speak slowly." → Speak aloud: `천천히 말해 주세요.` (*Please speak slowly.*)
Prompt: "Request: Please say it once more." → Speak aloud: `다시 한번 말해 주세요.` (*Please say it once more.*)
Prompt: "State: I don't know well. Please help me." → Speak aloud: `잘 모르겠어요. 도와주세요.` (*I don't know well. Please help me.*)
Prompt: "Ask: How do you say this in Korean?" → Speak aloud: `이거 한국어로 어떻게 말해요?` (*How do you say this in Korean?*)
**Reading Passage:** "외국인 유학생을 위한 생생 한국어 팁 (Live Korean Tips for Foreign Students)"
Text: `한국어를 배울 때 모르는 단어가 나오거나 상대방의 말이 너무 빠르면 당황하지 마세요. 한국 사람들은 외국인이 한국어로 노력하는 모습을 매우 좋아합니다. "천천히 말씀해 주세요" 또는 "다시 한번 말씀해 주시겠어요?"라고 정중하게 부탁하면 누구나 친절하게 다시 설명해 줍니다. 모르는 것을 두려워하지 말고 적극적으로 질문하세요!`

Translation: *When learning Korean, if unfamiliar words appear or the other person speaks too fast, do not panic. Korean people love seeing foreigners make an effort in Korean. If you politely request "Please speak slowly" or "Could you please say it once more?", anyone will kindly explain again. Do not fear not knowing, and ask questions actively!*
Check: What should you say when someone speaks too fast in Korean? → Answer: `천천히 말씀해 주세요 (Please speak slowly)` (*"천천히 말씀해 주세요"라고 정중하게 부탁하면*)
Check: How do Korean people feel when foreigners try speaking Korean? → Answer: `매우 좋아해요 (They like it very much)` (*한국 사람들은 외국인이 한국어로 노력하는 모습을 매우 좋아합니다.*)
**Guided Writing Task:** Write 4 sentences explaining what you do when you cannot understand Korean words in class or on the street.
Sample Model Answer: `저는 한국어 수업에서 모르는 단어가 있으면 손을 들어요. 선생님께 "선생님, 다시 한번 천천히 말씀해 주세요"라고 부탁해요. 그리고 한국어 사전을 찾아서 뜻을 확인해요. 새로운 단어를 단어장에 꼭 적고 매일 복습해요.`

modules.title: 16.2 — Putting Your Day Together: Capstone Narrative (나의 하루 종합 이야기)

elements.text: **Situation & Objective.** Synthesize Level 1 vocabulary, particles (은/는, 이/가, 을/를, 에, 에서, 의, (으)로), present, past, and future into a connected life story.

items.text: **Dialogue Practice:** Listen to and practice the dialogue between Interviewer (면접관) and Sarah (사라) and Interviewer (면접관) and Sarah (사라) and Interviewer (면접관).
`사라 씨, 1급 과정을 마친 소감이 어때요? 자신에 대해 소개해 보세요.` (Sarah, how do you feel finishing the Level 1 course? Please introduce yourself.) — *Note: 소감 = feelings/impressions; 소개해 보세요 = please introduce.*
`처음에는 한글도 몰랐지만 지금은 한국어로 인사하고 식당에서 주문할 수 있어요.` (At first I didn't even know Hangul, but now I can greet in Korean and order food at restaurants.) — *Note: 주문할 수 있어요 = can order.*
`한국 생활은 어때요? 어제와 주말에는 무엇을 했어요?` (How is life in Korea? What did you do yesterday and over the weekend?) — *Note: Comprehensive interview question testing past tense narrative.*

`어제는 도서관에서 시험공부를 했고, 지난 주말에는 친구들과 경복궁에 가서 사진을 찍었어요. 내일은 동아리 친구들과 삼겹살을 먹을 거예요!` (Yesterday I studied for exams at the library, and last weekend I went to Gyeongbokgung with friends and took photos. Tomorrow I will eat pork belly with club friends!) — *Note: Integrated use of past, present, and future.*
`정말 훌륭합니다! 1급 과정을 완벽하게 수료하셨습니다. 축하합니다!` (Truly outstanding! You have completely passed the Level 1 course. Congratulations!) — *Note: 수료하셨습니다 = You have graduated/completed the course.*

**Cultural Etiquette & Pragmatics:** Graduating Level 1 signifies full survival competence (A1 proficiency): you can navigate Seoul independently, shop, order food, commute across lines, discuss past events, make appointments, and form authentic personal friendships.
**Core Target Words:** Memorise and pronounce all target words for this lesson:
`수료 / 졸업` (suryo / joreop, Hanja: 修了 / 卒業) [Noun]: course completion / graduation — e.g., "한국어 1급 과정을 성공적으로 수료했어요." (*I successfully completed the Level 1 Korean course.*)
`자신감` (jasin-gam, Hanja: 自信感) [Noun]: confidence — e.g., "한국어 말하기에 자신감이 생겼어요." (*I developed confidence in Korean speaking.*)
`축하합니다 / 축하해요` (chukahamnida / chukahaeyo, Hanja: 祝賀) [Expression]: congratulations! — e.g., "1급 완주를 진심으로 축하합니다!" (*Warmest congratulations on finishing Level 1!*)
**Grammar Pattern: `Integrated Level 1 Particle & Tense Matrix`** (Complete mastery of Present, Past, and Future with all 8 core particles)
Formula: `Present (아요/어요) + Past (았/었어요) + Future ((으)ㄹ 거예요)`
Explanation: The ultimate synthesis of beginner Korean communication.
Rule: Topic/Focus: 은/는
Rule: Subject identifier: 이/가
Rule: Direct object: 을/를
Rule: Static location / Time / Destination: 에
Rule: Dynamic action place: 에서
Rule: Possession: 의
Rule: Method/Direction: (으)로
Rule: Connector: 하고 / 와 / 과 / 그리고 / 하지만

Example: `저는 어제 도서관에서 책을 읽었어요. 그리고 내일은 공원에 갈 거예요.` — *I read books at the library yesterday. And tomorrow I am going to go to the park.* [Integrates past, connectors, location markers, and future intention.]
**Shadowing & Repetition Drill:** Deliver full connected sentences transitioning effortlessly across present, past, and future.
Prompt: "Introduce yourself: I am Sarah, American, and studying Korean." → Speak aloud: `저는 사라예요. 미국 사람이고 한국어를 열심히 공부해요.` (*I am Sarah. I am American and studying Korean diligently.*)
Prompt: "State past: Yesterday I went to Hongdae and bought clothes." → Speak aloud: `어제 홍대에 가서 옷을 샀어요.` (*Yesterday I went to Hongdae and bought clothes.*)
Prompt: "State future: Tomorrow I will go to Busan by KTX train." → Speak aloud: `내일은 KTX 기차로 부산에 갈 거예요.` (*Tomorrow I will go to Busan by KTX train.*)
Prompt: "Express wish: I want to speak Korean very fluently." → Speak aloud: `한국어를 정말 유창하게 잘하고 싶어요.` (*I want to speak Korean very fluently.*)
**Reading Passage:** "나의 한국어 성장 일기: 1급을 마치며 (My Korean Growth Diary: Finishing Level 1)"

Text: `처음 서울에 왔을 때 저는 한국어를 한마디도 할 수 없었습니다. 하지만 1급 16개 단원을 매일 꾸준히 공부하면서 모든 것이 달라졌습니다. 이제는 혼자서 카페에 가서 아메리카노를 주문하고, 식당에서 좋아하는 찌개를 시킵니다. 지하철 노선도를 보고 원하는 역으로 쉽게 갈 수 있습니다. 어제는 한국인 친구에게 카카오톡 메시지를 한글로 직접 보냈습니다. 다음 2급 과정에서도 포기하지 않고 더욱 열심히 공부할 것입니다!`

Translation: *When I first came to Seoul, I could not speak a single word of Korean. However, as I studied the 16 units of Level 1 diligently every day, everything changed. Now, I go to cafes alone and order Americanos, and order my favorite stews at restaurants. Looking at the subway map, I can easily go to my desired station. Yesterday, I directly sent a KakaoTalk message in Hangul to a Korean friend. In the upcoming Level 2 course, I will not give up and will study even harder!*
Check: What can the writer do alone now at cafes? → Answer: `아메리카노를 주문해요 (Order an Americano)` (*혼자서 카페에 가서 아메리카노를 주문하고*)
Check: What did the writer do yesterday with a Korean friend? → Answer: `한글로 카카오톡 메시지를 보냈어요 (Sent a KakaoTalk message in Hangul)` (*어제는 한국인 친구에게 카카오톡 메시지를 한글로 직접 보냈습니다.*)

**Guided Writing Task:** Write a comprehensive 10-sentence self-introduction and life essay combining your name, nationality, routine, what you did last weekend, and what you will do next week in Korean.

Sample Model Answer: `안녕하세요? 제 이름은 데이비드입니다. 저는 캐나다 사람이고 서울대학교 어학당 학생입니다. 저는 매일 아침 일곱 시 반에 일어나요. 낮에는 어학당 교실에서 한국어를 열심히 공부해요. 제 취미는 음악 감상과 축구예요. 어제는 홍대에서 친구와 함께 쇼핑을 했어요. 따뜻한 김치찌개도 아주 맛있게 먹었어요. 다음 주말에는 KTX 기차를 타고 부산에 갈 거예요. 그곳에서 푸른 바다를 보고 맛있는 해산물을 먹고 싶어요. 만나서 정말 반갑습니다!`

elements.text: **Objective.** Consolidate all 16 units of Level 1 into an end-to-end spoken simulation portfolio and a 12-sentence connected Korean life essay.

items.text: **Checkpoint A Passed:** Read Hangul accurately, introduce name/country/job, and ask about objects.
**Checkpoint B Passed:** Order drinks and meals, ask prices with Sino-Korean Won numbers, and describe room/family.
**Checkpoint C Passed:** Recount past events with 았/었어요, schedule appointments with time/day particles, and state hobbies.
**Checkpoint D Passed:** Conduct full exit interview with directions, future plans -(으)ㄹ 거예요, and conversation repair.

questions.question: Q: What is the fundamental difference between the topic particle 은/는 and the subject particle 이/가?
A: 은/는 sets the topic or contrastive focus of the sentence, whereas 이/가 identifies the specific grammatical subject.
Q: When do you use Native Korean numbers vs Sino-Korean numbers?
A: Native numbers are used for counting items/people and clock hours (시). Sino-Korean numbers are used for money (원), minutes (분), dates (년/월/일), and phone numbers.
Q: You enter a cafe in Seoul and want two iced Americanos and one slice of cheesecake to go. What do you say?
A: "아이스 아메리카노 두 잔하고 치즈케이크 하나 포장해 주세요."

assessment.title: Checkpoint D — Checkpoint D: Integrated Final Assessment (Level 1 Comprehensive Exit Exam)

items.text: **Scenario:** Official SNU Level 1 Oral Proficiency Interview with a native examiner.
**Prompt:** Deliver a comprehensive 2-minute spoken introduction covering: name & background, daily schedule, yesterday's outing, directions to your favorite place, and future plans.

Deliver unprompted: `안녕하세요? 저는 캐나다에서 온 데이비드라고 합니다. 서울대학교 어학당에서 한국어를 공부하고 있습니다. 저는 보통 아침 일곱 시 반에 일어나서 학교에 갑니다. 어제는 수업이 끝난 후에 명동에 가서 쇼핑을 했습니다. 지하철 4호선으로 갔는데 약 이십 분 걸렸습니다. 옷 한 벌과 신발 한 켤레를 샀습니다. 내일은 동아리 친구들과 잠실야구장에 갈 거예요. 한국어로 대화하는 것이 정말 즐겁고, 앞으로 2급에서도 열심히 공부할 것입니다. 감사합니다!` (*Hello? I am called David from Canada. I am studying Korean at the SNU Language Education Center. I usually wake up at 7:30 AM and go to school. Yesterday after class finished, I went to Myeongdong and shopped. I went by subway Line 4 and it took about twenty minutes. I bought one outfit and one pair of shoes. Tomorrow I am going to go to Jamsil Baseball Stadium with club friends. Conversing in Korean is truly enjoyable, and I will continue studying hard in Level 2. Thank you!*)
**Prompt:** Write a comprehensive 12-sentence final graduation essay summarizing your life in Korea, routine, past memories, favorite places, and future ambitions. (100–140 Korean words)

Submit written draft: `안녕하세요? 제 이름은 사라입니다. 저는 미국에서 왔고 서울에 살고 있습니다. 한국에 처음 왔을 때는 한글을 읽을 수 없었습니다. 하지만 지금은 한국어로 인사하고 식당에서 맛있는 음식을 주문할 수 있습니다. 저는 아침마다 학교에 가고 도서관에서 친구들과 열심히 공부합니다. 지난 주말에는 부산 해운대에 다녀왔습니다. KTX 기차로 두 시간 반 걸렸습니다. 바다가 정말 아름다웠고 해산물도 맛있게 먹었습니다. 다음 방학에는 제주도에 꼭 여행 가고 싶습니다. 한국어 공부는 아주 흥미롭고 재미있습니다. 1급을 무사히 마치게 되어 매우 기쁩니다.`

levels.title: THE GRAMMAR ENGINE I
levels.goal: Stop memorising sentences and start generating them. By the end you can conjugate any regular verb into any of three tenses, negate four ways, and place every core particle correctly.

dashboard.core tools: Anki, recorder, tutor weekly, *Korean Grammar in Use – Beginning*
dashboard.final outcome: 200 verbs conjugated correctly across tense, negation, and modality, with no reference.

sections.title: The verb: dictionary form, stem, and classes

items.text: Dictionary form ends in **-다**: 가다, 먹다, 하다.
The **stem** is the dictionary form minus 다: 가, 먹, 하.
All endings attach to the stem. The dictionary form is a citation form, never used in speech except in writing and in the plain-style declarative.

rows: conjugate like verbs but do not take imperatives or progressives
irregular in form, not in meaning
behave like verbs, but 있다 as "have" takes 이/가

elements.text: **The trap:** Korean adjectives are verbs. `예뻐요` is a complete sentence — *she is pretty*. There is no "to be" inserted. English speakers add one for months.
**Module completion gate (2.1).** You classify 30 given verbs into action/descriptive, and write the stem of each.

modules.title: The ㅡ and ㄷ families (handled fully in 2.8)

items.text: 쓰다 → 써요, 크다 → 커요, 바쁘다 → 바빠요.
듣다 → 들어요, 걷다 → 걸어요.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (2.2).** Twenty-five verbs conjugated to the polite present in under three minutes, out loud, with 90% accuracy.
`stem + 았/었 + 어요`, with the same vowel test as the present.

items.text: `추워요` (it is cold) → `추웠어요` (it was cold).
`맛있어요` → `맛있었어요`.
Past adjectives are how you describe a completed experience: `정말 재미있었어요` — *it was really fun*.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (2.3).** Narrate yesterday in ten connected past-tense sentences, spoken, with no more than two errors.

items.text: Consonant stem → -을 거예요; vowel stem → -ㄹ 거예요.
먹다 → 먹을 거예요 · 가다 → 갈 거예요 · 하다 → 할 거예요.
Past form: -ㄹ 거였어요 = *was going to*.
`제가 할게요` — *I'll do it* (because you asked, or as a promise).
It only appears in the first person, and it is about the listener's expectation.

elements.text: **The distinction in one line:** `할 거예요` = my plan; `하겠습니다` = my determination, formally; `할게요` = my promise to you.
**Module completion gate (2.4).** Describe next weekend in eight sentences, using all three futures at least once each, without slipping into the present.

rows: I can't eat (allergy, no time, unavailable)

items.text: This distinction is not optional. Using 안 when you mean 못 sounds like stubbornness.
안 and 못 go immediately before the verb, never before the object: `밥을 안 먹어요` ✓, `안 밥을 먹어요` ✗.
With 하다 verbs, the 안 goes before 하다: `공부 안 해요`.
Past negation is formed on the tense: 안 갔어요, 못 갔어요, 가지 않았어요, 가지 못했어요.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (2.5).** Twenty sentences negated both ways, with 안/못 chosen correctly and the placement never wrong.

items.text: After a consonant 을, after a vowel 를.
Only transitive verbs take it.
Memorise verbs with their frame: `밥을 먹다`, not `먹다`.
Marks what the sentence is *about*, and often contrasts.
`저는 학생이에요` — *as for me, I'm a student*.
It can replace 이/가 or 을/를 in the same slot: `밥은 먹어요` — *as for rice, I do eat it*.
Marks the doer or the bearer of a state, and signals *this is the answer to the question*.
`누가 왔어요?` → `민수 씨가 왔어요.` (not 는)
`비가 와요` — new information, no contrast.

elements.text: **Do not try to master this at L2.** Learn the five situations above, and let the rest come from exposure between L2 and L7. Fluency in 은/는 vs 이/가 is a late-stage skill, and no amount of rule-reading replaces hearing 1,000 examples.
**Module completion gate (2.6).** You choose the correct particle in 20 out of 25 given sentences and can explain the choice in the five-situation table.

rows: 세 시에 · 학교에 가요 · 집에 있어요

items.text: **에 vs 에서.** Movement toward or existence at a place → 에. An action performed there → 에서.
**만 vs 밖에.** Both mean "only", but 밖에 always requires a negative verb: `물밖에 없어요`.
**하고 vs 와/과.** Same meaning; 하고 is spoken and can be used with any noun, 와/과 is written and more formal.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (2.7).** 25 sentences with particles blanked out, 22+ correct, with the reason stated for each.

items.text: **Exceptions (regular):** 입다 → 입어요, 잡다 → 잡아요, 좁다 → 좁아요, 씹다 → 씹어요.
**Exceptions:** 받다 → 받아요, 닫다 → 닫아요, 믿다 → 믿어요.
**Exceptions:** 웃다 → 웃어요, 벗다 → 벗어요.
**Exception:** 따르다 → 따라요.
Rule: if the preceding syllable has ㅏ/ㅗ, take -아요; otherwise -어요.
ㄹ drops before ㄴ, ㅂ, ㅅ endings: 살다 → 사세요 (not 살으세요), 알다 → 아는 (not 알는), 만들다 → 만드세요.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (2.8).** Thirty irregular verbs conjugated across present, past, and future at 90% accuracy, with the ㅂ and ㄷ exceptions named from memory.

items.text: `-(으)ㄹ 수 있다` — there is a way: 할 수 있어요.
`-(으)ㄹ 수 없다` — there is no way.
`못` — I personally cannot, right now.
Produce all four from any verb without hesitation. This grid is one of the highest-frequency things an intermediate speaker does.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (2.9).** The four-way grid produced for ten verbs, spoken, in under three minutes.

items.text: Add -시- to the stem when the *subject* is respected: 가다 → 가세요, 하다 → 하세요, 먹다 → 드세요.
`선생님이 오세요` — the teacher comes. `친구가 와요` — a friend comes.
이/가 → **께서**: `선생님께서 오세요`.
에게 → **께**: `선생님께 드렸어요`.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (2.10).** You convert ten plain sentences into honorific ones, changing the verb, the particle, and the vocabulary where required.

sections.title: Level 2 assessment
sections.objective: **Level 2 completion rule.** You must be able to conjugate a *new* verb you have never seen, correctly, from first principles. If you pass the test by memory of the 200 verbs in the bank, you have learned a list, not a system.

elements.text: **Objective.** A verified system, not a list.

items.text: **The verb bank.** 200 verbs, each with stem, class, and present/past/future forms.

**The production log.** 100 original sentences using the level's patterns, each recorded.
**The error ledger.** Every conjugation error, with the family it belongs to.

levels.title: THE GRAMMAR ENGINE II
levels.goal: Connect clauses into discourse, handle all the irregulars fluently, use honorifics in the full system, and tell a three-minute story about your own life that a native speaker would call fluent.

dashboard.core tools: Anki, recorder, weekly tutor, graded readers from L3 onward
dashboard.final outcome: Clause linking, all six irregulars automatic, honorifics in full use, and a spoken narrative that holds together.

sections.title: Clause linking I: and, but, so

items.text: Attaches to the stem with no tense: 먹**고**, 가**고**, 하**고**.
Tense appears only on the final verb: `밥을 먹고 학교에 갔어요`.
It sequences, it does not cause. `비가 오고 추워요` — it rains and (also) it's cold.
`비싸지만 좋아요` — it's expensive but I like it.
Can attach to past stems: `갔지만`.
The most versatile connector in the language, and the last one learners acquire.
Background: `지금 바쁜데요…` — *I'm busy right now (so…)*
Contrast: `한국어는 어려운데 재미있어요`.
Softening a request: `죄송한데요, 다시 말씀해 주시겠어요?`
Conjugation: verb stem + 는데; descriptive stem + -(으)ㄴ데; past + -았/었는데.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (3.1).** Twenty linked sentences using -고, -지만, -는데 correctly, with the tense only on the final verb.

sections.title: Reason and cause: the three-way distinction

rows: **cannot** be followed by an imperative or a proposal
reason the listener should accept; discovery
can be followed by imperatives and suggestions

items.text: `비가 와서 못 갔어요` ✓ (statement)
`비가 오니까 우산을 가져가세요` ✓ (imperative — only 니까 works)
`비가 와서 우산을 가져가세요` ✗ (grammatically wrong)
Second use of -니까: discovery. `가 보니까 사람이 없었어요` — *I went and found nobody there.*

elements.text: **Module completion gate (3.2).** You choose correctly between 서 and 니까 in 15 sentences, and you can state the imperative restriction without notes.

items.text: -아/어 보다 — try: 먹어 봤어요 (I've tried it).
-고 싶다 — want: 가고 싶어요.
-고 싶어하다 — third person: 그 사람은 가고 싶어해요. You cannot use 싶다 about someone else's inner state.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (3.3).** Ten purpose sentences, ten intention sentences, and the third-person rule produced correctly.

items.text: Time clauses take tense only where the time reference differs from the main clause: `비가 왔을 때 집에 있었어요` (it rained, I was home — both past).
`-면` takes no tense at all: 비가 오면, never 비가 왔으면 (that would be counterfactual, a different pattern at L10).

elements.text: **Module completion gate (3.4).** A six-sentence narrative using at least five different time patterns, with no tense error in the subordinate clause.

rows: often with certain verbs (시작하다, 좋아하다, 어렵다)
formal, written, and in some fixed patterns

items.text: -는 것이 좋겠어요 — you'd better
-기로 하다 — decide to
-기 시작하다 — begin to
-기 때문에 — because (formal)
-(으)ㅁ에도 불구하고 — despite

elements.text: **Module completion gate (3.5).** You convert ten sentences into nominalised forms and use three fixed patterns correctly.

items.text: Note the collision: `-(으)ㄴ` is past for verbs and present for adjectives.
`-던` = used to, or was in the middle of: `내가 살던 집` — the house I used to live in.
`어제 만난 사람이 선생님이에요` — the person I met yesterday is a teacher.
Korean puts the whole relative clause before the noun, with no "who/which". Long modifiers are the main reason reading comprehension slows at intermediate level.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (3.6).** Fifteen noun phrases built from clauses, then used in full sentences.

items.text: All three operate at once. A sentence can be simultaneously subject-honorific, object-honorific, and hearer-polite.
The classic error: over-honorifying yourself. `저께서` is wrong — you never honour your own actions with 께서 in the same way.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (3.7).** Ten sentences converted into full honorific form, using all three axes, with no over-honorification of the self.
**Module completion gate (3.8).** Ten comparisons using five different patterns, spoken, with no English word order bleeding in.

rows: but, by the way — the most common turn in speech

items.text: 저기… · 음… · 뭐라고 할까… · 그러니까… · 약간…
Using fillers deliberately is a fluency marker, not a weakness. Silent pauses read as failure; filled pauses read as thinking.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (3.9).** A 90-second monologue using at least six discourse markers naturally, with no dead air longer than 2 seconds.

sections.title: Level 3 assessment
sections.objective: **Level 3 completion rule.** A native speaker listens once and can retell your story accurately. That is the only test that matters at this level.

elements.text: **Objective.** A three-minute spoken narrative that a native speaker would call fluent.

items.text: **The story.** A true story from your life, 3 minutes, told without notes, recorded on video.
**The transcript.** Written out in Hangeul, with a gloss and a grammar annotation for every clause connector.
**The structure.** A clear beginning, three developments, and an ending — marked explicitly in the transcript.
**The connector inventory.** Every linking pattern used, with a count, targeting at least ten distinct patterns.
**The tense audit.** All three tenses used correctly; the narrative must have a past main line and a present reflection.
**The revision log.** Three recorded takes with the improvements listed between them.
**The comprehension check.** A native speaker or advanced learner listens once and retells the story — the retelling must be accurate.

elements.value: the listener retelling is the gate. If a native speaker cannot retell your story, the grammar may be correct but the discourse is not.

levels.title: DAILY LIFE DOMAINS
levels.goal: Handle the twelve situations that make up an actual life in Korea. Not tourist Korean — the Korean of a lease, a prescription, a bank transfer, and a phone call from someone who expects an answer.

dashboard.main project: **`life-kit`** — twelve domains, each with vocabulary, dialogues, and a recorded performance
dashboard.final outcome: Twelve scripted situations performed unscripted, with 85%+ task success.

modules.title: Transfers, balances, and the numbers that matter

items.text: `이체해 주세요.` — Please transfer it.
`잔액이 얼마예요?` — What's my balance?
`달러를 원으로 바꾸고 싶어요.` — I'd like to change dollars to won.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (4.2).** You complete an account-opening conversation and a currency exchange, and you correctly write down a balance heard once at normal speed.

items.text: `어디가 아프세요?` — Where does it hurt? (the first question, always)
`언제부터 아프셨어요?` — Since when?
`열이 나고 기침이 나요.` — I have a fever and a cough.
`이틀 전부터 아팠어요.` — I've been sick since two days ago.
`이 약을 하루에 세 번 식후에 드세요.` — Take this three times a day after meals.
`처방전 주세요.` — Please give me the prescription.
`보험이 돼요?` — Does insurance cover this?
`진료비가 얼마예요?` — How much is the consultation?
`이 처방전으로 약을 주세요.` — Please fill this prescription.
`이 약은 어떻게 먹어요?` — How do I take this?
`식전 / 식후` — before / after meals
`하루에 두 번` — twice a day
`부작용이 있어요?` — Are there side effects?
**119** is fire and ambulance.

sections.title: Level 4 assessment
sections.objective: **Level 4 completion rule.** You must complete a domain you have *not* rehearsed, using circumlocution, in under ten minutes. That is the difference between a phrasebook and a language.

elements.text: **Objective.** Twelve domains, performed rather than listed.

items.text: **Twelve domain files.** Housing, banking, health, transport, bureaucracy, work, study, phone, shopping, food, social, and one domain of your own choosing.
**Per domain:** 20 words, 10 sentences, one dialogue (both roles), and one recorded performance of 60–90 seconds.
**The number drill.** Fifty domain numbers — deposits, balances, fares, dosages, times — heard once and written correctly.
**The failure log.** Every time a real or role-played interaction broke down: what was said, what you meant, what would have worked.
**The register log.** One note per domain on which register applies and why.
**The pressure test.** Five domains selected at random, performed cold, with a tutor who does not follow the script.

levels.title: LISTENING AND PRONUNCIATION MASTERY
levels.goal: Close the gap between the Korean you can read and the Korean you can hear. By the end of this level you understand natural-speed everyday speech at 90%, catch the contractions that are never written, recognise the major dialects by ear, and produce rhythm and intonation that no longer sounds translated.

dashboard.study commitment: 2–3 hours per day, with at least 60 minutes of that on audio
dashboard.core tools: Recorder, headphones, a drama, a podcast, a news app, a tutor
dashboard.final outcome: 90% comprehension of everyday dialogue at native speed; 80% on news; dialect recognition at 80%; a shadowing sample that a native speaker rates as natural.

rows: you cannot match the sound to the written word

items.text: Transcribe 60 seconds, score it, and record the number. Every session. The curve is the point.
Classify every miss: **phoneme** (didn't hear the sound), **contraction** (didn't recognise the form), **lexical** (didn't know the word), **speed** (lost the thread).
The classification tells you what to study. A phoneme problem is a pronunciation problem; a lexical problem is a vocabulary problem; they need different fixes.
60% of your listening time should be **material you understand 70–90% of** — the comprehension zone.
40% should be **material you understand 40–70% of** — the stretch zone.
Material you understand 100% of is entertainment, not practice. That is fine, but it does not count.

items.text: `그게 아니에요` — that's not it (from 그것이).

sections.title: Contractions II: endings, and the verb at speed

modules.title: The ones that will ambush you

items.text: `-잖아요` is not a question. It means *as you know* or *I told you*. `내가 말했잖아요` — I told you, didn't I.
`-거든요` explains or defends: `지금 바쁘거든요` — because I'm busy, you see. It expects no reply.
`-긴요` dismisses: `재미있긴요` — fun? Not really.
`-다면서요` reports hearsay: `한국에 간다면서요?` — I heard you're going to Korea?
`-더라고요` reports something you experienced yourself: `생각보다 비싸더라고요` — it was more expensive than I expected.

rows: [뭐 하는 거야] with the 하는 compressed

A ㄴ appears where there is none, between a consonant-final word and an ㅇ-initial word.

items.text: This is the rule that makes 나뭇잎 unrecognisable if you are listening for [나무십]. Korean speakers hear [나문닙] and do not notice the ㅅ at all.

`아니에요` → [아녜요].

items.text: Korean is spoken in **phrase groups** of roughly 3–7 syllables, not word by word.
A phrase group is marked by a slight lengthening of the final syllable and a small pitch movement.
`어제는 / 친구를 만나서 / 같이 밥을 먹었어요` — three groups, not nine words.

items.text: **Announcements:** listen once, write the station, the direction, and the transfer. 95% target.

Transcribe a real phone call (with permission) end to end.

levels.title: READING AND WRITING FOUNDATIONS
levels.goal: Read a news brief and a short story with 90% comprehension; write a 300-word diary, a formal email, and a message thread — each in the correct register, with correct spacing.

dashboard.core tools: A news app, graded readers, a notebook, a tutor for corrections
dashboard.main project: **`text-lab`** — a reading log, a diary, an email, and an error taxonomy
dashboard.final outcome: 90% comprehension of a news brief; 300 words of your own prose with ≤ 5 errors; correct spacing and register.

rows: read the first sentence of each paragraph, then the last paragraph
look for numbers, names, and Sino-Korean content words
sentence by sentence, with a dictionary

items.text: Most learners read everything in close-reading mode, which is slow and exhausting. Practise all three deliberately.
A news brief should be skimmed first, then scanned for the who/what/when, then close-read only the paragraph that matters.
Set a threshold: at 90% known words, keep going and infer. At 70%, look up.
Infer from three cues: the Sino-Korean morphemes, the particle pattern, and the sentence position.
`그 회사는 신제품을 출시했다` — if you don't know 출시, the particles tell you it is a verb acting on 신제품, and 하다 tells you it is a Sino-Korean noun-verb. That is often enough.

elements.text: Before reading a long sentence, find:

items.text: The **final verb** — it carries tense, register, and negation.
The **subject particle** (이/가/께서) or topic (은/는).
The **object particle** (을/를).
Any **modifier ending** (-는, -(으)ㄴ, -(으)ㄹ) — everything before it is a clause.
The **connector** (-지만, -는데, -아서) — it tells you the relationship to the next clause.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (6.1).** You skim a 300-word news brief in 30 seconds, state its topic in one Korean sentence, then locate three specific facts by scanning.

rows: `정부, 예산 확대` — no ending at all

items.text: Headlines delete verbs: `정부, 내년 예산 10% 확대` — *government, next year's budget 10% expanded*.
They use the comma to replace a topic marker: `서울시, 지하철 요금 인상` — *Seoul city, subway fares to rise*.
`-할 듯`, `-키로`, `-중` are headline-only forms.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (6.2).** Given ten short texts, you identify the type and the register from the first two lines, with 9/10 correct.

rows: Particles attach to the preceding word
할 수 있다 · 할 것 같다 · 먹을 만큼
Auxiliary verbs are separated (attached is permitted)
Numerals and counters are separated (attached is permitted after digits)
Proper names are written as one unit
Compound nouns are written as one unit
이 사람 · 그 책 · 저 집
Units of time and date attach

elements.text: **Module completion gate (6.3).** You correct 25 spacing errors in a supplied text at 90%+ and state the rule for each correction.

sections.title: The written style: -다 and its registers

items.text: The -다 style is the **default for written prose**: diaries, reports, novels, news.
It is not rude. It is not speech. It is the register of the written page, and confusing the two is the most common stylistic error at this level.
Speech uses 해요체/합니다체; writing uses -다; the two are not interchangeable.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (6.4).** You rewrite a spoken paragraph in -다 style, changing every verb, without altering the meaning.

rows: used more sparingly than in English
quotation within a quotation, or emphasis

items.text: No space before punctuation: `갔어요.` not `갔어요 .`
Korean uses fewer commas than English. Where English needs a comma, Korean often uses a particle instead.
Arabic numerals for prices, dates, phone numbers, and statistics: `15,000원`, `2026년 10월 22일`.
Sino-Korean words for small numbers in prose: `세 명`, `두 시간`.
In formal or literary text, numbers under ten are often written in words.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (6.5).** You format a 150-word text with correct punctuation, numeral style, and quotation marks, and it passes a native read without correction.

items.text: Write in -다 style, not 해요체. Diaries are prose.
Five to eight sentences is enough. Daily beats long.
Use only grammar you have *produced* before. A diary is for consolidation, not experimentation.
Add one sentence per entry using a pattern from the current level. This is how new grammar enters production.
Keep every entry. The Day 1 to Day 100 comparison is the most motivating artefact you will have.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (6.6).** Ten consecutive diary entries, 5+ sentences each, in -다 style, with no more than three errors per entry after correction.

modules.title: The ten phrases that do the work

items.text: `다름이 아니라` — the thing is (soft opener)
`문의드리고 싶은 것이 있습니다` — I'd like to ask about something
`혹시 가능하실까요?` — would it by any chance be possible?
`바쁘시겠지만` — I know you're busy, but
`확인 부탁드립니다` — please check / confirm
`회신 부탁드립니다` — please reply
`이해해 주시면 감사하겠습니다` — I'd be grateful if you understood
`불편을 드려 죄송합니다` — sorry for the inconvenience
`잘 부탁드립니다` — I look forward to working with you
`___ 드림` — from ___ (the closing signature)

modules.title: The three registers of a message

elements.text: **Module completion gate (6.7).** You write a formal enquiry email, a professional message, and a casual message thread, and a native speaker finds no register error in any of the three.

items.text: Sentences run to 40+ syllables, with two or three embedded clauses.
The verb is at the end, so the meaning arrives last. You must hold the pieces in working memory.
Free indirect speech puts a character's thoughts in the narrator's grammar, without quotation marks.
Read the same short story twice: once for the plot with a dictionary, once for the sentences without one.
Mark every sentence over 30 syllables. Those are the ones to parse on paper.
Poetry at L6 is recognition, not mastery. Read it aloud for sound; the meaning comes later.
Korean poetry uses inversion (`하늘을 나는 새` reversed as `나는 새, 하늘을`), archaic endings (-하노라, -리라), and line breaks that carry meaning.
One poem per week, read aloud, not analysed.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (6.8).** You read a 1,000-word short story and write a 150-word summary in Korean with 90% comprehension, plus three sentences on the writing style.

items.text: Most abstract vocabulary is Sino-Korean, built from characters you will formally study at L11.
You can already decode a lot of it: 학교 = 學校 (study + school), 전화 = 電話 (electric + speech), 대학 = 大學 (great + study).
Learning the top 100 characters at L11 will multiply your vocabulary by roughly three. For now, notice the pattern: the same syllable carries the same meaning across dozens of words.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (6.9).** Given ten noun roots, you generate the 하다 verb, the 되다 passive, and the -적 adjective where possible, and explain what each suffix does.

rows: tense must match the time word

modules.title: The ten spelling errors everyone makes

rows: 안 is an adverb; 않 is a verb stem
돼 is a contraction of 되어
does each paragraph have one idea?

items.text: Read the text aloud. Spacing errors and awkward endings are audible even when invisible.
Keep an error count per category. The category that repeats is your next study unit.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (6.10).** You edit your own 300-word text down to ≤ 5 errors across all categories, with every remaining error explained.

sections.title: Level 6 assessment
sections.objective: **Level 6 completion rule.** You must write 300 words with five errors or fewer, and every remaining error must be *explainable*. An error you can explain is a level of control; an error you cannot is a habit.

elements.text: **Objective.** A body of written work, corrected and classified, plus evidence of reading.

items.text: **Twenty diary entries**, five sentences minimum, in -다 style, with corrections applied.
**One 300-word essay** on a personal topic, in -다 style, structured in three paragraphs.
**One formal email** — a real enquiry to a real or simulated institution.
**One message thread** — ten exchanges with a native speaker, in the correct casual register.
**One 500-word reading summary** of a short story, with three sentences on style.
**The error taxonomy** — every error from the level, classified, with a count per category.
**The spacing pass** — your own 300-word text with every spacing decision marked and justified.

Write the same essay in two registers — -다 and 합니다체 — and compare.

levels.title: DISCOURSE AND CONNECTORS
levels.goal: Hold the floor. Say something for five minutes that has a beginning, three reasons, a concession, and an end — in the right register, without the listener having to work to follow you.

dashboard.core tools: Recorder, tutor twice weekly, a Korean debate or discussion podcast
dashboard.main project: **`argument-lab`** — a five-minute argument with a Q&A
dashboard.final outcome: Five minutes of structured speech on an unprepared topic, with six connectors and one concession.

sections.title: The architecture of a Korean answer

rows: signals that a long answer is coming, buys time
the claim, stated early — not at the end
two or three, each with a marker
shows you have considered the other side

items.text: Unlike English academic style, the position comes **early**. A Korean listener who waits 90 seconds for the thesis assumes you do not have one.
The concession is not optional. An answer with no concession reads as naive.
The close restates, it does not add a new point.
Every part has its own ending, and the register has to stay consistent across all five.
The connectives carry much of the meaning, so a wrong one changes the argument, not just the grammar.
Korean discourse is more **listener-oriented**: you signal your direction constantly (`크게 두 가지가 있는데요…`) rather than surprising the listener.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (7.1).** You deliver a 90-second answer using all five parts, labelled out loud ("여기서부터 이유입니다"), and a listener can name your position after hearing it once.

sections.title: Cause and reason: the refined set

rows: reason the listener should accept; discovery
a reason that *occupied* you, usually with a negative result
subject must be the same, present/past only
an unwelcome cause with a bad outcome
because I saw/heard that, so I acted
first person action in the result

modules.title: The three you will actually use

items.text: **-느라고** takes the blame: `전화 받느라고 못 봤어요` — I didn't see it because I was on the phone.
**-는 바람에** assigns an external cause to a bad result: `지하철이 멈추는 바람에 늦었어요`.
**-길래** reports a perceived cause: `맛있어 보이길래 샀어요` — it looked good so I bought it.

elements.text: **The constraint that matters:** -느라고 and -는 바람에 cannot be followed by a request or a command. If you add `-세요`, the sentence collapses. Same restriction as -아/어서, and the same reason: the speaker is reporting, not directing.
**Module completion gate (7.2).** Fifteen cause sentences, each using a *different* pattern, with the nuance explained in one clause.

rows: 네 말이 맞다 해도 문제는 남아요

items.text: `물론 ___지만, 그래도 ___` — of course X, but even so Y. This is the single most useful argumentative structure in Korean.
`-기는 하지만` is the softened version and is what makes you sound reasonable rather than combative.
`-는데도` is *despite*, and it carries frustration. Do not use it about a person in a formal setting.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (7.3).** Ten concessions, each conceding a real point and then contradicting it, delivered to a tutor who argues back.

modules.title: The two that carry the most meaning

items.text: **-았/었더니** combines a past action with a discovery, and the second clause must be a *result you observed*: `전화했더니 안 받더라고요`.
**-(으)ㄹ수록** is a rhetorical favourite: `생각할수록 화가 나요` — the more I think, the angrier I get.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (7.4).** A six-sentence narrative using five different sequence connectors, with no tense error in the subordinate clauses.

rows: It wouldn't be a bad idea

items.text: In Korean professional speech, the stronger the disagreement, the softer the wording. Bluntness is not honesty — it is a register error.
`-것 같아요` is not weakness. It is the default stance of a polite adult expressing an opinion.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (7.5).** You disagree with ten statements, each at a different level of directness, and state which level suits which setting.

rows: 제 생각에는 · 개인적으로는 · 이 문제에 대해
첫째 · 둘째 · 셋째 · 먼저 · 다음으로 · 마지막으로

items.text: Rehearse the skeleton on five different topics. The topics do not matter; the shape does.
The concession is where most learners fall apart, because it requires switching sides for two sentences while keeping the register.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (7.6).** A five-minute argument on a prepared topic, recorded, scored against the skeleton with every part present.

rows: 그 지적은 타당합니다 / 그 부분은 맞습니다
그 얘기도 중요하지만, 제가 말씀드린 건
그 부분은 제가 잘 모르겠습니다. 확인해 보겠습니다

items.text: Do not restart the whole argument when interrupted. Answer the specific objection, then return with `그래서 처음에 말씀드린 것처럼…`.
`그 부분은 제가 잘 모르겠습니다` is a strong answer, not a weak one. Confident ignorance beats invented facts.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (7.7).** You argue a position while a tutor interrupts three times with objections, and you return to your thread each time without restarting.

rows: but, by the way — the commonest turn in speech
kind of, a bit — the universal softener
like, or something — intensifier in slang
now, then — a filler that means nothing

items.text: A silent pause reads as failure; a filled pause reads as thinking. This is the single biggest cheap improvement available at this level.
`약간` and `좀` make almost any sentence sound more natural and less aggressive.
`막` and `완전` belong to casual speech only — using them in a formal setting is a register error, not a vocabulary error.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (7.8).** A three-minute monologue with no dead air over two seconds, using at least eight different markers.

items.text: `아, 그게 아니라` — no, that's not it (the commonest repair)
`다시 말하면` — let me rephrase
`제가 말을 잘못했는데` — I said that badly
`그게 아니라, ___` — it's not that, it's ___
Repairing is a *fluency* behaviour. Learners who never repair sound worse than learners who repair often.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (7.9).** You deliver a two-minute answer containing at least two self-repairs, both smooth enough that the argument does not break.

items.text: Prepare nothing. A partner names a topic; you speak for the target time.
Topics should be ordinary: remote work, learning languages, city versus countryside, social media, university education, AI, food culture, exercise, travel, money.
Record every attempt. The measure is *time sustained without a break longer than three seconds*.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (7.10).** Five minutes on an unprepared topic, recorded, with ≥ 4.5 minutes of speech and no break over three seconds.

sections.title: Level 7 assessment
sections.objective: **Level 7 completion rule.** You must sustain five minutes on a topic you did not prepare. A rehearsed speech is a performance; this level is about thinking aloud.

elements.text: **Objective.** A recorded argument with a live Q&A, scored on structure.

items.text: **The prepared argument.** Five minutes on a topic of your choice, with the full five-part skeleton.
**The unprepared argument.** Five minutes on a topic given at random, forty seconds of thinking time.
**The concession drill.** Three recorded clips where you concede a point, then contradict it.
**The Q&A.** Ten minutes of questions from a tutor, including two hostile ones.
**The connector inventory.** Every connector used, with a count and a context.
**The self-review.** A transcript of the prepared argument with the skeleton annotated in the margin.
**The repair log.** Every self-repair, hesitation, and breakdown, with what you should have said.

Soften: "이건 틀렸어요".

levels.title: REPORTED SPEECH, PASSIVE, AND CAUSATIVE
levels.goal: Move other people's words, and change the direction of a verb. By the end you report what someone said with the correct hearsay marker, describe being acted upon without sounding like a translated English sentence, and distinguish the passive from the causative where Korean uses the same suffix for both.

dashboard.core tools: Recorder, tutor twice weekly, *Korean Grammar in Use – Intermediate*, a news app
dashboard.main project: **`voice-lab`** — a retelling, a news summary, and a voice audit
dashboard.final outcome: Accurate reported speech, four passive forms, six causative forms, and a working sense of when Korean prefers the active.

rows: 간다고 했어요 — he said he's going
간냐고 물었어요 — she asked if I'm going
가자고 했어요 — he suggested we go
가라고 했어요 — he told me to go

items.text: Korean does **not** backshift tense the way English does. `간다고 했어요` = *he said he is going / was going*. The time is carried by the outer verb and the context.
To be explicit: past `갔다고 했어요`, future `갈 거라고 했어요`.
The outer verb can be anything: 말하다, 하다, 생각하다, 믿다, 듣다, 물어보다, 쓰다.

modules.title: The copula and the irregular quotes

elements.text: **The one everyone gets wrong:** 이다 takes **-라고**, not -다고. `학생이라고 했어요`, never `학생이다고 했어요`.
**Module completion gate (8.1).** Twenty sentences converted from direct to reported speech, all four quote types, with the copula correct every time.

rows: 내일 온대요 — I hear they're coming tomorrow
내일 온다더라고요 — they told me they're coming
내일 온다면서요? — so you're coming tomorrow?
내일 온다잖아요 — I told you they're coming tomorrow

items.text: **-대요 vs -더라고요** is the distinction that separates an intermediate speaker from an advanced one. -대요 = I heard it from somewhere. -더라고요 = I saw/heard it for myself, and I'm telling you what I found.
**-다면서요** is a confirmation, and it carries a mild challenge: *I heard X — is that right?*

elements.text: **Module completion gate (8.2).** Given ten situations, you choose between -대요, -더라고요, -다면서요, and -다고요?, with the reason stated.

items.text: 말하다 · 이야기하다 · 전하다 · 알려 주다 · 물어보다 · 대답하다 · 주장하다 · 강조하다 · 부인하다 · 인정하다 · 약속하다
News register: -다고 밝혔다 (announced), -다고 전했다 (reported), -다고 주장했다 (claimed), -다고 반박했다 (countered).

elements.text: **Module completion gate (8.3).** You retell a three-minute conversation in ninety seconds, with at least five quotes, using the correct quote type for each and no lost nuance.

sections.title: Passive I: the four short suffixes

rows: to be caught, read, closed, sold
to be held, chased, wound, cut off

items.text: **The warning:** 보이다 does not mean "is seen" in most sentences. `그 책이 잘 보여요` = the book is visible / looks good. Korean uses 보이다 far more often as *appear* than as *be seen*.
Passive sentences in Korean almost always take **이/가**, not 을/를: `문이 열렸어요`, never 문을 열렸어요.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (8.4).** Twenty active → passive conversions, all four suffixes, with the particle changed correctly.

items.text: -아/어지다 is about **state change**, not about being acted upon. This is the passive-like form Korean uses constantly and English has no single equivalent for.
`한국어가 늘었어요` = my Korean improved. `한국어가 늘어졌어요` ✗ — some verbs take -았/었 directly, not -아/어지다.

modules.title: -게 되다: come to be, ended up

rows: I ended up going to Korea

items.text: -게 되다 describes a change of circumstance with no agent, and it is the polite way to describe something that happened *to* you. It removes responsibility: `늦게 됐어요` sounds softer than `늦었어요`.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (8.5).** Fifteen sentences using -아/어지다 and -게 되다, with the state-change versus circumstance distinction made explicit.

rows: to put to sleep, wake, stand up

elements.text: **Module completion gate (8.6).** Twenty causative conversions across all six suffixes, each in a full sentence with a clear agent and patient.

rows: 아이를 웃게 했어요 — I made the child laugh
내일까지 끝내도록 하세요 — see that it's finished by tomorrow

items.text: -게 하다 is neutral: it can mean *make* or *let*, depending on context. `가게 했어요` = I let him go / I made him go. Add context.
-도록 하다 is the instruction form, and it is what you use in a workplace or a written notice.

rows: Physical action on a person or animal
Anything not covered by a suffix

elements.text: **Module completion gate (8.7).** Ten sentences using -게 하다 and -도록 하다, with a justification for choosing them over a suffix form.

sections.title: The ambiguity: same suffix, two directions

rows: to be seen, to be visible

items.text: **The particle.** 이/가 subject → usually passive; 을/를 object present → usually causative.
**The agent.** If there is an explicit agent with 에게/한테, causative is more likely.
**Plausibility.** `옷이 감겼어요` (the clothes got wound) vs `실을 감겼어요` (I wound the thread).
These forms are memorised as *words*, not derived. Build a list, learn the pairs, and let usage settle it.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (8.8).** Given fifteen sentences, you identify each as passive or causative, and state which of the three disambiguation cues decided it.

items.text: Korean uses the passive far less than English. Where English says "the window was broken by the storm", Korean says `폭풍 때문에 창문이 깨졌어요` — the storm caused the window to break.
Where English says "I was told that…", Korean says `___라고 들었어요` — I heard that…
Where English says "it is believed that…", Korean says `___라고 합니다` — they say…

modules.title: The four replacements for the passive

elements.text: **Module completion gate (8.9).** You rewrite ten passive English sentences into natural Korean, and none of them uses a mechanical suffix passive.

items.text: These forms are **evidential markers**: they tell the reader how the paper knows. Getting them wrong is a factual error, not a stylistic one.
`주장했다` versus `밝혔다` is the difference between "claims" and "announced" — a newspaper choosing one is making an editorial statement.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (8.10).** You read a 400-word news brief and list five evidential markers, saying what each implies about the source.

sections.title: Level 8 assessment
sections.objective: **Level 8 completion rule.** You must produce a retelling in which a listener who was *not* present can identify who said what. Attribution is the whole point.

elements.text: **Objective.** Prove control of reported speech, passive, and causative in production and in reading.

items.text: **The retelling.** A three-minute conversation retold in 90 seconds, with five quotes of at least three different types.

**The causative corpus.** Twenty causative sentences across the six suffixes, plus -게 하다 and -도록 하다.
**The ambiguity audit.** Fifteen ambiguous forms classified, with the disambiguation cue named.

levels.title: REGISTER AND NUANCE
levels.goal: Say the same thing four different ways, and know which one a situation demands. By the end of this level you move between 해요체, 합니다체, 해체, and 반말 without a slip, and you can hear the difference between a neutral statement, a reproach, a discovery, and a joke — which in Korean is carried almost entirely by the final ending.

dashboard.core tools: Recorder, two tutors (one for formal role-play), drama with subtitles off, a workplace dialogue corpus
dashboard.main project: **`register-lab`** — one piece of content, four registers
dashboard.final outcome: Four registers controlled; twelve nuance endings read correctly; honorifics used without over- or under-honorifying.

rows: presentations, news, first meetings, military, service
older-generation address to a junior, historical drama

items.text: You need to *produce* three: 합니다체, 해요체, 해체/반말.
You need to *read* all six, because novels, dramas, and documents use registers nobody speaks.

modules.title: The same sentence in four registers

items.text: Nothing changes except the ending. That is the whole difficulty: the ending carries the social relationship.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (9.1).** Ten sentences rendered in all four registers, spoken, with no cross-contamination between them.

rows: how well do you know them?

items.text: **The corridor rule:** the same person takes 합니다체 in a meeting and 해요체 in a corridor. Register tracks setting as well as relationship.
**The stranger rule:** never 반말 with a stranger of any age, including a child you do not know.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (9.2).** Twenty scenarios, each with the correct register and address term, in under five minutes.

rows: You use 해요체 with everyone, always
The other person says `말 놓으세요` / `우리 말 놓을까요?` / `편하게 하세요`
You switch — **but only after one more exchange of 해요체**, as a courtesy
If they are older, you still use honorifics within 반말: `형, 밥 먹었어?`

items.text: Being invited is not the same as being required. With someone much older, stay in 해요체 even if invited — the offer is politeness, not instruction.
You never initiate the switch with someone older. Ever.

elements.text: This is the combination learners miss: 반말 grammar with honorific vocabulary.

items.text: 반말 refers to the *ending*, not to disrespect. Dropping the honorific vocabulary at the same time is the actual error.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (9.3).** You simulate the full switch: five exchanges in 해요체, the invitation, then five in 반말 with honorific vocabulary retained.

rows: a boss enters the room mid-conversation
you drop to 합니다체 to show seriousness

items.text: `죄송합니다만` — sorry, but (the formal reset)
`실례지만` — excuse me (formal opener to a stranger)
`그런데요` — by the way (soft return to 해요체)
`편하게 말씀하셔도 됩니다` — you may speak casually to me (you grant it to someone younger)

elements.text: **Module completion gate (9.4).** A role-play where a third party enters mid-conversation and you switch register within two sentences, twice.

I remember it being, with contrast

modules.title: The four that carry the most social weight

items.text: **-네요** is the politeness of noticing. Saying `맛있네요` instead of `맛있어요` makes you gracious.
**-잖아요** is a reproach dressed as a reminder. Use it with people you know; it is confrontational with strangers.
**-거든요** ends a topic. It says *this is my reason, and I am not inviting discussion*.
**-기는요** is the correct response to a compliment, and refusing it too firmly is its own error.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (9.5).** Ten situations, ten endings, each chosen for its social function rather than its translation.

sections.title: Nuance endings II: stance and evaluation

rows: as I did it, I found
it is in the nature of things

items.text: **-다 보면** for encouragement: `연습하다 보면 늘어요` — you'll improve if you keep practising.
**-ㄹ 텐데** for a considerate request: `바쁠 텐데 죄송해요` — I know you're probably busy, sorry.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (9.6).** Ten sentences using four different stance endings, each with the stance named aloud.
**Error 1 — over-honorifying yourself.**

items.text: `저께서 하겠습니다` ✗ — you never honour your own subject with 께서.
`제가 하겠습니다` ✓
Humble verbs lower *you*: 드리다, 뵙다, 여쭙다, 모시다.

elements.text: **Error 2 — under-honorifying the subject while being polite to the hearer.**

items.text: `선생님이 밥을 먹어요` ✗ — polite to you, but the teacher is not honoured.
`선생님께서 진지를 드세요` ✓

elements.text: **Module completion gate (9.7).** Ten sentences converted to full honorific form, using all three axes, with no over-honorification of the self.

sections.title: Reading tone: what is not said

items.text: A Korean no is rarely the word 아니요. It is a delay, a difficulty, or a deferral. Learning to hear it is a listening skill as much as a cultural one.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (9.8).** Given ten indirect refusals, you state what each means, and which you would use with a boss versus a friend.
**Module completion gate (9.9).** You handle a customer complaint and a workplace refusal, both in the correct institutional register.

sections.title: Slang, swearing, and what not to say

items.text: **Understand everything; produce almost nothing.** Slang dates fast, and a foreigner using 2020s slang in 2030 sounds worse than a foreigner speaking plainly.
Swearing: learn to recognise it so you are not caught off guard. Do not produce it.
The one exception: `대박` and `헐` are safe in casual company and will make people laugh.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (9.10).** You identify ten slang expressions from a drama clip, and state which register each belongs to.

sections.title: Level 9 assessment
sections.objective: **Level 9 completion rule.** Zero register slips. Not "few". This is the one level where the pass mark is absolute, because a slip is the thing a native listener remembers.

elements.text: **Objective.** One piece of content, delivered four ways, with an audit of every choice.

items.text: **One content unit** — a 200-word message, e.g. rescheduling a meeting, making a complaint, or declining an invitation.

**Four recordings** of the spoken versions, each with the register stated at the start.
**The switch log:** two role-plays where you change register mid-conversation, with the trigger named.
**The nuance set:** twelve sentences, each using a different nuance ending, with the social effect explained.
**The honorific audit:** ten sentences, with every honorific choice annotated by axis.
**The register map:** twenty situations, each with the correct register, address term, and one reason.
