levels.title: ADVANCED GRAMMAR PATTERNS
levels.goal: Master the TOPIK Level 4–5 grammar architecture: multi-clause hypothetical conditions, nuanced supposition, regret, inevitability, and concessive constructions. Transition from "correct sentences" to expressing exact degrees of probability, intention, and emotional stance.
levels.prerequisites: Level 9 passed. Clear grasp of quoted speech, formal registers, and intermediate conjunctions.

dashboard.core tools: *Korean Grammar in Use – Advanced*, Anki grammar sentence cloze, speech recorder
dashboard.main project: `grammar-engine-ii` — live oral drill matrix of 80 advanced grammar patterns
dashboard.final outcome: Spontaneously deploy complex grammatical combinations without hesitation.

items.text: Understand `-(으)ㄹ 텐데` as combining future expectation/supposition `-(으)ㄹ 터이다` with background connector `-ㄴ/은/는데`.
Contrast `비가 올 텐데 우산을 가져가세요` (strong anticipation offering advice) with `비가 올 텐데요` (sentence ending expressing concern or presumption).
Drill the past supposition variant: `-았/었을 텐데` (e.g. `많이 피곤했을 텐데 푹 쉬세요`).
Understand `-(으)ㄴ/는 모양이다` as deduction based on observable external signs or evidence.
Contrast with `-나 보다` (informal, intuitive deduction) vs `-(으)ㄴ/는 모양이다` (written/spoken, based on visible cues).
Conjugate correctly across tenses: `-은 모양이다` (past), `-는 모양이다` (present verb), `-(으)ㄴ 모양이다` (adjective), `-(으)ㄹ 모양이다` (imminent future).

elements.text: **Module completion gate (10.1).** Record 6 spontaneous sentences explaining real situations using `-(으)ㄹ 텐데` and `-(으)ㄴ/는 모양이다` without looking at notes.

modules.title: Virtual Equivalence: -(으)ㄴ/는 셈이다 and -(으)ㄴ 셈 치다

items.text: Master `-(으)ㄴ/는 셈이다` ("it amounts to", "practically considered as"): `거의 다 끝난 셈이다` (it's practically finished).
Master `-(으)ㄴ 셈 치다` ("let's consider it as...", "pretend that"): `속는 셈 치고 한번 믿어 보세요` (give it the benefit of the doubt).

modules.title: Narrow Escapes and Remorse: -(으)ㄹ 뻔했다 and -(으)ㄹ 걸 그랬다

items.text: Master `-(으)ㄹ 뻔했다` for events that almost happened (usually accompanied by `하마터면`, `거의`): `늦잠을 자서 비행기를 놓칠 뻔했다`.
Master `-(으)ㄹ 걸 그랬다` for expressing regret about an unchosen path: `좀 더 일찍 출발할 걸 그랬어요`.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (10.2).** Create a 2-minute oral monologue describing an emergency or close call using both `-(으)ㄹ 뻔했다` and `-(으)ㄴ 셈이다`.

items.text: Use `-기 마련이다` for natural laws and inevitable outcomes: `시간이 지나면 상처는 아물기 마련이다`.
Contrast with `-(으)ㄴ/는 법이다` ("it is the way of things"): `사람은 누구나 실수하기 마련이다 / 마련인 법이다`.

modules.title: Limit and Monopolisation: -기 십상이다 and -기 일쑤이다

items.text: Use `-기 십상이다` for high probabilities of negative outcomes: `급하게 서두르면 실수하기 십상이다`.
Use `-기 일쑤이다` for chronic undesirable habitual actions: `그는 약속 시간을 어기기 일쑤였다`.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (10.3).** State 4 universal principles of human behaviour using `-기 마련이다` and `-는 법이다`.

items.text: Master `-더라도` ("even if", "granted that"): `아무리 힘들더라도 끝까지 완수해야 합니다`.
Master the elevated written concessive `-(으)ㄹ망정` / `-(으)ㄹ지언정` ("even though I may... I will never..."): `굶어 죽을망정 부정한 돈은 받지 않겠다`.
Master `-느니 (차라리)` ("rather than doing X, I would rather do Y"): `그런 대우를 받느니 차라리 회사를 그만두겠다`.
Contrast with `-기보다는` (mild preference) vs `-느니 차라리` (categorical aversion).

elements.text: **Module completion gate (10.4).** Roleplay a difficult ethical decision using `-느니 차라리` and `-더라도`.

items.text: Master `-는 김에` ("while taking the opportunity of X"): `서점에 가는 김에 제 책도 한 권 사다 주세요`.
Master `-는 길에` ("on one's physical way to/from"): `퇴근하는 길에 마트에 들렀어요`.
Master `-(으)ㄴ/는 척하다` ("pretend to"): `알면서도 모르는 척했다`, `바쁜 척하지 마세요`.
Apply past, present, and adjective forms correctly: `아는 척하다`, `들은 척도 안 하다`.
Master `-(으)ㄹ수록` ("the more... the more..."): `한국어는 배울수록 흥미진진하다`.
Apply to double-clause structures: `연습을 많이 하면 할수록 실력이 늡니다`.
Master `-(으)ㄹ 정도로` / `-(으)ㄹ 정도이다` ("to the extent that..."): `숨이 턱에 찰 정도로 뛰었다`.
Construct idioms of physical extent: `눈코 뜰 새 없이 바쁠 정도이다`.
Master `-기는커녕` ("far from doing X, cannot even do Y"): `상금은커녕 본전도 못 건졌다`, `쉬기는커녕 밤을 새웠다`.
Pair with negative endings: `못하다`, `없다`, `않다`.
Master `-(으)ㄴ/는 한편` ("on one hand... on the other hand..."): `신제품 개발에 주력하는 한편 해외 시장 개척에도 힘쓰고 있다`.
Master `-느라고` for subject continuity where energy in clause 1 causes an adverse clause 2: `시험공부 하느라고 잠을 못 잤어요`.
Enforce the three structural constraints: identical subjects, action verbs only, negative/burdensome result.
Master `-다면서요?` / `-라면서요?` to verify hearsay with the interlocutor: `다음 달에 한국으로 전근 가신다면서요?`.

levels.title: THE SINO-KOREAN VOCABULARY ENGINE
levels.goal: Decode 1,800 Hanja roots to unlock exponential vocabulary growth. In this level, polysyllabic Sino-Korean words (which comprise over 60% of modern Korean vocabulary) stop being isolated strings of sound and become transparent morphological compounds.
levels.prerequisites: Level 10 complete. Ability to read complex grammatical sentences.

dashboard.core tools: Naver Hanja Dictionary, Hanja root flashcard deck (300 core characters), news editorials
dashboard.main project: `hanja-lexicon` — personal 300-root cross-reference network decoding 1,500 advanced words
dashboard.final outcome: Guess the precise meaning of 80% of unfamiliar Korean newspaper headlines on sight.

sections.title: The Mechanics of Hanja in Modern Korean

items.text: Understand that Korean does not require writing Chinese characters by hand; it requires **auditory and semantic root recognition**.
Understand homophonic divergence: why `전` can mean 前 (front/before), 電 (electricity), 全 (entire), or 戰 (war).
Learn the context-clue heuristic: identifying the root family by surrounding topic domain.
Master negative prefixes: 不/부/불 (부족, 불가능, 불안), 無/무 (무료, 무단, 무한), 非/비 (비공식, 비정상), 未/미 (미완성, 미성년).
Master directional and temporal prefixes: 前/전 (전임, 전직), 後/후 (후배, 후유증), 再/재 (재발, 재시험).

sections.title: Top Productive Roots: State, People, and Society

items.text: Map 學 (학 - study/learn): 학생, 학교, 학문, 장학금, 과학, 철학, 어학, 독학.
Map 國 (국 - country/nation): 한국, 외국, 국민, 국적, 국경, 귀국, 출국, 선진국.
Map 生 (생 - life/birth): 생활, 생물, 생명, 탄생, 생산, 평생, 일생.
Map 人 (인 - person/human): 인간, 인기, 인류, 외국인, 증인, 주인공, 개인.

modules.title: Social Organization: 會, 社, 員, 團

items.text: Map 會 (회 - meet/gather): 회사, 사회, 회의, 기회, 총회, 회원, 동호회.
Map 社 (사 - society/company): 사회, 사옥, 사원, 사장, 언론사, 신문사.

items.text: Map 話 (화 - speech/dialogue): 대화, 전화, 화제, 회화, 신화.
Map 語 (어 - word/language): 한국어, 단어, 어휘, 속어, 언어, 국어.

items.text: Map 經 (경 - pass through/manage): 경제, 경영, 경험, 경력, 신경.
Map 濟 (제 - aid/cross): 경제, 구제, 결제.
Map 費 (비 - cost/expense): 비용, 학비, 생활비, 소비, 낭비, 회비.

items.text: Map 法 (법 - law/method): 법률, 헌법, 방법, 문법, 합법, 불법.
Map 制 (제 - control/system): 제도, 통제, 제한, 제작, 절제.
Map 規 (규 - standard/compass): 규칙, 규정, 규모, 규제.

modules.title: Elements: 水, 火, 木, 金, 土, 電

items.text: Map 水 (수 - water): 생수, 수영, 음료수, 홍수, 침수, 해수.
Map 電 (전 - electricity): 전기, 전화, 전자, 전철, 전구, 발전소.
Map 金 (금 - gold/metal/money): 황금, 현금, 금융, 요금, 입금, 송금.

modules.title: Form and Character: 形, 狀, 性, 質

items.text: Map 形 (형 - form/shape): 인형, 형태, 형식, 지형, 변형.
Map 性 (성 - nature/gender): 성격, 성별, 남성, 여성, 가능성, 특성, 개성.
Map 質 (질 - quality/matter): 질문, 품질, 본질, 물질, 성질.
Step 1: Syllable isolation (break down 4-syllable term into morphemic pairs).
Step 2: Domain matching (determine if context is legal, economic, medical, or philosophical).
Step 3: Semantic synthesis (assemble the root meanings into an intuitive definition).
Practice deconstructing: `초소형` (超-小-型: ultra-small-model), `무단횡단` (無-斷-橫-斷: un-authorized-cross-cut).
Understand why Korean news headlines eliminate particles and rely 90% on Hanja compounds.
Decrypt headline strings: `한미정상회담 합의문 발표`, `물가상승률 둔화세 지속`.
Identify single-character headline shorthands: 美 (미국), 中 (중국), 日 (일본), 北 (북한), 檢 (검찰), 警 (경찰).

levels.title: IDIOMS, PROVERBS, AND EXPRESSIVE LANGUAGE
levels.goal: Acquire the cultural and rhetorical layer that separates mechanical fluency from native-adjacent expressive mastery: four-character idioms (사자성어), living proverbs (속담), evocative sound-symbolic words (의성어·의태어), and writing in plain form (해라체).
levels.prerequisites: Level 11 passed. Solid command of 300+ Hanja roots.

dashboard.core tools: Korean literature excerpts, editorial columns, proverbs corpus, voice recorder
dashboard.main project: `expressive-voice` — a 1,200-word published-grade opinion column in 해라체
dashboard.final outcome: Spontaneously weave 사자성어 and 속담 into conversational debates and write compelling analytical Korean.

modules.title: The Classical Canon: Irony, Resilience, and Folly

items.text: Master the 20 foundational 사자성어 of modern discourse:
`일석이조` (一石二鳥) — killing two birds with one stone.
`작심삼일` (作心三日) — giving up after three days.
`고진감래` (苦盡甘來) — sweet comes after bitter; hard work pays off.
`동문서답` (東問西答) — answering something totally irrelevant.
`우이독경` (牛耳讀經) — reading scriptures into a cow's ear (talking to a brick wall).
`새옹지마` (塞翁之馬) — fortune and misfortune are unpredictable.
`십시일반` (十匙一飯) — ten spoons make one meal; pooling resources.
`동상이몽` (同床異夢) — same bed, different dreams (working together with different motives).
Drill deploying these idioms in modern workplace and conversational contexts.

sections.title: Rhetorical Idioms for Persuasion and Debate

items.text: Master idioms used in editorial writing and high-level debate:
`어불성설` (語不成說) — illogical, absurd claim.
`자승자박` (自繩自縛) — caught in one's own trap.
`적반하장` (賊反荷杖) — the thief blaming the owner; sheer audacity.
`역지사지` (易地思之) — putting oneself in another's shoes.
`탁상공론` (卓上空論) — armchair theory divorced from reality.
`일장춘몽` (一場春夢) — an empty transient spring dream.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (12.2).** Deliver a 3-minute oral critique of an unrealistic government policy using `탁상공론`, `적반하장`, and `역지사지`.

items.text: `가는 말이 고와야 오는 말이 곱다` — speak nicely to receive kindness.
`발 없는 말이 천 리 간다` — words travel fast; beware of gossip.
`말 한마디에 천 냥 빚도 갚는다` — a tactful word resolves immense debt.
`호랑이도 제 말 하면 온다` — speak of the devil.
`낮말은 새가 듣고 밤말은 쥐가 듣는다` — walls have ears.
`시작이 반이다` — well begun is half done.
`티끌 모아 태산` — tiny dust motes gather into Mount Tai.
`우물 안 개구리` — frog in a well (narrow horizons).
`소 잃고 외양간 고친다` — mending the barn after losing the cow.
`원숭이도 나무에서 떨어진다` — even monkeys fall from trees (experts make mistakes).
Understand bright vowels (ㅏ, ㅗ) vs dark vowels (ㅓ, ㅜ):
`반짝반짝` (bright, cheerful sparkle) vs `번쩍번쩍` (heavy, intense flashing).
`찰랑찰랑` (gentle shallow lapping) vs `출렁출렁` (deep heavy waves).
`살금살금` (light stealthy tiptoeing) vs `슬금슬금` (covert, sluggish creeping).
Master psychological mimetics:
`두근두근` (heart pounding with excitement/nervousness).
`안절부절` (restlessly agitated, can't sit still).
`오락가락` (back and forth, confused, intermittent).
`조마조마` (on tenterhooks, nervous anxiety).

sections.title: The Plain Form Writing System: 해라체 Mastery

modules.title: Syntax of 해라체 for Non-Fiction and Essays

items.text: Master declarative endings: Verb `-ㄴ/는다` (간다, 먹는다), Adjective `-다` (예쁘다, 높다), Past `-았다/었다`, Future `-겠다` / `-(으)ㄹ 것이다`.
Master interrogative and indirect rhetorical questions: `-는가?`, `-(으)ㄴ가?`.
Understand register consistency: never mixing `-ㅂ니다` or `-요` into a 해라체 essay.

modules.title: Constructing Flow and Pacing in Korean Non-Fiction

items.text: Master connective progression: `이에 따라`, `반면`, `더욱이`, `궁극적으로`.
Balance active sentences with topic-fronted assertions.

items.text: Exactly 1,200–1,500 words written in immaculate, uninterrupted 해라체.
Natural incorporation of target idioms without appearing forced or archaic.

Recorded 7-minute expressive audio reading of the essay with dignified cadence and authoritative pacing.

questions.question: When a business competitor copies your product after mocking it, which idiom applies: `적반하장` or `동상이몽`?

What visual picture does `살금살금` paint compared to `성큼성큼`?
Why does `반짝반짝` sound lighter than `번쩍번쩍`?
Conjugate into 해라체: `살다` (live), `만들다` (make), `바쁘다` (busy), `아름답다` (beautiful).
Fix this sentence for an essay: `이 문제는 심각하다고 생각해요.`
Why must adjectives take `-다` rather than `-ㄴ다` in 해라체 present tense?

levels.title: PROFESSIONAL KOREAN
levels.goal: Operate inside a Korean organisation. Not "survive a business trip" — function as a colleague: attend and run meetings, present to a room that outranks you, write documents that get approved, negotiate without rupturing the relationship, and interview for a job.

dashboard.core tools: A professional tutor (ideally someone who has worked in a Korean company), business-writing samples, a recorder, mock meetings
dashboard.main project: **`professional-kit`** — a meeting, a presentation, a proposal, and an interview
dashboard.final outcome: Run a 20-minute meeting, present for 15 minutes, write a 3,000-word report, negotiate a disagreement, and pass a mock interview.

items.text: Rank determines register, seating, who speaks first, who pours, and who pays. It is not decoration.
A person's rank is part of their name in address: `김 부장님`, never `김 씨` to a superior.
Modern companies (startups, foreign firms) flatten this. Ask which culture you are in; do not assume.

rows: 이름 + 씨, or just 이름 once close

items.text: **Never** use a person's bare name at work unless they are clearly junior and you are close.
`님` attaches to titles, not to surnames alone. `김 님` is wrong; `김 부장님` is right.
When in doubt: `선생님` is never wrong and never too formal.

rows: The senior speaks last in a decision
do not conclude before they have
the youngest often takes notes and reports
"그 부분은 조금 더 검토해 볼 필요가 있을 것 같습니다"
correction happens privately, never in a meeting

items.text: `저희` (our, humble) is the default for company, team, and department: `저희 팀`, `저희 회사`.
`우리` is warmer and used inside a team, but `저희` is safer with clients.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (13.1).** You explain the rank ladder, address ten people correctly by rank and relationship, and identify four indirect refusals in a meeting transcript.

items.text: 회의 meeting · 회의실 meeting room · 안건 agenda item · 발제 presentation of a topic · 논의 discussion · 결정 decision · 보고 report · 피드백 feedback · 액션 아이템 action item · 마감 deadline · 참석 attendance · 불참 absence · 대리 참석 attending on behalf · 속기 minutes · 정리 summary

rows: 오늘 회의를 시작하겠습니다. 안건은 세 가지입니다.
말씀은 이해했습니다만, 한 가지 우려되는 점이 있습니다.

modules.title: Contributing as the most junior person in the room

items.text: You will be the least senior. Your job is not to be quiet; it is to be **specific and brief**.
The two moves that work: ask a clarifying question (`확인차 여쭤보겠습니다만, ___은 어느 정도 규모인가요?`), and offer a concrete fact (`제가 확인해 보니 ___였습니다`).
Never open a disagreement with `아니요`. Open with `말씀 감사합니다. 다만 …`
If you have not understood an action item, say so immediately: `제가 이해한 게 맞는지 확인하고 싶습니다.`

elements.text: **Module completion gate (13.2).** You participate in a 20-minute simulated meeting: make two clarifying questions, one contribution, and one soft disagreement, and correctly summarise the action items assigned to you.

rows: 좋은 질문입니다. 그 부분은 별도로 확인해서 말씀드리겠습니다.
state the recommendation in the first two minutes
과도한 자신감 reads badly; use -라고 판단됩니다
say how many parts before you begin
a number alone is not an argument
end with what you want, explicitly

elements.text: **Module completion gate (13.3).** A 15-minute presentation on a real topic, recorded, with the structure above and eight presentation phrases used naturally.

rows: what we will build and why
the proposal, with options and a recommendation

items.text: The title states the conclusion: `A/B 테스트 결과, 신규 UI가 전환율 12% 개선` — not `A/B 테스트 결과 보고`.
The 요약 must stand alone. Many executives read only it.
`드림` is the standard sign-off. `올림` is more formal and older-fashioned.
Subject lines carry the action and the object, in brackets. `[보고]`, `[요청]`, `[회신]`, `[긴급]`.

elements.text: **Module completion gate (13.4).** You write a 200-word request email and a 1,500-word report, both approved by a professional native reviewer with no register or structure corrections.

items.text: 협상 negotiation · 조건 condition · 양보 concession · 조율 coordination · 합의 agreement · 절충 compromise · 대안 alternative · 요구 demand · 우선순위 priority · 마지노선 bottom line · 윈윈 win-win · 장기적 long-term
**Never say no directly.** Say `어렵습니다` and immediately offer an alternative.
**The silence after an offer is a tool.** Do not fill it.
**Leave them a way to agree.** Frame the concession as their decision, not your demand: `이렇게 하시면 어떨까요?`

elements.text: **Module completion gate (13.5).** A 15-minute negotiation role-play where you must obtain a 20% discount or a deadline extension, recorded, with both an alternative and a conditional offer used.

items.text: `넵` is the standard acknowledgement — it is polite, not slang. `네` is slightly formal, `응` is 반말.
`확인했습니다` and `알겠습니다` are the two acknowledgements that matter. `알겠습니다` accepts the task; `확인했습니다` only confirms receipt.
Voice notes are normal in Korean workplace messaging. Record one short and clear, never rambling.

rows: 지금 자리에 안 계신데, 메모 남겨 드릴까요?

elements.text: **Module completion gate (13.6).** You take a message on a work call, repeat it back accurately, and send the corresponding chat message in the correct register.

rows: senior sits farthest from the door
you pour for others; never for yourself
two hands, or one hand supporting the glass
조금만 주세요 / 저는 물로 하겠습니다 — never a bare no
declining is normal; leaving early needs a reason and a bow

items.text: **Safe topics:** weather, food, weekend plans, sports, travel, the commute.
**Ask about them, not yourself:** `주말에 뭐 하셨어요?` is the workhorse.
**Avoid:** politics, religion, salary, someone's age unless they raise it, and personal appearance.
**Self-deprecation works.** Korean humility norms mean a small joke at your own expense lands well: `제 한국어는 아직 멀었어요.`

elements.text: **Module completion gate (13.7).** You sustain fifteen minutes of workplace small talk with a native, covering four safe topics, with no dead air over four seconds.

rows: one page, photo, education-first for new grads
the most important document in Korean hiring

elements.text: **The 자기소개서 structure** — this is a genre with expected sections:

rows: your background, briefly, in a way that explains your values
a real weakness with a fix
what you did and what it produced
what you will do in the first two years

items.text: Korean cover letters are formulaic by design. The formula is not optional; the differentiation happens inside it.
Quantify everything. `매출 15% 증가에 기여` beats `열심히 일했습니다`.
The 90-second self-introduction: name and background → one concrete achievement with a number → why this role → close with enthusiasm. Rehearse to exactly 90 seconds.
Always have two questions ready, and never ask about salary in the first interview.
`궁금한 점 없습니다` is a weak answer. Have questions.

rows: 현재 ___을 받고 있고, 업무 범위를 고려하면 ___입니다.
면접을 더 진행한 뒤 논의하는 게 좋을 것 같습니다.

levels.title: MEDIA, LITERATURE, AND ACADEMIC KOREAN
levels.goal: Read the Korean that is written to be *read*, not spoken. By the end of this level you read a newspaper editorial and identify its argument, a short story and identify its narrative technique, a journal abstract and extract the method, and a poem and hear what it does with sound — and you can write an abstract and a literary analysis of your own.

dashboard.core tools: A newspaper, two novels, a poetry collection, a journal database (DBpia, RISS), a literary tutor
dashboard.main project: **`canon-lab`** — an analysis, a translation, and an abstract
dashboard.final outcome: Ten editorials analysed, two novels read, twenty poems read aloud, one abstract written, one story translated.

modules.title: The anatomy of a news article

rows: 政府, 明年 豫算 10% 擴大

items.text: The comma replaces the topic marker: `政府,` = 정부는.
Verbs vanish. Reconstruct them from the noun: `擴大` = 확대한다.
`與` (ruling party) and `野` (opposition) appear as single characters. Learn these two and half of political headlines open up.
`... 中` = in progress; `... 豫定` = scheduled; `... 檢討` = under review.

modules.title: The six decisions every translation makes

items.text: **Register.** 해요체, -다, or 합니다체? It changes the character.
**Rhythm.** Korean sentences are longer. Split them or keep them?
**Idioms.** Translate the meaning, or the image?
**Cultural terms.** Explain, transliterate, or substitute?
**Honorifics.** English has no system; how is hierarchy preserved?
**What to lose.** Something always goes.

sections.objective: **Level 14 completion rule.** You read a novel chapter without a dictionary and understand not only what happened but *how it was told*. That is the difference between reading Korean and reading literature in Korean.

levels.title: TOPIK II MASTERY
levels.goal: Score 230 or above on a full, timed, cold TOPIK II paper. Not 230 on a practice set you have seen before, and not 230 assembled from your best section scores on different days — 230 in one sitting, under exam conditions, with the clock running.
levels.prerequisites: Level 14 complete. In practice this means: you can read a newspaper editorial without a dictionary (L14), you know 300 Hanja at recall (L11), and you have written 1,200 words of 해라체 argument that a native did not correct for grammar (L12).

dashboard.study commitment: 2–3 hours per day, one full mock every two weeks
dashboard.core tools: Official past papers (at least 10 sets), an answer sheet, a stopwatch, a marker who scores 쓰기
dashboard.main project: **`topik-kit`** — three full timed mocks, a writing portfolio, and an error ledger
dashboard.final outcome: ≥ 230/300 on a paper you have never seen, with 쓰기 ≥ 72.

rows: Comprehension at native speed, once, with no replay
Controlled production under severe time pressure
Speed-reading and inference, not careful reading

elements.text: **Total: 300 points, 180 minutes, one sitting, one morning.**

rows: Can function in daily life; cannot work in Korean
Can hold a job with support; reads simple work documents
Can work independently; reads newspapers with effort
Can work at professional level; reads academic and literary text

elements.text: **Your target is 230. That is 77% — not 90%.** This single fact changes strategy completely. You are not trying to be excellent. You are trying to be *unbreakable in the parts you control*.
The most useful thing you can do in your first week is decide, in advance and on paper, which questions you intend to get right.

rows: Q1–35 with high confidence, 10 of Q36–50
Q1–40 with high confidence, 5 of Q41–50
Q51, Q52, Q53 near-perfect, Q54 at 60%

elements.text: **The arithmetic that decides your life for 180 minutes:** you can leave the last ten questions of 읽기 blank and still score 6, provided 쓰기 holds. You cannot leave 쓰기 to chance, because the section is only four questions — one bad essay costs you 20 points, which is ten reading questions' worth of margin.

rows: Doors close. Late arrivals are refused — no exceptions, no appeals

elements.label: Things that are not obvious until they cost you
elements.value: you must write your answers on the OMR sheet as you go, because there is no separate transfer time at the end. Bring a correction tape, not correction fluid — fluid is banned in most centres. Your ID must be the exact one you registered with.

items.text: Download three official past papers. Do not open them yet.
Sit one paper cold, untimed, and score it honestly. Record the section subtotals. This is your baseline, and it will be worse than you expect — that is the point.
Write your intended question-by-question strategy on one page, in pencil, and revise it after every mock.
You have a written baseline score for all three sections.
You can state, without looking, the point value of a single reading question and the total margin between 190 and 230.
You have read the official candidate rules for your test centre.

sections.title: 듣기: the anatomy of the section

rows: Choose the matching picture or graphic
vocabulary of everyday objects and places
the polite-but-wrong answer is always present
Identify where the conversation is happening / what follows
requires inference from register and vocabulary
Identify the man's or woman's central point
the other speaker says the plausible wrong answer
the opening sentence is a decoy
numbers are said once and often corrected
60–90 seconds of continuous native speech per item

modules.title: What you are allowed to read

elements.text: You get the answer options **before** the audio starts, and there is a short gap. That gap is the whole exam.
**The 30-second pre-read.** Read the four options, not to understand them but to build a prediction list:

headers: What you extract before the audio
rows: the topic field — one of these four will be said
`찬성한다` `반대한다` `우려한다` `기대한다` → listen for stance markers, not content
write the four numbers down; the audio will say all four, one of them twice
listen for the particle `에서` and the place-vocabulary field

modules.title: The three distractors the exam always uses

elements.text: Every wrong answer in block D–H is one of these. Learn to recognise them and the section gets dramatically easier.

rows: an option that restates the *other* speaker's position accurately
check *whose* idea the question asks about — usually one named sex
a statement that is factually in the audio but is not the answer to *this* question
read the question stem first, not the options
an option that is true but goes one step too far — `항상` `절대` `모든` `반드시`
extreme quantifiers are almost never correct

elements.text: **The single most reliable listening rule:** if an option contains `항상`, `절대`, `모두`, or `반드시`, it is wrong unless the speaker literally used that word. The exam writers use absolutes as a trap because they are easy to construct and easy to detect.

items.text: Take one past paper's 듣기 and do the first twenty questions with the transcript visible. Mark every place where the correct answer was paraphrased rather than repeated. You will find that almost none are verbatim.
Do the same twenty questions again with audio only. Compare.
Build a list of fifty attitude verbs and their typical audio cues (`걱정스럽다` → `-ㄹ까 봐`, `아쉽다` → `-았/었으면`, `기대된다` → `-ㄹ 것 같다`).
You can name the eight blocks and what each one tests.
You score ≥ 85/100 on a 듣기 section you have not heard before.
You have caught at least five "overreach" options in a single paper and can point to the word that gave them away.

sections.title: 듣기: the tactics that survive the audio

elements.text: When you miss something, you get **four seconds** to decide: keep listening or abandon the question. Most candidates lose five questions' worth of points by still processing question 34 while question 35 is playing.

elements.label: The decision rule
elements.value: if you cannot reconstruct the answer from your notes within four seconds of the audio ending, mark a guess and move. A guess is worth 0 or 2. A lost question 35 because you were still on 34 is also 0 or 2 — but you have now lost the option of guessing well.

modules.title: Note-taking that fits on one line

elements.text: You are not transcribing. You are writing a skeleton.

elements.label: Rule
elements.value: one line per question, maximum four words. If you are writing a sentence, you are not listening.

elements.text: Blocks G and H ask `남자의 태도는?` or `여자의 중심 생각은?` far more often than they ask for facts. The answer is almost always carried by one of these markers, not by the content.

rows: reluctant concession → the real point is after it
unintended consequence → usually the cause they admit
hedged opinion → the speaker's actual view
the speaker is about to contradict something said earlier
refusal to commit → answer is usually "uncertain"

modules.title: Numbers, times, and the correction reflex

elements.text: Korean exam audio says a number and then corrects it roughly a third of the time: `세 시... 아, 세 시 반이죠.` If you write the first number down and stop listening, you lose the question.

elements.label: The rule
elements.value: when you hear a number, hold your pencil above the paper. Write only after the next clause finishes.

items.text: Transcribe five block-H monologues in full, then compare against the official transcript. Count your errors by type: vocabulary, grammar, speed, or attention.
Do a full 듣기 section at 1.0× speed, then again at 1.15×. The second run is harder than the exam — it is training, not simulation.
Keep a "missed because" tally for every mock: unknown word / too fast / lost my place / misread the question.
Fewer than three "lost my place" errors across a full section.
You can identify speaker stance from the marker alone, with the content removed, on ten items.
듣기 ≥ 85/100 on two consecutive unseen papers.

sections.title: 읽기: the clock is the opponent

elements.text: Eighty-four seconds. A Korean newspaper paragraph is roughly 45 seconds of careful reading for a competent reader — and the later passages are longer, denser, and often technical.

elements.label: The consequence
elements.value: the passages in blocks A–E must be read in 40–50 seconds, because block H passages need 3–4 minutes each. If you spend 3 minutes on question 12, you have already failed question 45.

rows: three options are colloquially plausible but formally wrong
the correct slot is often *not* where the topic seems to shift
one option is true but not in this passage
the topic is the noun that repeats, not the first noun
the first sentence is usually not the one that starts with a connector
Insert a sentence into a paragraph
Choose the grammar form for the blank
three options paraphrase the same clause
Match a statement to a passage or a graph plus passage
the graph carries half the answer
requires reading the whole passage once
3–4 minutes each, and they are worth the same 2 points
Read the question and options first. You now know what to hunt for
Read the passage *for the answer*, not for comprehension. Headings, connectors, and the sentence containing the keyword
Eliminate the overreach and the true-but-irrelevant. If two remain, choose the one that matches the passage's *scope*
Fill the OMR. Never defer — you will not come back

elements.label: Hard rule for block K
elements.value: if you reach question 42 with fewer than 20 minutes remaining, you answer the remaining questions by keyword matching only — read the question stem, find the keyword's sentence, read that sentence and one before it, answer. You will get about half. That is 4–5 points you would otherwise lose to blank answers.

items.text: Do a full 읽기 section with a visible stopwatch, and write the timestamp when you finish each question. You are looking for the questions that ate 4 minutes.
Do blocks A–G only, 27 questions, in 25 minutes. Repeat until you finish with two minutes spare.
Read one block-K passage from a past paper with no time limit, then read it again with a 3-minute limit. Note what you had to give up.
You finish all 50 questions in 70 minutes on three consecutive attempts, guessing no more than six.
읽기 ≥ 80/100 on an unseen paper.
You can name, from memory, the four-step method and the block-K fallback.

elements.text: The single most learnable question type on the paper. The inserted sentence must attach to *something* — a pronoun, a repeated noun, or a connector.

headers: What to look for in the sentence being inserted
rows: there must be an antecedent immediately before the slot
a description must precede; a general claim must follow
the previous sentence must contain the opposite
the previous sentence must contain the cause
the previous sentence must contain the general claim being exemplified
the slot is where the paragraph's *topic* changes — usually last

elements.text: Do not read them in order. Find the sentence that **cannot** come first — the one that opens with a connector or a pronoun — and build outward from it.
Method:

items.text: Cross out every sentence beginning with a connector. Those are not first.
Find the sentence with a bare noun subject and no back-reference. That is usually first.
Chain by pronoun and by `-는데` / `-지만` / `-어서`.
Check the last sentence ends the paragraph's argument, not merely a detail.

elements.text: These test register and collocation, not meaning. All four options fit semantically. The deciding factors:

rows: is the passage 해요체, 합니다체, or 해라체? A `-습니다` form in a 해라체 passage is wrong regardless of meaning
`-에 달려 있다`, `-을 수밖에 없다`, `-기 마련이다` take fixed partners
the blank must agree with the tense established two sentences earlier
`-더라` implies hearsay or recollection; `-겠-` implies intention or supposition

elements.text: These come from real sources: economics, science, sociology, literary criticism. The vocabulary is beyond the 6,000-word list, and that is deliberate — the exam tests whether you can survive unknown words.

elements.label: The three-sentence strategy
elements.value: read sentence 1 (the claim), the sentence containing the keyword from the question, and the last sentence (the conclusion). Skip the middle. In most block-K passages, the middle is elaboration, and the same 2 points ride on the edges.

items.text: Take ten insert-the-sentence questions and, before answering, underline every deictic and connector. Answer using only the underlined words. Score yourself.
Take five block-K passages and write a one-line summary of each in Korean, 15 words maximum.
Build a personal list of 200 words that have appeared in block-K passages and that you did not know. Sort by frequency across papers.
You solve insert-the-sentence questions at ≥ 80% accuracy.
You can identify the first sentence of an ordering question in under 15 seconds.
You have a 200-word block-K vocabulary list in your SRS.

modules.title: The rules that are actually scored

rows: a `-습니다` clause in a 해요체 notice loses the point even if perfect
if the preceding clause is `-는데`, your clause must respect that relation
you are completing a clause; a full stop in the middle loses the point
the blank is not a summarising exercise
one misspelling typically costs the point, not half of it

elements.label: Minute 1
elements.value: read both passages and identify the register. Write it in the margin.

elements.label: Minute 2

elements.label: Minutes 3–4

items.text: Take ten Q51–52 pairs from past papers. For each, write the register and blank type before writing the answer.
Have a tutor mark them against the official rubric, not against "does it sound right".
Write twenty of them in one sitting, timed at two minutes per question.
18 of 20 on a set of ten Q51–52 pairs, marked by someone else.
You never lose a point to register mismatch across a full mock.

sections.title: 쓰기 Q53: describing data in 300 characters

elements.text: You are shown a graph, chart, or table — often with a survey premise — and asked to describe it in **200–300 characters**. It is worth **30 points**.

**The rule that decides everything:** you describe the data. You do not explain it, interpret it, or give an opinion about it. A single sentence beginning `이는 ... 때문인 것으로 보인다` is a deduction the rubric does not reward and can cost you points for straying from the task.

rows: what the data is, when, of whom
the largest or the headline number
the second figure, ideally compared to the first
the change, the smallest, the exception
`가장 높은 것으로 나타났다` `가장 많은 비율을 차지했다`
`-에 비해 두 배 이상 높았다` `-보다 약간 높은 수준이었다`
the task says describe; the rubric rewards relevance to the task
the rubric requires all major items, even briefly
below 200 characters reads as an incomplete response
`나타났다` five times reads as a low proficiency; vary it

items.text: Take six past Q53 prompts. Write each in exactly 250 characters. Count characters, not words.
Write the same prompt three ways: emphasising the largest figure, the change over time, and the contrast. Notice the task usually specifies which.
Have each marked against the official 30-point rubric, and record which of the four blocks lost points.
Six Q53 responses, all between 220 and 290 characters, none containing a causal explanation.
≥ 24/30 on a marked response.
You can write a Q53 in eleven minutes, leaving four for checking.

elements.text: A short topic statement — usually a social issue with two sides or a proposed change — and an instruction to give your opinion with reasons. **600–700 characters. 50 points. About 30 minutes.**

modules.title: The rubric, in the order it is scored

elements.text: Scoring is on three axes. Candidates obsess over grammar and ignore the first two, which are worth more.

rows: Did you answer *the question asked*, with reasons and examples relevant to it?
Is there an introduction, a body with distinct points, and a conclusion that closes?
Grammar accuracy, vocabulary range, spelling, appropriate register

elements.text: **The insight:** an essay with simple but correct grammar and a clear two-reason structure beats an essay with ambitious grammar and one reason. Difficulty is not rewarded. Completion is.

rows: restate the issue, state your position
`최근 ...이 늘면서 ...에 대한 논의가 활발해지고 있다. 나는 ...라고 생각한다.`
strongest reason plus a concrete example
second reason, or the opposing view and why it fails
restate the position, add a forward-looking close

modules.title: The essay rules that are not about grammar

rows: Use 합니다체 or 해라체, never mix
mixed register is the most common deduction
it reads as a register error, not a typo
the 구성 score rewards visible structure
the lower bound is a floor, not a target
it wastes characters and gains nothing
Leave two minutes to check spelling
`-되` vs `-돼` and `-로서` vs `-로써` are exam favourites

items.text: Write the same prompt twice: once with two reasons, once with one reason and a rebuttal. Have both marked. Learn which structure your marker rewards.
Write ten prompts in thirty minutes each, across two weeks. Increase the count to two per session by week four.
Build a personal bank of ten examples — Korean-specific, concrete, and reusable across prompts (an education policy, a workplace case, a technology change, a demographic fact).
Ten timed essays, all 600–700 characters, all scoring ≥ 35/50.
Zero register mixing across three consecutive essays.
You can plan a Q54 in four minutes on a prompt you have never seen.

sections.title: The vocabulary and grammar the exam actually reuses

elements.text: TOPIK reading and listening are built from a small pool of formal verbs. Learn them as collocations, not as words.

rows: the standard reporting verb of survey data
a critic pointed out — implies fault

elements.text: **Why this matters:** in block K, roughly one question per paper turns on distinguishing `주장했다` from `밝혔다`. One is a claim, the other is a statement of fact by an institution, and the correct answer depends on which.

rows: `-므로` cannot be followed by an imperative
`-는데` can also mean background, not contrast

elements.text: TOPIK passages mix registers deliberately. Before answering any question about a long passage, identify its register in the margin:
**One mark in the margin, every passage, every time.** Register errors are where most candidates lose block-G points, and register identification is a two-second habit.

items.text: Extract every `-다고 ...했다` construction from five past papers. Build a verb list with the noun it governs.
Take ten block-K passages and label the register of each in one word before answering.
Build a 300-item exam vocabulary deck from the words that repeat across three papers — not from a general word list.
You can produce the ten academic reporting verbs with their collocations, cold.
You identify register in under three seconds on any passage.
Your exam deck contains 300 words sourced from real papers, not from a textbook.

rows: Section drills: 듣기 blocks A–F only
Section drills: 읽기 blocks A–G only, 25 min

Full mock, timed, in exam conditions (morning, no phone, OMR sheet)

elements.text: Every wrong answer gets one line: **question number · block · why · the fix**.

rows: missed the pronoun `이러한` pointing back two sentences
always scan backwards two sentences for a deictic antecedent

elements.text: By week 8 you will have 100–150 lines. The **block counts** tell you exactly what to drill; the *reasons* tell you whether the problem is vocabulary, method, or time.

rows: no new material; one light review of your 쓰기 phrase bank
arrive 40 minutes early; ID in hand; no caffeine spike if you are a nervous test-taker
pre-read options; four-second rule; never leave a blank
do not discuss answers with anyone — it costs you focus and gains nothing
Q51–52 first (4 min), Q53 second (15 min), Q54 last (30 min), 1 minute buffer
blocks A–G fast, then block K with the keyword method; fill every OMR cell
check that no answer is unfilled. A blank is a guaranteed zero; a guess is a coin flip

items.text: Do the four scheduled full mocks. Score each section separately and plot the trend.
Do one mock in a room you do not control, with noise, to rehearse the real centre.
Rehearse the OMR transfer: 50 answers in under four minutes, neatly.
Four full timed mocks completed, ascending or stable.
Error ledger with ≥ 100 entries and block counts.
A mock score ≥ 230 with 쓰기 ≥ 72.

sections.title: If you already have TOPIK 5: the last thirty points

elements.text: Almost nobody is stuck because of listening. The distribution of the missing 30 points is remarkably consistent:

rows: under-length, one reason only, or register mixing
running out of time, guessing the last ten

elements.text: **Conclusion: the fix is almost always 쓰기 and reading speed, in that order.**

rows: blocks A–G in 25 minutes, daily, plus five block-K passages
two full mocks, error-ledger only, no new material
markers recognise them; content score collapses when the template does not fit the prompt
Doing more full mocks without reviewing them
volume without an error ledger produces the same score repeatedly
TOPIK 6 is not a grammar exam; it is a stamina and speed exam
novels are slow, and the exam is fast; use newspapers and past papers

Write the three-week plan with dates and drills.

읽기 block K accuracy ≥ 60%.

levels.title: TRANSLATION AND INTERPRETATION
levels.goal: Move meaning between Korean and one other language without losing the things that make it mean. By the end you can translate a 3,000-word document with a translator's note explaining every hard choice, and perform fifteen minutes of consecutive interpreting from audio you have never heard.
levels.prerequisites: Level 15 complete. In practice: TOPIK 6 level (230+), and — the part that actually matters — you can read a Korean sentence and say what it *does*, not only what it says.

dashboard.core tools: Parallel corpora, a glossary spreadsheet, a recorder, an interpreting tutor, published translations to compare against
dashboard.main project: **`bridge-kit`** — a translation portfolio, a 300-term glossary, and a recorded consecutive performance
dashboard.final outcome: Three translated texts with notes, a 15-minute consecutive interpretation at ≥ 80% content accuracy, and a 300-term glossary.

rows: a correct sentence that reads like a translation
a pause long enough to lose the room

modules.title: The four things that must survive

elements.text: A translation succeeds if these four cross the bridge. They are listed in order of how often they are abandoned.

headers: What it looks like when lost
rows: the facts are wrong — a hard failure, rare
a corporate apology reads like a text message, or a poem reads like a manual
the politeness, the threat, the joke, the reluctance — all gone
the sentence is correct and unreadable; a native would never have written it

elements.text: **The amateur trade:** sacrifice 2, 3, and 4 to preserve 1. **The professional trade:** sacrifice surface form to preserve all four.

modules.title: The unit is the sentence, and sometimes the paragraph

elements.text: Literal translation fails because Korean and English do not share sentence boundaries. A Korean sentence may contain four clauses that English would split into three sentences. A single English sentence may collapse into one Korean clause plus a trailing `-는데`.

elements.label: The rule
elements.value: if you find yourself translating clause by clause and the result is grammatical but strange, the boundary is wrong, not the words.

items.text: Take one paragraph of Korean newspaper prose and one of English newspaper prose on the same event. Compare sentence counts. Notice the ratio.
Translate a 150-word Korean paragraph three ways: maximally literal, maximally free, and balanced. Have a native read all three and tell you which one they would have written.
Write down, in one sentence each, what you think the four invariants mean for a business email.
You can state the four invariants without notes.
You can identify which invariant a given bad translation sacrificed.
You have produced three versions of one paragraph and can justify the balanced one.

rows: must be carried by verb choice or context
register is often invisible in English until it is wrong
the humility is lost unless the verb is upgraded
past tense plus a hint of personal witness ("I remember", "I found")
bare past tense that loses the witnessing

elements.text: English requires a subject. Korean drops it. When you translate into Korean, you must decide — every time — whether `you` becomes `너`, `당신`, `여러분`, a title, or nothing at all.

rows: `당신` is confrontational outside arguments and translations
drop the pronoun; let the verb carry it

elements.text: **The rule:** in Korean, `당신` and `너` are *marked*. Their absence is the default. If your Korean translation is full of `당신`, it was translated from English.

items.text: Take ten English sentences containing "you" and translate them into Korean without using `당신` once. Justify each choice.
Take a Korean customer-service notice in 해요체 and a corporate apology in 합니다체. Translate both into English and make the register difference visible to a reader who does not know Korean.
Find five Korean sentences with `-시-` and translate them so that a reader can tell who is being honoured.
Zero instances of `당신` in a 500-character Korean translation, unless deliberately marked.
A native reader can tell your 해요체 from your 합니다체 translation without seeing the source.
You can name the register of any Korean passage on sight.

sections.title: Korean into English: three structural problems

elements.text: Korean marks topic (`-은/는`) and subject (`-이/가`) separately. English marks only subject. The consequence: Korean sentences begin with a topic that is not the grammatical subject, and a literal translation produces a sentence with no engine.

elements.label: The method
elements.value: find the `-이/가` phrase. That is your English subject. The `-은/는` phrase becomes the object, the time expression, or the place.

elements.text: Korean drops subjects, objects, and sometimes verbs entirely. English cannot. When you translate, you must *supply* what Korean omitted — and get it wrong about 20% of the time if you are careless.
**The three questions to ask of every clause:**

items.text: Who is doing this?
What are they doing it to?
Is this a new fact or a continuation?

elements.text: If a Korean passage says `그렇게 하기로 했다` with no subject, the answer is in the previous sentence, and you must carry it forward into English.
This is the hardest structural feature of Korean, and the one that makes machine translation fail visibly.

elements.code: 그가 작년에 처음 만났다고 말했던 그 사람이 지금 우리 회사에서 일하고 있다.

elements.text: Everything before `그 사람` is a relative clause stacked onto a noun. English cannot do this. The **unpack-and-rebuild** method:

rows: Find the head noun — here `그 사람`
List the clauses attached to it, in order
Decide which becomes a relative clause, which becomes a separate sentence, which becomes an appositive
Rebuild in English order — usually head noun first, then clauses to the right

elements.label: Result
elements.value: "The man he said he'd first met last year now works at our company." Or, better, split: "He said he'd first met the man last year. That man now works at our company."

elements.text: **Rule of thumb:** a Korean modifier chain longer than three clauses becomes two English sentences. Native English writers do not stack; they serialise.

items.text: Take ten Korean sentences with `-은/는` topics that are not subjects. Translate them with the `-이/가` rule and check against a published translation.
Take five modifier chains of three or more clauses and unpack each into two or three English sentences.

Take a published Korean→English translation of a novel paragraph and back-translate it into Korean. Compare with the original. Note every place the translator chose differently from the source structure.
Ten topic-prominence sentences translated without a single "As for..." construction.
Five modifier chains unpacked, none exceeding two clauses in English.
A back-translation that recovers ≥ 90% of the original's propositions.

sections.title: English into Korean: the harder direction

elements.text: English has `a`, `the`, and zero article. Korean has `이`, `그`, `저`, and — most often — nothing.

rows: first mention takes no determiner; use a counter

elements.label: The rule
elements.value: English articles map to Korean *information structure*, not to Korean words. First mention → no marker or a counter. Second mention → `그`. Generic → bare noun with `-은/는`.

elements.text: English puts relatives to the right of the noun; Korean puts them to the left and without a relative pronoun. This is where machine translation produces Korean that is technically parseable and completely foreign.

rows: "The report that the team submitted last week was rejected."
"Anyone who wants to join should sign up."
"A policy that would help small businesses"

elements.label: Three fixes
elements.value: delete the `그`; choose the correct particle (`-이/가` vs `-은/는`) by information structure; and replace the literal verb with the collocation Koreans actually use (`거절되다` → `반려되다` in a corporate document).

elements.text: English prefers passive in formal writing; Korean prefers active with a plural subject, or the `-어지다` / `-게 되다` construction, or an impersonal noun.

rows: "It was decided that the meeting would be postponed."

elements.text: After a first draft, run four checks in this order. They catch about 80% of translationese.

rows: delete most; Korean repeats the noun or drops it
does every `-은/는` mark a topic, and every `-이/가` a new fact?
swap the ones that are decorative
is the verb a translation of an English verb, or the verb a Korean would use?
does every sentence end the way this register ends?
`-입니다` in a report, `-한다` in an editorial

items.text: Translate 500 words of an English news article into Korean, then run the four-pass Koreanify. Keep both drafts and count the changes.
Collect ten sentences of published English→Korean translation (from a bilingual book or a company website) and mark the places where the translator Koreanified rather than translated literally.
Have a native read your draft aloud and stop you at every sentence they would not have written. Those are your real errors, and they are usually not grammar.
A 500-word translation with fewer than five sentences a native would not have written.
Zero unnecessary `그` / `그녀`.
You can run the four passes in under twenty minutes on 500 words.

sections.title: Terminology: the glossary is the deliverable

elements.text: In a 40,000-word technical document, a term translated two ways is a defect, even if both are defensible. The reader builds a mental map; an inconsistent map costs them comprehension.

elements.label: The 10-term rule
elements.value: if a document uses a technical term more than ten times, it goes in the glossary before you translate sentence one.

elements.text: Never accept a dictionary's first suggestion. Verify every term against three independent sources.

rows: the official definition and the standard rendering
it is often the schoolbook version, not the industry version
**Industry usage** (the client's own documents, competitor sites, trade press)
it may be inconsistent, and may be wrong
**Parallel text** (a bilingual document using the same term)
proof that the term functions in context
parallel texts are scarce outside a few domains

elements.label: When the three disagree
elements.value: the client's usage wins for the client's document, and you flag it in the note.

rows: a party affected by a decision
`선물` is a gift, not "a present" in the financial sense
check the domain before the dictionary
gloss them separately, with the verb they take
`AI` is fine; `KPI` needs `핵심성과지표` on first use
`전자상거래` vs `이커머스` in the same client's materials
follow the client, note the inconsistency
`컨설팅` over `자문` in business, but `자문` in law

items.text: Build a 300-term glossary in one domain — pick one and stay in it (legal, medical, semiconductor, or game localisation).
For each term, record all three sources and the decision.
Translate a 1,000-word document using only glossary-approved terms, and count your deviations.
A 300-term glossary with three sources per entry.
A 1,000-word translation with zero unflagged terminological deviations.
You can explain why consistency outranks elegance in a technical document.

sections.title: The untranslatable: 정, 한, 눈치, and the rest

rows: it is not love, and it is not friendship; it accumulates
it is collective and historical as much as personal
the ability to read a situation without being told
"social awareness" loses the speed and the self-interest
`우리 엄마` is "my mum"; it is not a possessive but a belonging
`밥 먹었어?` is a greeting, not a question about food
implies noticing what was not meant to be noticed
the text is about the concept itself
reads as exotic in a news piece
the function matters more than the name
drop it, add the nuance elsewhere
it appears once and carries no argument

items.text: **Does the term carry an argument?** If yes, it must be visible. Transliterate or calque.
**Does it appear once?** If yes, functional equivalent is safest.
**Is the reader an outsider?** Then gloss at first use, once, in parentheses.
**Is the reader an insider?** Then never gloss; they will find it condescending.
Translate a 300-word Korean essay about 정 into English twice: once transliterating, once with a functional equivalent. Have a bilingual reader judge which serves the essay.
Collect ten Korean culture-bound terms and assign a strategy to each, with a written reason.
Find a published translation of a Korean novel and catalogue how the translator handled the food vocabulary.
Ten terms, each with a strategy and a justification.
Two complete versions of one culture-bound passage, and a defensible choice between them.
You can explain the outsider/insider gloss rule without notes.

elements.text: **This level targets consecutive.** Simultaneous requires a dedicated programme and is out of scope here — but note that consecutive practice is what makes simultaneous possible later.
You are not writing words. You are writing **structure**: who, did what, to whom, why, and the connector between ideas.

rows: a new speaker or agent gets a new line, always
a diagonal slash through the line
the single most dangerous thing to miss
names cannot be reconstructed from initials

elements.label: The layout rule
elements.value: notes go down the page in a vertical line, one idea per line, connectors in the left margin. This is what lets you read your notes back in the order the speaker said things.

rows: you have notes and cannot read them
simplify the notation; practise reading notes 10 minutes later
you fall 90 seconds behind and stop hearing
drop to the gist; a summarised segment beats a lost one
you say something confident and wrong
when uncertain, say "the speaker said X, and I want to confirm the figure" — never invent

elements.text: **The interpreter's first duty is not to lie.** A confident wrong number in a negotiation is worse than a request to repeat. Practise the sentence that buys you time, in both languages, until it is automatic.

rows: a news bulletin, your native language
a 5-minute Korean talk with numbers and names

elements.text: **Record every attempt.** The gap between what you think you said and what you actually said is where the learning is.

items.text: Build your notation system on paper and commit to it for two weeks. Do not change it mid-drill.
Do rung 1 and rung 2 daily for a week. Score yourself against the source transcript.
Record a 3-minute consecutive performance of a Korean news segment and have a bilingual listener mark it for accuracy, completeness, and delivery.
A notation system you can read back after 10 minutes with ≥ 90% accuracy.
Rung 4 at ≥ 80% content accuracy, three times.
Zero invented facts across five recorded performances.

sections.title: Sight translation and the timed pressure of the booth

elements.text: You cannot revise, you cannot search, and the audience hears your thinking. The skill is **chunking**: read a clause, hold it, say it, move on — while reading the next clause with the other eye.

headers: Why it is separate from translation
rows: you must break the sentence *before* you know how it ends
a hard term must be handled without a pause
hesitation reads as incompetence, even when the content is right

elements.text: You are usually given 1–3 minutes with the text before speaking. Spend it like this:

rows: read the title, the first sentence, and the last sentence — that is the argument
scan for numbers, names, and terms — mark them, because they cannot be improvised
read the first two paragraphs closely; the rest you will read cold

elements.text: When you hit a term you do not know, you have three options, in this order of preference:

items.text: **Circumlocute**: "a type of chemical used in semiconductor cleaning" — say what it does.
**Preserve and move**: say the term in the source language and continue — legitimate in a technical setting.
**Flag**: "the exact term here is technical; I'll come back to it" — and do come back.

elements.label: Never
elements.value: invent a term that sounds plausible. A wrong drug name or a wrong legal term is a real-world harm.

items.text: Sight-translate one Korean newspaper article per day for two weeks, recorded, cold.
Sight-translate a legal or medical text and use the circumlocution protocol on every unknown term.
Have a bilingual listener mark your delivery for hesitation markers and fillers.
Ten recorded sight translations.
Fewer than three invented terms across all ten.
Delivery with no pause longer than four seconds.

sections.title: Editing, revision, and the translator's note

rows: omissions, additions, wrong numbers, wrong names, mistranslated negation
sentences the target reader would not write

elements.text: **Read the target text alone on pass 2.** If you read source and target side by side you will see what you meant to write, not what is there.
A proper note has four parts, in this order:

rows: audience, purpose, register of the source and target
"a corporate apology, addressed to customers, formal in both languages"
the three to five hard choices and why
"정 rendered as 'attachment' rather than 'affection' to avoid romantic connotation"
"the honorific distinction between the CEO and the manager is not recoverable in English"
what you would ask the client
"whether the date in paragraph 3 is the signing or the effective date"

elements.text: **Why the note matters more than it looks:** a client who can see your reasoning can defend the translation to their own boss. A translator who never states a decision gets overruled on style by someone who has not read the source.

modules.title: The things a client actually complains about

rows: translationese — the four-pass Koreanify was skipped
register was not established before translating
no glossary, or the glossary was built from a dictionary
sentence boundaries were preserved instead of restructured
"It's fine but we can't use it"
the purpose of the text was never asked about

items.text: Translate a 1,000-word text and submit it with a full four-part note.
Have a native read the target text and mark every sentence they would rewrite. Count how many are accuracy errors versus fluency errors. The ratio tells you what to work on.
Take a published translation and write the translator's note it would have had.
Three translations with complete notes.
A revision cycle where pass 2 finds no accuracy errors that pass 1 missed.
One translation a professional would sign.

rows: Read the source and decide whether it is machine-appropriate (a manual, yes; a poem, no)
Machine-translate, then **never accept a segment without reading the source beside it**
Use the output as a first draft, not a translation
Run the four-pass Koreanify on every machine segment
Log every recurring machine error in your glossary — the machines repeat themselves, and so do their mistakes

elements.text: **The error signature of Korean machine translation:**

rows: the model does not track speaker relationships

modules.title: What you are still responsible for

elements.text: Everything the tool cannot see: who the reader is, what the document is for, which of two equal readings is the intended one, and whether a sentence will embarrass the client. **The tool produces text. You produce a translation.**

items.text: Machine-translate 800 words, then edit it properly. Time both stages. Note which stage is longer — it is usually editing.
Catalogue fifteen machine errors by type using the table above.
Build a "machine error" sheet and add to it every week.
An edited machine translation that a native cannot identify as machine-assisted.
A 15-item error catalogue with types.
A written rule for which document types you will not machine-translate.

sections.title: The portfolio, and the professional path

rows: demonstrates that you can write copy that sells
demonstrates judgement — the thing that distinguishes you
demonstrates that you can do it live

elements.text: Professional translation rates in Korea are usually quoted per **자** (character, in the Korean source) for Korean→foreign, and per word for foreign→Korean. At a beginner-professional stage, the more important number is your **daily capacity**: most translators produce 2,000–3,000 자 per day of publishable output, and a beginner produces half that.

elements.label: The rule for pricing your first jobs
elements.value: price the work, not the hours, and never accept a rate you cannot sustain over a month of full-time work.

rows: a company's global team, a publisher, a broadcaster
a portfolio plus a test translation
a portfolio, a specialisation, and reliability
domain knowledge plus a certification route

items.text: Assemble the five portfolio pieces. Have a professional read them and tell you which one you should lead with.
Write a 200-word translator's bio in both languages.
Take one paid test translation, even at a low rate, and treat the deadline as absolute.
A complete five-piece portfolio.
One recorded consecutive performance in it.
A written answer to "what is your specialisation, and why".
