A publisher offers to pay per word of the English target. Why might that be a bad deal for a Korean source, and what would you counter with?

levels.title: NATIVE-ADJACENT FLUENCY
levels.goal: Be mistaken for a native for a sustained stretch — not on the phone for thirty seconds, and not because you said one idiom correctly, but for twenty minutes in a conversation you did not prepare.  **What this level is not.** It is not accent elimination. Some learners reach near-native prosody and some never do, and the difference is mostly age of onset and ear. Accent is the least important thing in this level and the thing learners obsess over most. **Being mistaken for native and being native-adjacent are different targets, and only the second one is required here.**

dashboard.study commitment: 2 hours per day, at least half of it in live conversation
dashboard.core tools: Three native friends who will tell you the truth, a recorder you actually use, Korean-language media consumed for pleasure
dashboard.main project: **`fluency-proof`** — a 60-minute unprepared talk, a 3,000-word short story, and a native-blind test
dashboard.final outcome: Sixty minutes of speech with no preparation, a short story a Korean would finish reading, and a twenty-minute conversation in which the other person did not know.

rows: you speak for a minute without a visible search for grammar
you take your turn at the speed Koreans take theirs
no gap longer than 1.5 seconds in a three-way conversation
you hear what was not said
you correctly identify a refusal that used no negative word
you laugh at the right moment, not two seconds late
you switch level mid-conversation without thinking
honour a superior and joke with a peer in the same minute

modules.title: The five things that still mark you

elements.text: These are what a Korean hears as foreign, in roughly descending order of how often they occur. None of them are grammatical.

rows: every sentence has a subject, verb, and object
drop pronouns; let the verb carry the meaning
Korean is not stress-timed; the phrase carries the beat
too clear, too slow, no elision
saying the obvious, because you fear being misunderstood
trust the listener; cut a third

elements.text: The only honest measurement is this: **a Korean who does not know you talks to you for twenty minutes and does not ask where you are from.**
It is an unreliable test — a polite Korean may not ask even if they suspect. So use the four-probe version:

rows: a stranger on the phone does not detect you (no visual cues)
you follow a three-way conversation with overlapping speech and interruptions
you laugh before the punchline lands, because you saw it coming
a Korean corrects your Korean as if you were a native who misspoke, not a learner who erred

elements.text: **The fourth probe is the real one.** When a Korean says `그거 아니고...` rather than `외국인이시죠?`, you have crossed. It means they have stopped modelling you as a learner.

items.text: Record a five-minute unscripted monologue on a random topic, then listen for the five markers above. Count them.
Have a native friend rate you 1–5 on each of the five components. Ask them to be unkind; explain why you are asking.
Book one phone call with a stranger — a restaurant, a bank, a government office — where the only information is your voice.
A written self-assessment and a native assessment of all five components, with numbers.
Fewer than five textbook-completeness markers in five minutes of recorded speech.
One phone call completed where the other party did not identify you as foreign.

sections.title: The sound of real speech: reduction, elision, and speed

elements.text: Written Korean and spoken Korean differ systematically. These are the highest-frequency reductions, and using them is what makes speech sound natural.

rows: `그러면 안 돼` → `그럼 안 돼` → `그럼 안 댜`

elements.text: **Why this matters more than it looks:** a learner who speaks with textbook clarity sounds *careful*. Careful is the signal. Koreans reduce because the information is redundant; if you do not reduce, you sound like you are reading aloud.
Korean is a **phrase-timed** language with a light pitch accent that is not lexical, plus a final contour that carries politeness.

rows: rising = question or softening; falling = statement or finality
flat endings sound cold or robotic
each phrase resets high, then descends
monotonous descent across a whole sentence
the final syllable of a turn is stretched for politeness

elements.label: The drill that works
elements.value: shadow a news anchor for five minutes, then a drama scene, then a variety show. The three use different rhythms, and the third is what conversation actually sounds like.

items.text: Transcribe 60 seconds of a Korean variety show verbatim — including the reductions — then read your transcription aloud and compare with the audio.
Shadow (speak simultaneously, not repeat after) five minutes of audio daily for a month. This is the single highest-yield drill in this level.
Record yourself saying the same sentence five ways: flat, rising, with phrase breaks, fast, and warm. Have a native rank them.
Shadowing 5 minutes a day for 30 consecutive days, recorded.
A native listener identifies your speech as "natural" rather than "clear" on a blind listen.
You produce the twelve reductions in the table above without thinking.

modules.title: The four engines of Korean humour

rows: the familiar is inflated until it breaks
you lower yourself to raise the room
very common in group settings, and a social obligation
아재개그, which is a whole genre of deliberately bad puns
the joke is in the response, not the setup
variety shows are built on reaction, not material

modules.title: 아재개그, and why bad puns matter

elements.text: 아재개그 is a genre of pun so weak it becomes funny through the telling. It is a social ritual: the teller knows it is bad, the listener groans, and the groan is the point.

elements.label: Why you should learn three of them
elements.value: not because they are funny, but because deploying one is a recognised move in Korean social humour. It signals that you are *inside* the game rather than observing it. A foreigner who tells a bad 아재개그 and waits for the groan has made a cultural joke about the culture, which is a different and better joke than a good pun.

rows: the teller reacts *with* the room; deadpan is less common than shared laughter
you must recover fast, and self-deprecatingly
seniority matters — a junior jokes *at* themselves, not at the senior

elements.text: **The social constraint that surprises learners:** humour in Korean workplaces is often used to *soften a request or a criticism*, not to entertain. Reading a joke as entertainment when it is actually an instruction is a real professional hazard.

The hardest part is not producing jokes; it is laughing at the right moment. Korean humour is often carried by **tone and timing rather than content** — the same sentence is funny or serious depending on the lengthening of the final syllable.

elements.label: The habit
elements.value: when a group laughs and you did not, do not ask "what did they say". Ask "what was the *turn*". The joke is usually in the last three syllables, said slowly.

items.text: Watch one episode of a Korean variety show with Korean subtitles, then again with none. Note which jokes you missed and why: vocabulary, reference, or timing.
Learn three 아재개그 and deploy one in a real conversation. Record the reaction honestly.
Keep a "joke log": ten things that made a Korean laugh in your presence, and what the mechanism was.
You have made a Korean laugh at something you constructed, not repeated.
You can name the mechanism of ten jokes you heard.
You deferred a joke and it landed on the second attempt — and you know what changed.

elements.text: Underlying logic: the relationship survives the message. Direct refusal, direct criticism, and direct disagreement all risk the relationship, so they are routed through implication. This is not dishonesty — it is a different contract about what a sentence is *for*.

elements.label: Consequence
elements.value: the literal content of a Korean sentence and its social content can be opposite, and the listener is expected to resolve the difference.

elements.text: Five ways to say no, in ascending order of softness. All of them are no.

rows: I will look into it and contact you
no, and there will be no contact

elements.text: **The trap:** `긍정적으로 검토하겠습니다` sounds like a yes and is not. It means the matter is alive, not that it is approved. Learners who treat it as approval and then act on it do real professional damage.

rows: discomfort — someone senior disagrees and will not say so
disagreement; the sentence is deliberately unfinished
"I think you're wrong, and I will not argue"
"I don't want to be the one who says no"
a question about your decision — `절차는 어떻게 되나요?` can mean "this was wrong"
they are giving you a chance to correct yourself
you have crossed a line, and they are re-establishing distance

elements.text: You must send as well as receive. The three moves:

rows: `그날은 좀 어려울 것 같아요. 다음에 꼭 모셔 주세요.`
`말씀하신 부분도 맞는데, 혹시 이 부분은 어떻게 볼까요?`
`혹시 시간 되실 때 잠깐 뵐 수 있을까요?`

items.text: Take ten Korean refusals from dramas, emails, or real life and classify them on the ladder.
In your next three conversations, deliberately use a rung-3 or rung-4 refusal and observe whether it was understood.
Ask a Korean friend, after a meeting, "what did they actually mean by X". Compare with your reading. Do this ten times.
You correctly classify ten refusals, verified by a native.
You have declined something using a soft form and got the outcome you wanted.
You can state, in Korean, what `그럴 수도 있겠네요` means, without hedging.

elements.text: Natives switch constantly. The rule is not "one register per relationship" but "one register per *moment*".

rows: 합니다체, even between close colleagues, if a client is present
반말, usually by explicit offer: `말 놓으세요`
register frequently *drops* to 반말, which is the insult

elements.text: The transition to 반말 is a ritual, not a drift.

rows: `아직은 좀 그래요` — not an insult, a boundary

elements.text: **The error that matters:** a learner who drifts into 반말 because a senior used it once. The senior's 반말 is an offer, not an instruction; the junior waits for explicit permission or mirrors only after it is given — and even then, in a group with an older member present, the junior may hold 해요체.
The hardest thing to learn and the clearest native marker: honouring one person while addressing another in the same sentence.

rows: To a peer, about a senior
`과장님이 아까 말씀하셨는데, 우리도 준비하는 게 좋을 것 같아.`
To a senior, about a peer
`민준 씨가 확인한다고 했습니다.` — no `-시-`, because the subject is not honoured
honour the verb, neutralise the noun: `관계자분들께서 확인해 주셨습니다.`

elements.label: The rule
elements.value: `-시-` follows the *subject*, not the listener. Honouring the wrong person is a louder error than using the wrong ending.

rows: you keep 합니다체 with a friend after they have switched; it reads as coldness or distance
you use 반말 before the offer; it reads as disrespect, and no Korean will correct you to your face

items.text: Script a 90-second scene: you greet a client in 합니다체, turn to a colleague in 해요체, and answer your phone to a friend in 반말. Perform it, record it.
In one real day, note every register switch you observed — yours and others'. Aim for ten.
Have a native read a paragraph of your writing, then ask you to say the same content to three different people. Compare the three.
A recorded 90-second performance with three correct switches and zero drops.
Ten observed switches logged, with the trigger for each.
You can explain why `-시-` follows the subject and not the listener.

sections.title: Slang, youth language, and the decay curve

elements.text: Slang is the highest-risk vocabulary in the language for a foreign learner, because **getting it slightly wrong is worse than not using it at all.** A Korean who uses last year's slang to a twenty-year-old sounds like a visiting relative. A foreign learner who does it sounds like a textbook that has been taught by an older textbook.

elements.label: The rule
elements.value: learn to *understand* fifty slang terms and *use* five. Comprehension is safe; production is a minefield.

elements.text: These are recent, widely understood, and mostly stable enough to be recognisable for a while. Glosses are functional, not dictionary definitions.
Before you use any slang term, ask three questions:

rows: Would a 25-year-old use it without irony?
it is dated — understand it, don't produce it
it is too niche for general use
Would you use it in front of a client?

elements.label: The professional rule
elements.value: in any setting where money or hierarchy is involved, use no slang. `워라밸` and `N잡러` are borderline-acceptable workplace vocabulary; `쌉가능` is not.

elements.text: Slang decays at roughly five to seven years; some terms persist as "older person's slang", which is worse than disappearing.

rows: `눈치`, `정` — these are not slang, they are Korean

elements.label: Maintenance
elements.value: refresh your comprehension list twice a year from actual media, and never let your productive slang be older than two years.

items.text: Watch one episode of a current Korean variety show and list every term you did not know. Add ten per month to a comprehension-only deck.
Ask three Koreans of different ages whether they would use each of the fourteen terms above. Build the generational map yourself.
Write a 200-word dialogue between two 22-year-olds and have a 22-year-old mark it.
Fifty slang terms understood, five actively used, and a written note on what each of the five is safe for.
A three-generation check performed on ten terms with real informants.
You have never used slang in a professional email.

sections.title: Shared reference: the culture behind the words

modules.title: Why reference is harder than vocabulary

elements.text: A Korean sentence can contain a reference that carries half the meaning and none of the information. `요즘 애들은` presupposes a theory of generations. `우리 때는` presupposes a shared past. Neither can be looked up, because neither is a definition.
Koreans use generational labels as arguments. Each one carries a claim about who is responsible for what.

rows: those born in the 1960s, politically active in the 1980s
the generation that democratised; now the establishment
the cohort facing precarious work after 2008
those who have given up three or five things (dating, marriage, children, home, hope)
a blended millennial + Gen Z label
contested; many Koreans reject it as a media invention
the open-ended version: giving up N things

elements.text: **How to handle these:** use them to *read*, not to *speak*. Saying `MZ세대는...` in a room of people in their twenties is a known way to sound like a consultant. Saying it in an essay about workplace conflict is normal.
Every educated Korean has these as background. You do not need depth; you need recognition and the correct emotional register.

rows: collective trauma; `IMF 때` is a unit of hardship
the Han River Miracle, rapid industrialisation
pride, with an undertow of cost
national event; everyone has an opinion

elements.text: You cannot share a generation's television, but you can share its *current* references. The rule is topical, not historical: know what is on air now.

rows: the two or three currently discussed shows
one long-running show and one current hit
the front page of two papers, daily, including the comment section's tone
one sport, with the current national storyline
the current trend — what people queue for this year

items.text: Read one editorial and one entertainment headline daily for a month. Note every reference you had to look up; that list is your syllabus.
Ask a Korean friend to explain `MZ세대` and their opinion of the term. The opinion is the useful part.
Watch one episode of a currently airing drama with Korean subtitles and no dictionary, and write down every reference you missed.
You can explain six generational labels and why each is contested.
You can name the historical references above and the emotional register each requires.
You have a daily news habit in Korean that has survived a month.

sections.title: The long monologue: speaking for an hour

modules.title: Why an hour is a different skill

elements.text: Five minutes is a set piece. Sixty minutes is a *structure*. The failure mode is not grammar — it is running dry at minute twenty-two and then repeating yourself for forty minutes.

elements.label: The arithmetic
elements.value: at a normal speaking rate, sixty minutes is roughly 9,000–12,000 Korean syllables. You need enough *content*, not enough *words*.

elements.text: A long talk runs on four tanks, drawn in order, and each one refills the last.

rows: what you think and why in one sentence
three concrete examples, told as stories
what follows if you are right
returning to tank 2 with a new example

elements.label: The refill trick
elements.value: every time you feel the tank emptying, return to a *story*, not to abstraction. Stories are inexhaustible because detail is infinite. Abstractions are finite and you will hit the wall.

elements.text: What holds an hour together is not vocabulary but signposting. Have these automatic.
**Buying time is a skill, not a failure.** `잠깐 생각을 정리해 보면` said calmly reads as deliberation. Silence with a searching expression reads as a vocabulary gap. The difference is entirely in the phrase.

rows: a random prompt, recorded, one listener
no prep, two listeners, questions at the end

elements.text: **Record all of them.** Listen at 1× for grammar, and at 1× a second time for content — you will find that the grammar is fine and the content is thin, which is the actual problem to fix.

items.text: Do the twelve-week build. Do not skip the middle; the 30-minute wall is where the skill is made.
After each recording, count filler words per minute. Target under five.
Have a listener interrupt at three random points and ask a question. Resume without losing the thread.
Three recorded monologues of 45 minutes or longer.
One 60-minute talk with two listeners and live questions.
Filler rate under five per minute across a full recording.

sections.title: Writing a short story in Korean

modules.title: Why fiction is the hardest test

elements.text: Non-fiction lets you use the registers you have drilled. Fiction requires **voice** — a narrator whose sentences are consistent, whose omissions are deliberate, and whose dialogue sounds like people rather than like examples.

It also requires the thing that Korean short fiction does better than almost any other tradition: **restraint**. The Korean short story is often built around what is not said, and around a situation that does not resolve.

rows: a scene, not a thesis — the first sentence places you in a room
an ordinary situation with one pressure applied to it
a small fracture, not a plot twist — often one line of dialogue
open. The story stops; it does not conclude. Meaning is left with the reader
3,000–8,000 characters is the classic magazine range

elements.text: **The most common foreign mistake:** resolving the story. Korean short fiction frequently ends *before* the resolution, on an image. If your ending explains what it meant, cut it.

rows: the story turns on what the narrator cannot see
distance with access to one mind
older fiction; hard to sustain without sounding dated
the narrator absorbs the character's voice
the hardest and the most modern — see L14 §14.4

elements.text: Four rules, learned from reading rather than from grammar.

rows: the same line in 반말 and 해요체 is a different scene
real dialogue deflects; a direct answer reads as an exam
trailing off is how Korean dialogue avoids closure
`그가 말했다` is rarer in Korean fiction than in English; the line-break does the work
Transcribe a page of dialogue from a Korean novel you admire. Count the speech tags.
Write a 500-word scene with two characters and no plot.
Write 1,500 words with one pressure and no resolution.
Have a Korean writer mark it for voice, not grammar.

items.text: Read 현진건 「운수 좋은 날」 and 이효석 「메밀꽃 필 무렵」, then 윤흥길 「장마」. Note how each ends.
Write one scene per week for eight weeks, each 500–800 words, each with a different viewpoint.
Submit one story to a Korean writing group or a language-exchange critique circle. Take the criticism on structure, not on particles.
A 3,000-character story with a turn, an open ending, and dialogue a Korean would believe.
One native reader finishes it without stopping, and says so.
You can name the viewpoint and the voice strategy of your own story.

sections.title: Reading at native speed, and the invisible error

elements.label: Why speed matters beyond convenience
elements.value: below a threshold, reading is decoding and comprehension collapses. Above it, reading becomes *thinking*, and you can disagree with a text while reading it — which is the point of being literate in a language.

rows: title, first sentence of each paragraph, last paragraph
eyes on the left edge, hunting the keyword

elements.label: The rule that builds speed
elements.value: never re-read a sentence. If you missed it, keep going — the redundancy in real prose will recover the meaning. Re-reading is the habit that keeps learners at 120 characters/min forever.

elements.text: At this level, your errors stop being grammatical and become *slightly off* — the sentence a Korean would not have written, with nothing wrong with it.

rows: `-은/는` used for emphasis where it marks topic

elements.text: **The only reliable detector is a native reader.** Your own ear cannot hear these, which is why L18's teaching work is the real fix: explaining the language is how you finally see it.

items.text: Time yourself on five articles a week for a month. Record words per minute and comprehension after.
Write 500 words of opinion prose and have a native mark every sentence they would rewrite, with a reason. Categorise the reasons using the table above.
Read one novel in Korean with no dictionary, at speed, and accept 85% comprehension.
350 characters/min on news with ≥ 85% comprehension, measured.
Twenty labelled invisible errors, categorised, with fixes.
One novel finished without a dictionary.

modules.title: The five features of a foreign accent

rows: minimal-pair drills, spectrogram feedback, a coach
drill the unreleased stop; Korean stops are not aspirated finally
minimal pairs with a native, 20 reps each
this is where "sounds foreign" mostly lives, and it is the least fixable
No identifiable accent on short utterances
yes, with 6–12 months of focused prosody work
Mistaken for native on the phone, consistently
yes for some, no for others, and no amount of work guarantees it
Mistaken for native in a long conversation
depends more on 17.1–17.7 than on pronunciation

elements.text: **The thing to internalise:** accent is the *last* thing Koreans use to decide you are foreign. Rhythm, reference, and subtext come first. A learner with a slight accent who handles 눈치 perfectly is treated as a fluent speaker; a learner with perfect vowels who misses a refusal is treated as a foreigner who speaks well.

items.text: Record the same paragraph at the start and the end of twelve weeks. Play both to a native, blind, and ask which sounds more natural.
Do minimal-pair drills for the five tense consonants, 20 reps each, recorded.
Have a coach identify your top two features and ignore the rest for twelve weeks.
A before-and-after recording, judged by a blind native listener.
Two features identified, worked on, and measurably improved.
A written statement of what you have decided not to fix, and why.

levels.title: TEACHING AND LIFELONG MASTERY
levels.goal: Two things. First, be able to *explain* Korean — which is the deepest test of understanding there is, and the only one that exposes the gaps that fluency hides. Second, build the regime that keeps the language alive for decades, because the single most common outcome of reaching an advanced level is losing it by neglect.  **Why teaching is the final level.** A user of a language can be excellent and still not know why anything works. A teacher must be able to say what the rule is, when it bends, which exceptions matter, and why the learner's version was wrong rather than merely different. That knowledge cannot be faked, and building it fixes things fluency never touched.

dashboard.suggested duration: 3–6 months to the teaching certification; the maintenance regime is permanent
dashboard.study commitment: 2 hours per day, of which at least one hour is teaching or preparing to teach
dashboard.core tools: One or two real learners, a grammar reference (국립국어원, 한국어 문법 사전), a rubric you built, a recorder
dashboard.main project: **`the-teacher`** — a taught unit, a diagnosis, a curriculum, and a rubric
dashboard.final outcome: You taught a 60-minute lesson that worked, diagnosed a learner's error pattern, and can explain any structure on demand.

sections.title: What teaching demands that using does not

rows: you can name the structure and its constraints
you can tell *why* a learner produced this error
you know which order a learner should meet things in

elements.text: **The asymmetry that matters:** you learned Korean in an order nobody would design. You met `-는데` in a drama, `-더라` in a song, and the honorific system in a workplace. A teacher has to construct a better order than the one they lived through — and that requires knowing the dependencies, not just the facts.

modules.title: The three questions you must be able to answer

items.text: **What is the rule?** (form and meaning)
**When does it not apply?** (constraints, register, exceptions)
**Why did the learner get it wrong?** (diagnosis)

elements.text: If you can only answer question one, you are a native speaker with a textbook, which is not a teacher.

You will be worse than a native Korean teacher at explaining Korean culture and worse than a trained teacher at classroom management. What you have that neither has: **you did this recently, consciously, and from outside** — which means you remember what it was like not to know, and you know which explanations actually worked on you.
**Teach from that.** Your comparative advantage is not authority. It is the memory of confusion.

items.text: Take three structures you use automatically (`-는데`, `-더라`, `-시-`). Write the rule, the constraints, and three exceptions for each, without looking anything up. Then check yourself.
Find one learner and ask them to explain a grammar point they know well. Note what they cannot explain.
Write your "confusion memories": the five things that took you longest to understand, and what finally made them click.
Three structures documented with rule, constraints, and exceptions.
Five confusion memories written, each with the resolution.
You can state in one sentence what your comparative advantage is as a teacher.

sections.title: The metalanguage: saying how Korean works

elements.text: A Korean says `-시-` correctly and has no idea it is called 주체 높임 선어말어미. That is not ignorance — it is the normal condition of a native speaker. Explicit knowledge and implicit ability are stored separately, which is why every Korean teacher training programme teaches grammar that the trainees already use perfectly.

rows: the invariant part, the inflecting part
a noun that cannot stand alone
a form that requires a partner

elements.text: Every learner hits these, and every learner needs them explained in one page, not thirty.

**The teaching point learners never get:** the irregular classes are not lists to memorise. They are historical sound changes that applied to a *subset* of verbs, which is why `춥다` is irregular and `좁다` is not. Explaining that turns thirty memorised items into one rule with exceptions — which is what a teacher does and a textbook does not.

elements.label: The classic teaching error
elements.value: presenting honorifics as one system. They are four, they operate independently, and a sentence can honour the subject and insult the listener at the same time — which is exactly what a learner does when they use `-시-` with 반말.

items.text: Write a one-page grammar sheet for three structures, using the terminology above, and test it on a real learner.
Take a paragraph of your own Korean and label every ending as 선어말 or 어말.
Explain the ㅂ irregular class in under 90 seconds, out loud, without notes.
The eleven terms defined from memory, with examples.
The seven irregular classes explained with the reason, not just the rule.
One learner understood your explanation on the first attempt.

rows: the L1 pattern applied to Korean
English speaker: `나는 행복한이다` from "I am happy"
an error that has stopped responding to correction
the learner avoids the structure entirely
if it disappears when they slow down, it is performance; if it survives, it is competence

**Is it in a structure they avoid elsewhere?**

elements.text: You cannot diagnose from writing alone, because writing is edited. Sit with the learner and do three things:

items.text: **Elicit the structure** without naming it: "tell me about a time you almost missed a train".
**Ask them to self-correct**: "anything you'd change?" — this separates slips from gaps.
**Ask them to explain the rule**: a learner who can state the rule and still breaks it has a processing problem, not a knowledge problem, and the fix is fluency practice, not explanation.

elements.text: For each learner, keep one page:

rows: which grammar point it belongs to

elements.label: The rule
elements.value: work on **two** errors at a time. A learner given eight corrections fixes none of them.

items.text: Collect 200 words of a learner's writing and 3 minutes of their speech. Build the error profile.
Compare written and spoken: the difference is their *monitoring*, not their knowledge.

elements.text: Six moves, from least to most intrusive. Use the lowest rung that works.

rows: **Recast** — say it correctly, naturally, without comment
learner: `어제 영화 봤어요?` → you: `아, 어제 영화 봤어요?` (correcting tense by echo)
**Repeat the error with a rising tone**

elements.label: Why the ladder matters
elements.value: rungs 1–3 keep the conversation going and preserve face. Rungs 5–6 stop the flow, and a learner corrected at rung 5 five times in ten minutes will stop speaking. In a conversation class, live almost entirely on rungs 1–3 and save rung 5 for the review at the end.

modules.title: What to correct, and what to let go

rows: a slip the learner catches themselves
a one-off error in a hard sentence
register errors in a professional context

elements.text: **The rule of two:** two corrections per session, chosen deliberately, marked in your notes, revisited next time. A learner who fixes two things a week fixes a hundred things a year. A learner corrected on everything fixes nothing, because none of it is retained.

Research on corrective feedback is consistent on one point: **frequency of correction predicts uptake, and frequency of praise predicts willingness to speak.** You need both, and you need them in a ratio a learner can feel — roughly three positive or neutral interactions for every correction.
**It must be specific.** `잘했어요` is noise. `방금 '-는데'를 자연스럽게 썼어요. 그건 어려운 거예요` is information.
Fossilised errors need a different method, because correction has already failed.

rows: **Name it explicitly.** "You have a habit I want to break. It will feel wrong."
**Make it conscious.** Drill it in isolation, 20 reps, until it feels strange.
**Contrast it.** Put the correct and incorrect forms side by side, ten times.
**Monitor it.** For two weeks, every time they produce it, you raise one finger — no words.
**Re-test** in free speech after a month. If it returns, the fossil is deeper than the drill.

items.text: Record yourself teaching and count your rungs. Most new teachers live at rung 5 and think they are helping.

elements.label: The inversion that matters
elements.value: textbooks go language → task. Teaching goes task → language. The learner acquires the structure because they needed it five minutes ago, not because it was chapter four.

elements.text: A balanced course contains all four, in roughly equal time. Omit one and the learner stalls.

elements.label: The common design failure
elements.value: a course that is 80% language-focused learning — which is what most self-study and most bad textbooks are — produces learners who know about Korean and cannot use it.

elements.text: **The "notice" phase is the one teachers skip and the one that matters.** A structure they noticed themselves is retained; a structure they were told about is not.

elements.text: A usable rubric has **three or four criteria**, each with **four bands** and a **one-line descriptor per band**. More than four criteria and nobody reads it; fewer than three and it measures one thing.

elements.text: Score the same task at the start and end of a unit, with the same rubric. **The delta is the learning** — not the absolute score. A learner who moves from band 2 to band 3 on register has learned more than one who was already at band 4 and stayed there.

elements.text: The failure mode is presenting culture as rules: "Koreans always...", "you must never...". This produces learners who are anxious, who over-apply the rule in the wrong context, and who cannot read the exceptions — which are most of the cases.

rows: there are five ways to say no, and the choice depends on relationship and stakes
hierarchy is one axis among several, and it is negotiated, not fixed
"Koreans eat dog" / "Koreans are obsessed with beauty"
a stereotype with a partial fact inside it, which is the definition of a stereotype
true in some contexts, optional in others, and nobody notices if you do not

modules.title: The three-question method for any cultural claim

rows: age, region, class, generation — the claim is usually narrower than stated
every norm has exceptions, and the exceptions are the interesting part
mild awkwardness, or real offence — the learner needs the scale

elements.text: A learner who knows "Koreans use honorifics" will be lost the first time a boss uses 반말 to them. A learner who knows "honorifics track the *relationship*, and the relationship changes" will survive.

elements.label: The rule
elements.value: every cultural claim you teach must come with its exception, in the same lesson. A claim without an exception is a stereotype with good manners.

elements.text: You will be asked to explain things a Korean would never have to. That is an advantage: you can explain the *comparison*, which a native cannot. Do not fake authority you do not have — say "I notice that..." rather than "Koreans believe...".

sections.title: The decay curve, and the maintenance regime

rows: it is a motor and processing skill
motor memory is the most durable

elements.text: **The counter-intuitive result:** reading survives longest and speaking decays fastest, which is exactly backwards from how people maintain their languages. Almost everyone keeps reading and stops speaking, then wonders why they can no longer talk.
The maintenance regime is four floors. Miss one for a month and the building is fine. Miss one for a year and it is not.

rows: 30 minutes a day of Korean you did not choose for study
60 minutes a week of live speech with a native
10 minutes a day of SRS, or 20 minutes of writing
one new domain per year — a new field, a new register, a new genre

elements.label: The genius of the floors
elements.value: they are small enough to survive a bad week, which is the only reason any long-term regime works.

rows: the growth floor — take on a new domain
the output floor — a project that requires speech
a deliberate weakness — the thing you have avoided for years
consolidation — reread, re-record, compare with previous years

elements.text: Once a year, do the same four things and keep the recordings:

items.text: A 10-minute unscripted monologue on the same prompt.
A page of handwriting.
A cold reading of a newspaper editorial, timed.
A 5-minute conversation with a stranger.

elements.text: **Compare year on year.** Not with a target — with yourself. This is the only longitudinal measure that means anything, and almost nobody does it.

items.text: Write your four floors with actual times and actual people.
Record the four annual measures now, and date them.
Identify the skill you are most likely to let decay, and write the specific defence.

elements.text: When you come back after six months or three years, do not start where you left off. Start here:

rows: **Listening only.** 30 min/day, content you have already heard.
rebuilds the perception threshold fast, and it is the least threatening
**Speaking with a tolerant partner.** Someone who knew you before.
they remember your level and will not treat you as a beginner
**Reading, easy and pleasurable.** Not study material.
restores the habit, not the skill
**The diagnostic.** The four annual measures, compared with your last recordings.

elements.label: What not to do
elements.value: restart a grammar textbook. Your declarative knowledge survived. What decayed is retrieval speed, and only use restores it.

rows: maintaining, deepening one domain, becoming the person others ask

elements.text: **The shift at year six is the important one.** After that point, the language is not a project. It is a fact about you, maintained by the floors, deepened by the annual cycle, and occasionally tested by a year in which you did not use it at all.
Not fluency fireworks. Three quieter things:

rows: you read a novel and forget you are reading Korean
you catch a writer's bad sentence, and can say why
someone asks a question and you answer it in ninety seconds

projects.title: Level 0 Capstone: `sound-lab`

elements.text: **Objective.** Produce a recorded, reviewable corpus that proves the level's outcome — not a claim that you "know the alphabet".

items.text: **The alphabet corpus.** You record all 40 letters, isolated, in a single take, with no reading from a list you can see mid-recording.
**The minimal-pair corpus.** Ten triplets (가/카/까 and nine others) recorded twice, with a 2-second gap.
**The sound-rule corpus.** Twenty sentences, each containing at least one sound-change rule, recorded at natural speed.
**The reading corpus.** Three unseen passages of 100+ syllables, read aloud, timed, with the time and syllable count written down.
**The dictation log.** Ten sessions of 20 words, with accuracy per session and a running list of your recurring phoneme errors.
**The self-assessment.** One paragraph, written, naming your three weakest sounds and the drill you used for each.

Q: What is the fundamental difference between the topic particle 은/는 and the subject particle 이/가?
A: 은/는 sets the topic or contrastive focus of the sentence, whereas 이/가 identifies the specific grammatical subject.
Q: When do you use Native Korean numbers vs Sino-Korean numbers?
A: Native numbers are used for counting items/people and clock hours (시). Sino-Korean numbers are used for money (원), minutes (분), dates (년/월/일), and phone numbers.
Q: You enter a cafe in Seoul and want two iced Americanos and one slice of cheesecake to go. What do you say?
A: "아이스 아메리카노 두 잔하고 치즈케이크 하나 포장해 주세요."
